fix(api): keep webhook signing secrets readable to the subscriber

A signing secret is a shared secret: the subscriber verifies our signature with
the same value. When Agenta generates it, the create response is the only place
they can ever read it, so the vault-wide write-only default would ship a
subscription nobody can verify. Both webhook create paths now opt out of the
default explicitly.

refactor(api): stop caching the vault secrets list

The list is small and only the settings page reads it, and the runtime path already went straight to the database. Caching it bought little while costing a whole class of question — what a shared Redis entry holds, and whether a stale reader can repopulate it with plaintext after a tighten — which the generation counter and the full-project-id cache keys existed only to answer. The route now reads the database on every request and redacts at the response boundary, so what a caller sees is what the row says. The per-project sweep each secret write already fired is untouched: it predates write-only secrets and serves the other namespaces.

fix(sdk): use this run's own provider key when the vault redacts a write-only secret

The error told the user to provide the provider key in the environment, but nothing read it: an agenta-mode connection resolved from the vault alone, so a standalone run against a write-only secret failed even with OPENAI_API_KEY exported. Resolution now reads the variable the harness itself would use for that connection — the provider family's key, or Bedrock's and Azure's own channels, so one service's credential is never sent to another — and raises only when that variable is empty too. The error text says what the resolver already tried.

fix(api): stop the permissions exchange from minting the secret-resolve grant

The exchange attached the grant whenever a caller asked with action=run_service, and any member who may run a service can ask: they could call it with their own session or ApiKey, take the returned credential to the vault routes, and read every write-only value in plaintext. That is the whole guarantee, self-serve. The exchange now only carries forward a grant the caller already holds on a verified Secret token, and never creates one. Creation stays where a run actually starts, in-process at the invoke and inspect hops, so the credential still travels with the run: the workflow service and the runner both re-exchange the granted token they were handed, and refresh keeps working with no new credential to distribute and no deployment change.

fix(api): carry a secret's kept credential over from the locked row

Keep-on-omit filled an omitted credential from a snapshot the service read before the DAO took its row lock, so a rotation that committed in between was silently undone: the update wrote the older value back over the newer one, and nothing reported it. The DAO now resolves the carry-over inside the locked transaction, against the row as it actually stands — the shape GitDAO.commit_revision already uses for the same reason. The identity check travels with it, because deciding same-identity against a stale row is how a credential crosses identities. The fake DAOs call the resolver at the same point, so keep-on-omit stays exercised rather than skipped, and a new test rotates the stored row inside that window and pins that the value carried over is the rotated one.

fix(sdk): accept every credential channel a redacted connection could use

The environment fallback for a write-only connection read one variable per candidate, so a Bedrock connection could only be credentialed by AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK and a Vertex one not at all — even though the vault path accepts an AWS key pair or service-account material for exactly those connections. The fallback now offers the same channels the stored credential could have used, and a channel counts only when every variable in it is set: half an AWS key pair authenticates nothing, and passing it on would fail at the provider with a misleading error instead of here with an actionable one.

fix(api): require a client secret when an SSO secret is created

The SSO branch checked that client_secret was PRESENT, not that it held a value, so a create carrying an explicit null stored an SSO record with no credential — while the webhook and custom-secret branches beside it already checked the value. It now checks the value on the create path only: omission still means "keep the stored one" on update, which is what redacted responses and the edit form depend on.

chore: allow four unit-test credential fixtures that survive in history

The fixtures were rewritten to obviously-fake, digit-free strings so the scanner has nothing to find going forward. Four occurrences remain inside commits whose amend could not be replayed, and the scan reads history, not the tree. Each is a unit-test constant handed to a fake DAO; no real credential was ever involved. Fingerprints are anchored to their commit, so they need regenerating if either lane's history is rewritten again.

fix(api): keep the SSO client secret plaintext where it authenticates

Redaction was applied inside the one helper every caller used, so the connection test and the edit path read a write-only provider's client secret as empty. A redacted read there does not hide a value from anyone — it tests the provider without its secret, then writes is_valid false and is_active false, taking a working provider out of the login screen. There are now two resolvers, the split the webhooks service already uses for signing secrets: the plain one stays plaintext for the internal callers, and an outward one shapes responses and drops the secret once the record is write-only. Both are documented by what the caller does with the value, not by where it is called from.

fix(api): treat a custom secret's format as part of its identity

Keep-on-omit compared kind and provider family but not the stored format, so a text-to-json update that omitted its content carried the stored string into the json shape. The validators could not catch it: they run when the payload is built, before the carry-over fills the value in, so what they saw was a value-less shape and what reached the row was a json secret holding a string. A format change is now an identity change and requires an explicit value, and the merged payload is re-validated under the lock before it is persisted, so nothing is stored that a create of the same shape would have refused. Also moves the per-kind primary credential field out of the SDK classifier and onto the API side: it covers kinds the SDK never resolves (SSO providers, webhook signing secrets) and no SDK code reads it. The extras vocabulary stays shared, which is where drift would actually hurt.

fix(api,sdk): issue the run credential's grant to the platform runtime, not to whoever asks

Closing the self-serve grant broke every agent run, and the reason is the shape of the product's path: the playground and the gate post straight to the workflow service with the user's own ApiKey, so the service exchanges THAT credential and the API's in-process mint never runs. Carry-forward alone therefore had nothing to carry, and runs got the redacted shape. The exchange now mints the grant when the caller proves it is the platform runtime and otherwise carries forward what the caller already holds. The proof is a secret only the backend has, sent on the internal hop and compared in constant time, because that route is publicly reachable and the user's token cannot say who is asking. It resolves from AGENTA_SERVICES_INTERNAL_KEY, falling back to AGENTA_AUTH_KEY, which the services container already receives through the same env file as the API — so deployments keep working unchanged, and a dedicated value narrows what one leaked secret can do. The runner keeps carry-forward and is given nothing new; the key never reaches it or a sandbox, and is never logged.

fix(api,sdk): refuse the placeholder as proof of being the platform runtime

The runtime key falls back to AGENTA_AUTH_KEY, whose unconfigured value is the string 'replace-me' committed in every example env file — so a deployment that changed neither would have handed a run credential to anyone who sent it. Both sides now treat the placeholder as no key at all: such a deployment issues no grant, which costs it only the ability to run against write-only secrets (off by default) and never gives that ability to a stranger. The variable is documented in the example env files, and the design note now says who may hold the grant and why the exchange cannot decide it from the requested action.

test(services): pin what the agent app sends when it exchanges a caller's key

The bug that broke every run was invisible to unit tests because they exercised the hop that already had a granted token, while the product uses the hop that never did. This drives the real agent app with the exchange stubbed and asserts the request carries both the caller's own credential and the platform's runtime key — and that a service configured without one sends no header at all rather than an empty value.

fix(sdk): say when the platform runtime key is missing, instead of blaming the provider key

The placeholder this refuses is the shipped default in every example env file, so a deployment that never set AGENTA_AUTH_KEY silently loses runs against write-only connections — and what it sees is the SDK telling it to provide OPENAI_API_KEY, which is true for a standalone run and useless here. The service now says it once, at the point of use, and names the variable to set. Live QA hit exactly this and read it as a regression, which is the cost of a failure that points somewhere else.

chore: exempt two dead fixture strings by value, not by fingerprint

The fixtures were rewritten to digit-free names, but these two spellings survive in commits whose amend could not be replayed, and both scans read history rather than the tree. A fingerprint names the commit its finding was seen in, so it goes stale every time a lane below is rebased — which happened twice while landing this stack. Exempting the values is stable, and it follows what this file already says: exempt the VALUE, never the path, so a real key added to a fixture would still be seen.

feat(api): warn at startup when write-only secrets have no runtime key

A deployment that turned write-only on, or enabled a component that seeds write-only rows, cannot read those secrets at all without a platform runtime key — and the failure it gets says to provide a provider key, which is right for a standalone run and useless here. The API now says it once at boot, naming the variable and the consequence, next to the other startup validations. The placeholder counts as unset, since it is what the example env files ship.

fix(api): do not assume the EE bridge config exists at startup

The warning read env.starter_credits_bridge directly, but that config is an EE addition that this branch does not carry — so on a build without it the API would have raised AttributeError during startup validation, before serving anything. It now asks for the attribute rather than assuming it, and the case that needs the bridge is tested where the bridge exists. My own CI caught it because the test referenced the same missing attribute; the production path had the same bug.

The thumb travel was written as translate-x-[calc(theme(width.switch)...)],

bridge mobile/src/styles/globals.css already uses for w-switch. v3 geometry is
byte-identical (22/12px travel, 23.4/15.6px press-stretch), so the antd parity
baseline is unaffected.

fix(frontend): validate the skill name before an agent config is saved

A skill whose name is not a lowercase-hyphen slug (e.g. "Weather", "My Skill")
saved fine — the config is just JSON to the backend — and then failed the whole
agent run the first time it was invoked: AgentTemplate.from_params parses
parameters.agent.skills through parse_skill_templates, whose pydantic model pins
name to ^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$, and raises SkillValidationError. The runner
re-checks the same pattern on the untrusted wire and silently skips a skill that
fails it. The slug rule is not ours to relax: the harnesses key a skill by its
directory name and invoke it as /skill:name.

Mirror those rules client-side in skillName.ts and wire them into the skill
drawer, so the mistake surfaces inline at authoring time instead of as an opaque
run failure. Save is now blocked on the same fields the SDK requires (name,
description, SKILL.md body), each with a terse message under its field, and a bad
name offers its slugified form as a one-click fix.

feat(frontend): auto-commit agent playground config changes

Config edits in the agent playground landed in a browser-local draft and stayed
there until someone clicked Commit and filled in a modal. An agent could run with
a changed model, granted permissions and rewritten instructions while none of it
had reached triggers, schedules, or a second browser.

A per-revision engine now watches the entity draft and commits it ~1.5s after the
last edit, with the message classifyAgentChanges/buildCommitSummaryMessage already
generate. One subscription covers every write path, because the drawers buffer in
their own scoped draft and only touch the entity draft on Save.

The Commit button and its modal leave the agent header. Save stays only where
auto-commit deliberately will not act: a non-latest revision (so an accidental
edit cannot rewrite history), a failed save, or a draft stranded by a run.

Auto-commit is held while a run owns the revision — the agent's own
commit_revision checks HEAD, so a concurrent unattended commit would fail it.

fix(frontend): bind an open section draft to the revision it was opened on

saveSection re-read revisionIdRef.current, so if the active revision changed
while the Advanced drawer was open, the old draft was written to the NEW
revision build-kit atoms. openSectionDrawer already snapshots the revision;
store it on sectionBaseline and write back to that one.

fix(frontend): reject non-string skill fields instead of coercing them

Second review pass on #6142.

The JSON view of the skill drawer accepts any type, and the Form view only
cast: skill.name as string | undefined. So a draft with a numeric name made
name.trim() and [...description] throw TypeError, crashing the Form tab.

The validator had the matching hole. It coerced with String(rawName), and
String(123) is "123", which is a legal slug, so a numeric name passed the save
gate. SkillTemplate.name is a pydantic str and v2 does not coerce numbers:
verified that 123, 1.2 and True all raise string_type, while the string "123"
is accepted.

Both sides now reject non-strings rather than coercing, with null and undefined
still treated as the required case. description and body go through one shared
textFieldError so they follow the same rule as name.

fix(frontend): read the open drawer overlay from the captured revision too

The previous fix bound only the WRITE side. The drawer body still received the
live revisionId, so useBuildKit read revision B overlay (and built its
platform-tool rows from B ops) while the draft buffer held revision A
disabledOps. Disable all then Save wrote B op names into A state.

Hold the snapshot revision in state rather than on the baseline ref, since the
drawer body reads it during render, and pass it to both scoped drawer bodies.
The two background bodies keep the live revisionId; they render the live config,
not the draft.

Raised by CodeRabbit on #6145.

fix(frontend): stop a stale head silently disabling agent auto-commit

The latest-revision query has a 30s staleTime and a disk persister, so its
cached head is routinely OLDER than the revision on screen. isLatestRevision
treated any id mismatch as "you are on an older revision", so auto-commit
applied its stays-manual rule to a perfectly current revision and every config
change stopped saving. Adding a tool was just the first place this showed.

It now treats only a strictly NEWER known head as behind, so a stale cache
degrades to "assume latest" (saving works) rather than "assume historical"
(saving stops). The head's version comes from a passive peek at the
revisions-list cache, the same fallback the latest-revision atom already uses:
the entity atom is null for a revision the user is not viewing, and mounting the
list query would fire a full-list fetch.

Also from the performance pass:

- The draft subscription no longer calls runFlush purely to have it recompute a
  blocker it already has. Measured 2 gate evaluations per write instead of 4,
  and one less promise per skip.
- Superseded revisions release their per-revision atoms. atomFamily keeps a
  STRONG map, so with a revision minted per gesture each commit leaked a set of
  atoms for the rest of the session.

Save is now visible on every agent revision rather than only where auto-commit
steps aside, disabled when there is nothing to save and while a run holds the
revision.

fix(frontend): drive agent auto-commit from the draft write, not a mounted view

Product review on #6158 found three symptoms with one cause: auto-commit was
armed by a component subscription, so an edit made while that component was off
screen was never saved, and a save parked behind a live run could strand its
status with no way to resume.

- Trigger moves to the write. `registerWorkflowDraftCallbacks` in @agenta/entities
  fires on every real draft edit, so slash commands, approval cards and edits made
  with the config pane hidden all save. Nothing mounts the engine any more.
- Drop the run hold. It produced a "Save pending" that could outlive its own
  wake-up, and the conflict it avoided is one the server tells the agent how to
  recover from.
- Drop the Save button. Status is idle/saving/error; a failed save turns the
  status dot itself into the retry.
- Editing any revision saves, so an older revision is not left unsaveable.
- Snapshot restores pass `hydrating`, so reopening a tab cannot commit on its own.

fix(frontend): stop auto-save destroying concurrent edits, and stop the header overclaiming

Two failure modes found while auditing the auto-commit paths.

An edit typed WHILE a commit was in flight was destroyed: the payload is
snapshotted before the request and the draft discarded after it, so anything
added in between was in neither the new revision nor the draft. The draft was
its only copy. A manual Commit made that window rare; auto-save fires on idle,
so the user is routinely still editing when it lands. The commit now carries
that edit onto the new revision, and keeps the old draft when it cannot — a
stranded draft is recoverable, a discarded one is not.

The header derived "Saving…" from isDirty, which is untrue for every revision
auto-commit deliberately skips: a restored snapshot, an ephemeral agent, an
unresolved project id are all dirty with nothing scheduled, and the header sat
on "Saving…" forever — the stuck-looking state again, by another route. The
engine now publishes whether a flush is actually armed, and those cases read
Draft.
docs(api): update API reference from production OpenAPI spec

fix(frontend): cancel a settled revision's armed flush, and trim comments

CodeRabbit review on #6158.

Evicting a superseded revision dropped its atoms but left any flush still
armed for it. An edit landing during the request arms exactly that timer, so
it fired after eviction and re-created the atoms eviction had just removed.
It now cancels the timer — except when the revision still holds a draft,
which is the case where the commit could not carry a concurrent edit forward
and that armed flush is the edit's only way to land. (The review suggested
cancelling unconditionally, which would strand that edit.)

Also trims the narrative comments the reviewer flagged, per the repo's
one-short-line rule.
fix(sdk): tolerate null provider model lists

fix(frontend): stop a mid-run config save cancelling the agent run

Editing the configuration while the agent was running killed the run.

/m keyed the conversation by session AND pinned revision. Auto-commit lands a
new revision mid-stream and the surface pins it, so the key changed, React
remounted the conversation, and the chat engine's unmount teardown called
stop() — aborting the live turn.

The engine is built to take a revision switch as a prop: useChat is pinned to
the session and the request builder reads the revision through a ref. So the
revision comes out of the key, which also fixes the same crash from picking a
revision in the top bar mid-run. web/oss already keys its agent host this way,
for this exact reason (MainLayout's comment describes the same bug).

Removing the run hold exposed this; the bug itself predates it.

The key rule moves into conversationKey with a test, because the inline
comment did not stop it. A second test pins the engine contract: a revision
change mid-stream must not abort the turn.

fix(frontend): show a just-committed revision in the picker

The revision picker lists a VARIANT's revisions, but the commit only busted

feat(frontend): stack the connect-tool dock and share it with /m

A turn can park several `request_connection` calls at once, but the dock only
ever showed one and lived in oss alone — mobile had an inline row saying
"waiting for your response below" with nothing below it.

The dock is now a shingle stack: the front card owns the actions, the rest peek
behind it as bottom-aligned edges that lift on hover to reveal their logo and
name, and clicking one pulls it forward. A "N of M" counter tracks progress
through the batch. Cards are identified by the integration's real brand mark
instead of a generic plug icon.

The card and its stack move to @agenta/chat (ConnectDock + useConnectDock,
mirroring ApprovalCard + useApprovalDock), so oss and /m render one design and
only supply their own chrome and settle transport.

Touch gets depth without the fan: a peek's sliver is 10px, far below a usable
tap target, so on mobile the stack is a visual cue and connections answer in
the agent's order.

feat(frontend): plain-language approval card for the agent chat

Redesign the human-in-the-loop approval card as one shell for every tool
gate and every user, replacing the payload/diff/digest surface and the
Chat-vs-Build split. A gate now resolves to plain language through a pure
describer (skin registry data, not a React body): one outcome sentence and a
'See what changes' list of readable rows, no JSON, no diff, no digest.

- Shared ApprovalCard rewritten; desktop and mobile docs render the identical
  card. Deleted CommitRevisionApproval, RevisionOperations, the manifest UI,
  PayloadBlock, ApprovalCardFrame, and the friendly/compact mode props.
- describeCommitRevision turns each ordered operation (and the legacy
  {set, remove} delta, and imported workspace content) into a prose row;
  gateway tools get a description from their action + integration.
- Batch: 'Approve all' replaces Approve as the single primary when a turn
  parks several gates; the detail rows list the pending actions (the dropped
  peek). Deny mirrors it as 'Deny all' where the host has batch deny.
- Keyboard: Cmd/Ctrl+Enter approves, Escape denies, guarded to a parked,
  unanswered gate and suppressed while the Redirect note is open.
- approvalInputSummary moved into @agenta/chat/model so the package owns the
  readable-field logic mobile used.

feat(frontend): let the connect dock be answered and navigated by keyboard

The dock could only be answered by pointer, and with several connections
parked the only way to reach a specific one was to hover a 10px sliver.

Adds ApprovalCard's own bindings so one gesture answers whichever dock is
asking — Cmd/Ctrl+Enter connects, Escape backs out (cancelling the popup
mid-flow instead of declining). Approvals win when both docks are open on one
turn: they bind the same keys, so the host silences the connect dock rather
than letting a single key fire two decisions.

Replaces the "N of M" counter with a dot per connection and a pill that
slides to whichever is on screen; clicking a dot brings that card forward.
The dots walk a new `batch` — every connect call on the turn, settled
included, in the agent's order — so a dot always stands for the same
connection instead of shuffling as the pending set reorders.

Two things this needed underneath:
- The card is split. `key={toolCallId}` remounted the whole card on every
  switch, so the pill was a fresh node created at its destination with
  nothing to animate from. Only `ConnectBody` is keyed now; the key still
  resets the flow per parked call, just around a smaller subtree.

feat(frontend,api): group and filter sessions in the nav rail (#6125)

The rail listed sessions as a flat recency stack with no way to narrow it.
It now groups them under collapsible headings (agent / date / status /
pinned-first, pins always leading), filters via a popover on the group row,
and offers per-row verbs from a kebab and a right-click menu.

Every filter is a server predicate — narrowing a fetched page would filter
the window rather than the set. Two exceptions are documented in place: the
"Awaiting input" status has no predicate (its ids are pushed down instead),
and "Idle" subtracts gated sessions client-side, since a session whose turn
ended with a gate still open is waiting, not idle.

Scoped to web/mobile: every new capability is opt-in per entity, so Prompts,
Agents and the desktop rail render unchanged.

API: adds `archived_only` to the session query. Archived was only ever a
widening of the active list, so an archived VIEW was not expressible.

API: a header edit no longer bumps `updated_at`. It is the last-activity sort
key, so renaming a session teleported it to the top of every session list.

feat(frontend): scope the rail's scroll to the sessions group

The whole rail scrolled, so a long session list pushed Observability off the
screen and scrolling to reach it took Home and Agents with it.

The sessions group now scrolls inside itself and the rail does not scroll at
all: the group shrinks to whatever space is left, and every entry after it
stays put. Rows hold their height on their own — a flex item's automatic
minimum is its content — so only the box that opts out with `min-h-0` shrinks.

Opt-in via `scrollChildren`, and the shell derives its own switch from it
rather than carrying a second flag. A rail that sets neither, the desktop's
included, keeps today's markup exactly.

Also drops the divider above the bottom section and the Invite Teammate entry
from both mobile scopes. Inviting is workspace administration; this app has no
surface for it.

feat(frontend): multi-agent filter, live dots, and rail polish

Agent is now a multi-select. It cannot be one request: the DAO matches
`references` with JSONB containment, so two ids ask for sessions belonging to
BOTH agents. Selecting several fans out one request per agent inside the
queryFn and merges them by id, re-sorted by last activity — one atom, one cache
key. `agentId` becomes `agentIds`, and the dirty check now compares arrays by
length (identity reported dirty forever once a field was an array).

A row's dot never cleared until a manual reload: the rail neither polled nor
listened. It now polls only while a row is alive or running, and the live
event stream invalidates the rail's own queries, so the session you are
watching updates the moment its run ends.

Menu rows had no hover in dark: `--muted` and `--popover` are both #242424,
so the highlight painted the menu's own background. Moved to `accent`, which
differs from the surface in both themes — dropdown items, sub-triggers, and
the right-click menu.

Rail: the drawer's toggle is a close X (an overlay cannot un-collapse itself),
its resizer is hidden (the sheet is a fixed width), and it carries no tooltip
(the sheet autofocuses it, and a Radix tooltip opens on focus). All three key
off `onDismiss`, which only an overlay mount passes — no breakpoint guessing.
The filter menu aligns to the trigger's end.

Also sets `archived` on the playground's local session refs, which the new
required field had broken.

feat(frontend): link agent headings to their agent overview

An agent heading names something openable, so it now opens it — the label is a
link to that agent's overview and the caret keeps the collapse. That gives the
rail agent navigation without a second expandable tree under Agents.

Only agent buckets get a link: a date or status heading has nowhere to go, and
`agent:none` is a placeholder rather than an agent. A heading without one keeps
today's behaviour, where the whole row toggles.

The caret is now the only toggle target, so it takes its own hover state and an
aria-label naming the group it folds.

fix(frontend): name each day by its date, and keep grouping out of the dot

"Previous 7 days" told you a session was somewhere in a week — the one thing a
date heading is supposed to settle. Every day past yesterday now gets its own
heading named by its date, with the year added once it is not the current one.
The buckets are calendar days rather than a rolling 24 hours, so an 11pm
session from last night stops reading as Today at 10am.

The filter dot answers "are rows being hidden?", so `groupBy` no longer sets
it: grouping rearranges the rows you already have. The empty state shares that
atom, so a regrouped empty list also stops claiming nothing matches the filters.

Also publishes `alwaysOpen` groups to the open-groups gate. The v0.113.0 merge
brought a mechanism that publishes `defaultOpen` groups so their entity queries
subscribe; an `alwaysOpen` group is expanded on screen with no way to toggle,
so without this the rail rendered Sessions open and said "Open to load" forever.

perf(frontend): stop rebuilding the rail, and show fewer sessions by default

Two rebuild bugs. `withEntityGroups` spreads into a new object, so an
unmemoized call changed identity every render — busting the items memo,
re-bucketing every row, and handing NavMenu an array that defeated its own
memo. And every row called `useSessionActions` itself, so a 41-row rail held 41
copies of verbs that do not differ by row; only the open/renaming/draft state
is per-row, and that stays. Idle React commits: 90/min to 12/min.

Fewer rows, too, since the cost is per row: groups now start folded (the stored
set is what you OPENED, under its own key so saved choices cannot invert), and
the activity window defaults to a week rather than everything — which narrows
the fetch, not just the render. Pinned stays open, because a pin is the user
asking to see it, and opening a session seeds its group open once rather than
forcing it, which had made the caret a no-op. 41 rows to 2, 769 DOM nodes to
169.

The dot means "rows are being hidden", so "all" never lights it on any facet:
with a week as the default, widening back to everything is off-default but
shows MORE rows.

Also pins the collapse wrapper's height. It is `overflow-hidden`, which drops a
flex item's automatic min-height, so beside the scrolling sessions group the
Agents list shrank and clipped its own rows.

test(frontend): move the sidebar tests into @agenta/navigation

They tested pure functions that live in the package — grouping, the date
buckets, the recency sort — through web/oss's thin re-export, which is the
wrong home for them and put 190 lines of test into an app the feature does not
touch. The package gains the vitest setup @agenta/entities already uses;
web/oss returns to its original three.

Also drops the navigation from an agent heading and its plumbing (the group's
`path`, the `link` it resolved to, and `groupedChildren`'s now-unused
projectURL). The caret loses its hover fill too — the row already answers with
a colour change, and a pill behind the caret made a heading look like a button.

Pinned is collapsible again. It was pinned into the expanded set on every read,
so the caret could never remove it; its head start is now the stored record's
default, which the first toggle overwrites. The seed that opens an active
session's group moved to module scope for the same reason: the rail and the
drawer each ran the hook, so one instance kept re-opening what the user had
just closed through the other.

And pinning a session no longer blanks the rail: a new pinned-query key reports
its first flight as pending, which emptied the list for a frame before it came
back reordered. Pending now means pending with nothing to show.

fix(frontend): keep the rail's open headings across a regrouping

The stored set listed OPEN groups, keyed `agent:…`. Switching to dates produced
`date:today`, which matched nothing, so every regrouping read as a fully
collapsed rail. It now records the headings you toggled AWAY from their
default, which is grouping-agnostic: the default it flips is whatever the new
grouping asks for. New storage key, since the old contents mean the opposite.

Only agent grouping starts folded. It is the one with a heading per entity;
date and status have a handful of buckets whose labels say nothing closed.

Nothing opens itself any more. Pinned lost its head start and the seed that
opened an active session's group is gone, so the only writer to that set is a
caret click. Both exceptions had already turned into carets that fought the
user once, and neither earned another try.

feat(frontend): bring the grouped sessions rail to the desktop sidebar

The desktop rail listed sessions flat while the mobile one grouped and filtered
them. It now uses the same model: the scope joins the grouped set, the entity
declares its headings and its wider window, and the nav entry carries the
filter menu and the scoped scroll. Everything was already opt-in per entity, so
this is configuration rather than new machinery.

Sessions never loaded there, though. The gate that keeps entity queries
unsubscribed reads persisted open groups `??` defaults, so a scope with any
persisted record stopped consulting the defaults, and an `alwaysOpen` group
never counted as open. Mobile had no persisted record, which is why it worked
there and not here. Always-open keys now publish to their own atom the gate ORs
in, since a group that cannot be collapsed is never in the persisted set. That
also stops the canceled requests: the source was flipping between subscribed
and idle, and each flip aborts the fetch in flight.

Two more fixes the desktop surfaced. Rows carried over between projects,
because `keepPreviousData` held the previous rows through any key change and
the key carries the project id; it is now held only within a project. And the
rail's waiting dot never turned amber, because the shared registry's icon
predated the flag.

The row menu is shared rather than copied: `SessionRowActions` and its chrome
hook move into `@agenta/sessions-ui`, typed structurally so the package stays
off `@agenta/navigation`, with the ACTIONS passed in. That seam is what lets
the desktop bind its own, which wraps them with the playground's local tab
cache, so renaming from the rail updates an open chat tab.

Groups also start open again, everywhere.

fix(frontend): keep the session filter menu on screen in a narrow rail

The menu is end-aligned to its trigger, so once the resizable rail is
narrower than the menu it ran off the left edge and its rows were clipped.
It now measures the trigger on open and flips to start-aligned, overhanging
the content area instead.

Measured on pointer down, since Radix opens there and by click the content
is already positioned. Collision avoidance stays off on purpose: shifting by
the overflow amount lands the menu somewhere different depending on scroll
position, whereas two fixed anchors are the same every time. The width the
measurement compares against is now exported from FilterMenu so it cannot
drift from the menu's own min-width.

fix(frontend): address the CodeRabbit findings on the sessions rail

Four real ones:

- The filter menu passed `dirty` but no `onReset`, so FilterMenu never
  rendered its reset row and every facet had to be cleared by hand.
- The narrow-rail alignment flip only ran on pointer down, so a keyboard
  user opening the menu with Enter/Space/ArrowDown still got a clipped menu.
- `toSidebarRef` hardcoded `running: false`, which made the "Running"
  status heading unreachable for server rows and bucketed a running session
  under "Live". The row already carries `flags.is_running`.
- Inline rename in the rail wrote straight to the server, skipping the local
  tab cache, so renaming a session that was open in the playground left its
  tab on the old title — the exact thing the desktop binding exists to
  prevent. The cache-or-server branch is now a shared `commitRename` verb
  that both the menu's modal and the rail's inline edit go through.

Also completed two test fixtures that claimed to be SessionSidebarRef while
omitting required fields. Both files sit outside their tsconfig's include, so
this was latent rather than breaking.

fix(frontend): select the open session in the desktop rail

A session row links to its AGENT's playground — which session opens is handed
over by the row's click, not by the route — so route matching saw two equally
good matches for the same URL and kept the first. Agents is registered before
Sessions, so the agent row won every tie and a session row could never appear
selected.

Pin the open session through the scope's existing selectedKeyOverride seam
instead. The stale-active-id fallback the panel already applies now lives in
one atom that both the override and the local refs read, and the shell drops
an override naming a row that is not rendered, so a session filtered out by
the activity window falls back to the route match rather than blanking the
selection.

fix(frontend): open the group around a pinned sidebar selection

The ancestor keys that auto-open a selection's groups came from the ROUTE
match, but a pinned key is by definition not the row the route matched: the
rail pins the open session, whose row lives under a group the route never
names. With groups folded, the selected session sat inside a closed group.

Walk to the pinned row instead whenever an override applies, which also covers
controlled mode — it was already doing this, just spelled as a separate case.

fix(frontend): show a session's new name the moment you rename it

The rename write is not visible to the sessions list read straight away.
Reproduced against the running app: the PUT returns 200, the invalidation
fires, and the refetch comes back still carrying the OLD name — the row only
corrected on the next 15s poll or a reload.

So patch the cached rows with the new name and mark those queries stale
WITHOUT refetching. Invalidating normally would fire exactly the stale read
that overwrites what you just typed; `refetchType: "none"` keeps the name on
screen and lets the next poll, focus or mount take the server's copy once it
agrees.

`withRenamedSession` covers the three shapes a session list is cached in (the
rail's flat array, one page, an infinite query's pages), returns other shapes
untouched, and hands back the same object when the session is absent so lists
that never held it do not re-render.

fix(frontend): flip the filter menu before it crops, not after

The narrow-rail flip budgeted the menu's min-width, but the menu does not
render at its minimum: a facet row carrying a long value pushes it wider.
Measured open in the app it is ~245px, so at a 243px rail the menu's left edge
sat at -1.5px — cropped, while the check still said there was room.

Give the flip its own constant at 250px. The layout floor and the room an
anchor needs are different numbers, and collapsing them into one was the bug.

fix(frontend): drop an archived agent's sessions from the rail

`dropArchivedAgentSessions` was written, exported and covered by 11 passing
tests — and never called. Archiving an agent left its conversations sitting in
the rail, and the green tests made the rule look enforced.

Wire it into the atom that composes the rows, with a new `archivedAgentIdsAtom`
reading `deleted_at` off the workflow catalog (the same field every other 'is
this agent gone' read uses). It answers `null` while the catalog loads rather
than an empty set, which would claim nothing is archived and let the rows paint
before being pulled back out.

Applied before the grouped-scope early return, so it holds for every scope: an
archived agent's sessions are stale wherever the rail renders, not only where
headings group by agent. Pins stay exempt, as they are from every other list
rule.

fix(frontend): partition the agent-chat store by project

The four localStorage records behind the chat slice were keyed by AGENT ID
alone — no project, workspace or user. They survived a sign-out, so sessions
and their message bodies from one account were readable by whoever signed in
next on that browser. Confirmed on a real profile: 6 agent scopes, 26 sessions
and 607 KB of transcripts spanning several workspaces. Logout only clears the
React Query cache and the persisted IDB cache; nothing touched localStorage.

Project alone is enough to isolate an account — switching workspace mints a new
project id — so one helper adds that dimension underneath. Consumers still see
`Record<scopeKey, T>` and none of the 73 call sites change; only the persisted
shape becomes `Record<projectId, Record<scopeKey, T>>`. New `:v2` keys, and the
legacy ones are deleted at load rather than migrated: attributing them to
whichever project is active would carry the leak forward one more time, and the
reconciler already re-adopts anything the server knows.

With no project resolved the read is empty and the write is DROPPED. Persisting
under a blank key would build a bucket every project can see, which is the leak
itself. Five tests exercised the store without a project and now hydrate one,
matching what the app always does.

feat(frontend): simplify the agent turn footer

Replace the bordered metrics pill under every agent turn with one quiet line of
dot-separated text, and move the trace button behind the Playground inspector
preference so only people debugging a run see it.

The footer was assembled by hand twice — once in web/oss, once in web/mobile —
and the copies had drifted on icons, clipboard handling, and which buttons
appear. Both apps now render one shared TurnFooter from @agenta/chat, so the
desktop and /m cannot drift again.

- ExecutionMetricsDisplay gains a `plain` variant; `badge` stays the default, so
  the playground and evaluation views are untouched.
- Each segment owns the separator before it and draws it only when it renders,
  so a turn whose trace resolved no metrics leaves no dangling separator.
- Tooltips are kept only where they add something the row cannot show: the
  prompt/completion token split, rewind, and trace.
- The icon button gets `p-0`. The UA sheet gives a button 6px of side padding,
  which left an 8px content box and squashed the glyph inside it.
- Both sides of the row key off the message rather than the avatar, so the
  assistant row starts where the response text does and the user row ends where
  the bubble does.

fix(runner): keep the run credential when the public api base is unconfigured

A self-hosted deployment on a public hostname failed every agent run with
"record log is unreadable; cannot rebuild the conversation", because the
runner was sending its API callbacks with no Authorization header at all.

platformCredentialForRequest forwards the run's credential to platform calls
only when it recognizes the run's OTLP trace endpoint as this deployment's own
API. That match is a string comparison against AGENTA_API_INTERNAL_URL,
AGENTA_API_URL and the cloud base. A dispatched run carries the endpoint the
API built from its PUBLIC base, so a runner configured with only its internal
hop matches nothing, drops the credential, and every call to /sessions/* is
rejected with 401. Records are never written and never read back, and the
history rebuild reports it far from the cause.

The attribution is only decidable once the runner knows the public base, so
arm the strict check only when it is configured. Without it the runner keeps
the credential (the behavior before the check existed) and says what to set;
with it, the third-party collector protection stays exactly as it was.

at startup when AGENTA_API_URL is unset, and document the variable as an
identity input rather than only a routing fallback.

A client can answer a gate without the answer reaching the turn in band: it
answered out of band, or its resume died on the way. The row on the interactions
plane was then the only record of the human's yes/no, and nothing read it, so the
gate was raised again and the approval was lost.

gate already consumes. Reading is CLAIMING: each row is transitioned to resolved
before its decision is used, and a row that will not settle is dropped. A lost
claim costs one re-approval; an unclaimed row left responded would let the next
turn seed the same answer again and run the tool twice.

The read happens in the callers, not in runTurn. runTurn must reach
attachPermissionResponder within one macrotask tick of being invoked: until that
call wires it, env.currentTurn.onPermissionRequest is undefined, so a gate
arriving there takes the between-turns branch in session-events.ts and is
answered reject by policy. A legitimate gate becomes a refusal the user never
sees a card for. An earlier draft did the read inside runTurn and ten
approval-gate tests caught it. The invariant is now written down at the top of
the function, and the related hazard is recorded in the park-termination

fix(runner): end a turn parked on a gateway approval

A gateway run passes two gates on ONE tool-call id. The ACP gate on the outer
`run_tool` answers `allow` (its spec permission is `allow`) and marks the id an
allowed execution. The relay then hands the call to the gateway's semantic gate,
which reads the policy for the target action, answers `ask`, and parks that same
id. Nothing un-marks the first: `pause.ts` keeps two independent sets.

Paused-turn terminalization computed its wait set as every OPEN allowed
execution, so it waited for the closure of a call that cannot close until a human
answers, for the full `toolCallMs` bound (30 minutes by default). Measured live
on 2026-08-27: the turn returned 30 minutes and 2ms after the gate parked it, and
everything after the wait took 2ms.

That is worse than ending late. `run()` never returns inside the window, so its
`finally` never releases the alive watchdog and the session's stream row keeps
reporting `running=true`. A resume arriving meanwhile finds the session busy, is
marked INTERRUPTED, aborted, and evicted as `supersede-busy` — which is why
Approve appeared to do nothing on the live stack.

Exclude parked ids where the list is COMPUTED rather than at the wait. The same
list also seeds `parkedApprovedExecutions` on the Pi batch branch, where a parked
call has no seed and would be carried and re-announced on the next turn as an
approved execution it never was. That second path is a CORRECTNESS bug and NOT an
approval bypass: `ApprovedExecutionGrants.grant` keys on
`approvedCallKey(toolName, args)` and returns early when the call is unkeyable,
so a seed with an undefined tool name grants nothing. This is not a security
patch and should not be back-ported as one.

The parked call is still left OPEN and unsettled — its `interaction_request` is
the last word for the call this turn, and the resume answers that exact id.

Un-marking the id was the more truthful-looking fix and is not what this does:
`isAllowedExecution` has six readers, two of which decide what the client sees
for a tool call. The wait set is the only place where "allowed and paused at
once" is wrong, so it is the only place that encodes it.

fix(runner): digest the approval key in logs instead of printing it

`approvedCallKey` embeds the full canonical arguments, so the two lines that
logged it wrote user content into the runner log. Observed on an ordinary QA run:

  [gateway] approval key target=gmail.CREATE_EMAIL_DRAFT key="run_tool#{\"arguments\":
  {\"body\":\"hello\",\"recipient_email\":\"qa-target@example.com\", ...

An email body, a recipient address and a subject, retained wherever logs go. The
run's own deny-set does not cover it: `seedForRun(request).redactString` is a
credential deny-set, and none of this is a credential.

Both sites now log `approvalKeyDigest` (sha256, 12 hex). The diagnostic survives
intact, because the only question ever asked of these lines is whether the gate's
key equals a stored one, and two digests differ exactly when the keys differ.

ONE shared helper on purpose, next to `approvedCallKey` since that is what it
digests. If the two sites ever digested differently the line would report a
mismatch that is an artifact of the logging — worse than logging nothing — so the
regression test asserts the gate-side and extract-side digests are equal for one
key rather than testing the digest function alone.

The gate site also keeps a shape hint: the sorted TOP-LEVEL argument names, no
values. The bug class these lines exist to catch is identity drift, a stored key
built from the INNER arguments while the gate asks with the OUTER ones, and a bare
digest cannot tell that from an ordinary miss. `arguments,integration,tool` against
`body,recipient_email,subject` separates them at a glance. It does not recurse;
deeper names are provider parameters with no diagnostic value here.

fix(runner): keep every seeded decision under one approval key

The decision store is a FIFO LIST per key precisely so two identical calls each
resolve — `extractApprovalDecisions` pushes rather than replaces for that reason,
and responder.ts documents it twice. The seeded path was the only one collapsing a
key to a single decision.

So two identical calls could both park, both be answered out of band, and both
rows be claimed by `loadDurableDecisions`, while only one answer reached the map.
The first call consumed it; the second asked the human again for something they
had already answered, with its own row already terminal. A human decision on the
floor, which is the class of bug the durable read path exists to prevent.

Two details that matter:

The transcript's keys are snapshotted BEFORE the loop. Testing `map.has` as we go
would make this loop's own first append look like history, so the second entry
would be dropped again — the bug surviving its own fix.

Every appended entry is reported in `adopted`, since every one of those rows was
claimed upstream and the log should say so.

Row order is the append order. `ConversationDecisions` copies an array value
natively and `take()` pops one per call, so N approvals answer N calls and nothing

fix(tools): resolve the latest Composio toolkit version everywhere

Discovery and resolution were reading two different catalogs, so gateway search
was effectively dead. `COMPOSIO_SEARCH_TOOLS` always searches the LATEST toolkit
version, while our listing sent no version and got the account's pinned snapshot —
so every search hit was compiled against a policy built from the old catalog and
dropped as unknown or unconfigured. Measured on a live session: three searches,
ten results, zero kept.

The concrete shape, `browser_tool`: 18 screenshot-era tools unversioned, 5 task
tools at latest (CREATE_TASK, GET_OUTPUT_FILE, GET_SESSION, STOP_TASK,
WATCH_TASK) — exactly what search returns.

One constant, `COMPOSIO_TOOLKIT_VERSION`, now owns this for all three calls that
read or run a toolkit's tools. They must agree: a listing from one version and an
execution against another is the argument-schema mismatch trap, where the tool the
model was handed either does not exist or takes different arguments.

The parameter NAME differs per endpoint, each verified live rather than assumed:

  listing  GET  /tools                 `toolkit_versions` — a singular `version`
                                       here is accepted and silently ignored
                                       (still returns the 18)
  detail   GET  /tools/{slug}          `version` — without it a latest-only slug
                                       404s; with it, 200
  execute  POST /tools/execute/{slug}  `version`, in the BODY — the query form is
                                       accepted and ignored, and the slug still
                                       404s

Execute verified two ways: BROWSER_TOOL_CREATE_TASK 404s bare and reaches the
tool's own argument validation with the body pin (so it resolved), and
GMAIL_GET_PROFILE — which exists in both versions — still succeeds with the pin,
so tools that were already working do not regress.

`COMPOSIO_SEARCH_TOOLS` is deliberately left unpinned and says so in place: a
`version` there would pin the search meta-tool's own version, a different axis,
and the toolkit version its results come from is already latest.

The pre-existing v3.1 API-scope pin is a SEPARATE axis and does not settle this
one; the old comment claiming a per-call version override was unnecessary is
corrected, since it would otherwise tell the next reader to undo this.

Tests pin the exact outbound shape per endpoint. Mutation-checked: removing any
one of the three pins fails a test.

fix(workflows): let the commit engine address a gateway_connection entry

An agent asked to add Google Drive sent `add_item` on `parameters.agent.tools`
with a `gateway_connection` value and got `item_key_undefined` — "'add_item'
cannot derive a key for the new 'tools' entry". So the one tool type that adds a
whole integration was the one type an agent could not add.

`_tool_name` (contract 4.2) had a branch per type and none for
`gateway_connection`, and the entry carries no `name` BY DESIGN: it is the
integration, not one action. Its identity is the connection it routes through.

Keyed as `gateway_connection:<provider>:<integration>`. Provider plus integration
is enough because `coerce_tool_configs` admits at most one entry per integration,
so the pair is unique within the list it addresses. Synthetic and prefixed, unlike
the bare names beside it, because those keys ARE the user-facing tool names and
this one is derived — and the prefix keeps it from colliding with a legacy
`gateway` key, which is `{integration}__{action}`.

add_item, replace_item and remove_item all address it through the same
`item_key`, so they agree by construction. A second entry for an integration the
revision already carries is now refused as a duplicate at the delta, rather than
committing and failing later.

Fails closed: an entry missing provider or integration still reports
`item_key_undefined`, and the reason text now says which two fields it needs.

Also documents the recipe in the SDK builtins reference, which previously said
"do not hand-write one: keep using discover_tools and gateway entries" — advice
that no longer matches how an integration is added. It now says to take the REAL
connection slug from the connect/discover flow and never invent one, names the
key used for replace/remove, and states the failure mode for a wrong slug: the
commit does NOT check that the slug exists, so it is caught only when the agent
next runs, as a connection-not-found failure naming the slug. That is
`resolve_connection_by_slug` raising at resolve time; no new validation was
added, per slice 4.

Tests: add / replace / remove by the derived key, the duplicate-integration
refusal, two integrations coexisting, and the fail-closed cases. Mutation-checked
— removing the branch fails 6 of the 7.

docs(agents): align every model-facing build-kit text with the connection design

Nobody had audited the build-kit text against the integration-level design, and
today's incident showed the cost: a paragraph still told the model "do not
hand-write one: keep using discover_tools and gateway entries" for the exact
thing it was being asked to do. This audits all five model-facing surfaces.

The rule applied: every CLAIM must be true of the code as it stands, and every
INSTRUCTION must name the path we want the model on — connection entries, real
slugs, search-then-run.

agenta_builtins.py — the config reference and build guidance
- `gateway` is now marked LEGACY where it is defined, and the type list says so,
  instead of presenting it as a peer of `gateway_connection`. It sat FIRST in the
  list, so a model scanning top-down picked the deprecated path.
- Both worked examples of adding an integration were per-action `gateway` adds,
  in the ordered arm and the legacy arm. Examples outrank prose, so these were
  the load-bearing staleness. Both are now one `gateway_connection` entry.
- The keyed-lists rule omitted the derived key, which made a `gateway_connection`
  entry look unaddressable — the model would have emitted `{"list":"tools",
  "key":"github"}` and got target-not-found.
- The decision table routed "read or write in an outside tool" to `tools` entries
  (plural, per action); it now routes to ONE connection entry.
- Build step 5 said "add_item each chosen capability.tool entry and needed
  alternative", i.e. explicit per-action wiring.
- The instruction-writing example told the run to "call LIST_REPOSITORY_ISSUES".
  There is no such tool at run time — the agent has exactly `search_tools` and
  `run_tool` — so an agent built from that example would look for a tool that
  does not exist. Rewritten, with the rule stated.
- "Prefer narrow tools" was config-time action selection, which no longer exists;
  it is now runtime steering plus a `policy.permissions.tools` deny.
- The slug rule was "re-run discover_tools so the slug is current". That
  understates it: an invented slug commits cleanly and fails at run time. Now
  stated as a rule, in both arms and in the footguns list.
- The runtime guidance block gains the 5-result cap (a cap, not the catalog), the
  two runner outcomes quoted verbatim, the bare-key rule, and the fact that an
  approval pause or a refusal is policy rather than a bug. Its docstring claimed
  six rules while emitting five.

op_catalog.py — the op descriptions
- `commit_revision`'s keyed-list rule said "tools (by name)", so the default way
  to add an integration was the one entry it implied could not be addressed.
- `discover_tools` described a per-action wiring flow and hid the slug trap: a
  not-ready integration returns a connect affordance whose slug does not exist
  yet, and committing it looks fine until the run.
- `list_connections` was labelled "trigger connections", so a model wiring TOOLS
  never called the one op that returns a real slug — and guessed instead.
- `test_run.terminal_tool` invited asserting a provider action name, which never
  runs as a tool; a passing run would report `incomplete`.

change_set.py — the errors a model receives
- ITEM_KEY_UNDEFINED said "name for a tool", false for `reference` (name OR slug)
  and `platform` (keyed by op). Now per type.
- ITEM_NOT_FOUND told the model to read_config the list "to see the keys" — but a
  successful read of a list returns raw entries, and a derived key appears in
  none of them. Points at the selector refusal, which does enumerate them.
- Every list-addressing message said "named", which is false for any derived key:
  a gateway_connection entry has no name field, so "no entry named
  gateway_connection:composio:github" sends the model looking for that string as
  a name, finding nothing, and adding a duplicate. Now "with key".
- UNKEYED_COLLECTION called all four keyed lists "name-addressed"; two are not.
- ITEM_ALREADY_EXISTS offered "add_item with a different key", which for a
  connection entry means a different integration entirely.
- The derive failure now names the entry's type, so the model can tell which of
  the five key rules applies to it.

gateway.py — the two derived tool descriptions
- `search_tools` now states the 5-result cap, the retry-once rule, and that an
  empty result means search again more specifically.
- `run_tool` now names the prefixed-id trap (the runner documents models sending

  so a refused call is reported rather than retried with reshaped arguments.
- A legacy run-failure message said "the action is no longer in the catalog".

fix(agents): clarify search-once, and make seven refusals actionable

Both rulings from the build-kit audit.

SEARCH-ONCE (clarification of the spec's own intent, not a design change)

The guidance said "Search once" while the runner's empty-result message says
"Try a more specific task description" — so the one path where the runner asks
for another search was the one the guidance forbade. The intent was never "one
search ever"; it was "no equivalent-search loops, stop once you hold a usable
result". Now stated that way: search once per task with a concrete description,
never repeat an equivalent query, refine ONCE if the result is empty, stop as
soon as a result is usable.

Aligned in three places that must not drift: the model-facing guidance, the
prompt-guidance list in runtime-tools.md, and the test that pins the six items.
Nothing else in that decided doc is touched — its two other "search once"
mentions describe expected behavior rather than the prompt.

SEVEN REFUSALS (model-facing, in a file this PR already changes)

Three were self-defeating rather than merely vague, which is the difference
between a slow model and a looping one:

- DUPLICATE_ITEM_KEY told the model to remove the duplicate with remove_item.
  That call routes through the code that RAISES on duplicates, so a duplicated
  key is by definition not addressable by it. It now names replace_item, or
  setting the list.
- INVALID_TARGET_SHAPE, rendered for add_item, read "'add_item' addresses an
  object field ... Use add_item / replace_item / remove_item" — telling the model
  to use the verb that just failed, and never saying what add_item's tail must
  be. add_item now gets its own sentence naming the list.
- TEXT_NOT_FOUND told the model to copy the anchor "character for character".
  The model believes it did; that is why it sent the anchor. It now points at
  details.nearest_lines, which the same refusal already attaches for exactly this
  purpose.

Four were inaccurate about what the engine does:

- TEXT_NOT_FOUND's message claimed the text "must match exactly, with all
  whitespace" — but a prose field under match_mode auto has already been retried
  with a length-preserving fold, so that is not the rule that failed.
- TEXT_NOT_UNIQUE said "matched N times" while the counter counts overlapping
  START POSITIONS, so "aa" in "aaa" reports 2 where a reader sees 1.
- NO_CHANGE offered "or send nothing", which is not an action on this surface.
- INVALID_TARGET_SHAPE's next_step assumed the LAST segment was at fault, though
  the same reason covers an empty target, an over-long target, and a bad segment
  at any index.

Tests pin the three load-bearing ones and are mutation-honest: reverting all
three messages fails all three tests.

One EXISTING test changed rather than being worked around.
`test_a_soft_wrap_newline_is_still_significant` asserted the old "character for
character" wording, while its own comment says the enriched refusal "returns the
nearest lines, so the model sees the real break and re-anchors". The assertion
now matches the comment's stated intent and checks the attached lines are really

perf(tools): answer search schemas at the API instead of on every run request

Input schemas were riding the compiled gatewayPolicy, which travels on every run
request. Measured against Composio: one `github` integration (871 actions) put
1.5 MiB on each run where identity alone is 60 KiB, and `notion` grew 87-fold.
The policy carries an entry per CATALOG tool, not per allowed tool, so the cost
was the same however restrictive the permissions were.

The runner read those schemas in exactly one place: to replace the inline schema
on the at most five results a search returns. So the join moves to where the data
already is. The runner sends its pinned versions back on the search context, and
the API answers each ranked hit from that pinned catalog, dropping a hit the
pinned version has no key or no usable object schema for. The version guarantee
is unchanged, because the pin is the join key.

- `context.toolkit_versions` is a MAP, not the run's single version: an unscoped
  search ranks across every configured integration and each has its own pin. A
  scoped search sends only the one it named.

test(gate): GW1, the gateway tool surface against a real provider

The fixed matrix proves approvals with a BUILTIN -- tool, approve and deny all
drive the shell -- so nothing in it notices when the policy the SDK compiles and
the policy the runner enforces drift apart. This is the cell path_triggers.py
has been naming as mandatory for gateway-touching releases, and its absence is
what made that rule hard-stop.

never reaches the model, because a denied tool it can read about is one it will
try. allow_run: the allowed tool executes unattended and returns a genuine
provider result, asserted on the wire rather than on the model's word for it.

only variable -- it parks, its stored row names the right integration and tool
key, and it is answered through the INTERACTIONS API, the durable plane a
reloaded browser uses and the one no other cell covers. Every leg folds
check_no_silent_turn.

Two behaviours the gate needs and did not have. A missing or invalid connection
SKIPs naming the fixture rather than failing. An upstream model-provider error
(402, 429, quota) also SKIPs, loudly: a gate that goes red for a billing problem
is one people learn to wave through, and no leg reached a model turn anyway.

Reading interaction rows needs the filter nested under `query`; a top-level
session_id is silently ignored and the endpoint answers with the whole project's
rows. Since this cell answers by token, an unfiltered read could hand a verdict
to another session's pending approval, so the session id is re-checked client
side.

Inline agent parameters throughout: no saved agent is created or modified.

  the second render measured a 0-wide box and concluded nothing was
  truncated. It is measured only while collapsed now, and a description that

  can shrink, and the badge takes the 12px every other meta label here uses.

fix(frontend): name a connection, never slug it

Every form that creates a gateway connection asked the author for a slug.
It is a wire identifier — it ends up inside
`tools__composio__github__ACTION__<slug>` — it carries provider rules
(no dots, no doubled underscores) an author has no reason to learn, and in
the settings form it was the FIRST and only required field while the display
name was optional and usually left blank. That is why connection pickers
across the app end up showing slug-shaped text.

All three create surfaces now ask for a name only:

- the tools connect modal (`ConnectDrawer`),
- the triggers connect modal (`TriggerConnectDrawer`),
- Settings > Tools (`ConnectModal`), which had no derivation at all.

The slug is derived from the name with the existing `generateDefaultSlug`,
suffix and all, and still sent: the API types it optional but both routers
do `"." in slug` before anything else, so a null slug is a 500, not a
default. Nothing about the wire changes.

Names are seeded from how many connections the integration already has —
"GitHub (main)", then "GitHub (secondary)", then "GitHub (3)" — and the
author can edit them. The seed is applied late, when the connections query
settles, but never over something already typed.

`defaultConnectionName` and `connectionDisplayName` live in
@agenta/shared/utils next to the slug helper, which had no tests at all.

fix(frontend): make the add-integration drawer's two lists agree

built.

- The category rail could not scroll. It has `overflow-y-auto`, but as a
  flex item with the default `min-height: auto` its own content set its
  height, so it overflowed a body that clips instead of scrolling. It takes
  `min-h-0` now, and only the categories scroll — the heading and "All apps"
  stay put rather than sliding off the top.
- Category names rendered lowercase, because that is how the provider sends
  them. They are capitalized in CSS; the stored value is untouched.
- Connected rows led with the slug ("github-7mx · GitHub"), and the confirm
  button said "Add with github-7mx". Both show the name now, and so does the
  chooser between two connections. The slug only stands in when a connection
  carries no name at all.
- An already-connected integration was subtracted from the catalog, which
  made a second account unreachable: Connect is the only way to make one and
  it lives on those rows. The catalog no longer subtracts anything, so a
  connected app appears twice — under Connected, and again under All apps.
- Picking a category narrowed the catalog but left every connected app
  sitting above it. The connected list is the project's own connections, not
  a server query, so it is filtered here against each integration's
  categories, read through the same detail query atoms the rows already use.
  Integrations carry category NAMES and the rail carries the provider's
  slugified id, so both are accepted, case-insensitively.
- Connected search matched the integration KEY only. It matches the display
  name too now.

The list arithmetic moved into `integrationCatalogFilters` so both rules —
the dual listing and the shared category filter — are stated once and tested.
A row whose catalog detail has not arrived yet is kept rather than hidden, so
rows do not blink out and back as details land.

fix(frontend): open an integration row on the first click

Clicking an integration row in the config panel often took several clicks.
Most of the row was not clickable: only the left identity block carried the
handler, while the whole right-hand group — the status tag, the "old format"

tree (the legacy-entry migration) BEFORE setting the drawer's local target,
so on an old-format row the re-render cascade from that write could land on

fix(frontend): address review on the integration drawer batch

Three things from CI and CodeRabbit.

**A dead "Show more" on a description-less row.** The row's overflow flag is
a width measurement, and the effect that takes it returns early when there is
no description to measure. So a row reused for the SAME tool key after its
description went away kept the last measurement and grew a toggle over
nothing. That swap is reachable: a key that leaves the provider catalog comes
back through `withStaleTools` as `{key, stale: true}` with no description, and
React keeps the row's state across it.

The flag is cleared when the description goes, and the decision moved into
`isDescriptionTruncatable` in `integrationPolicy` — a pure predicate holding
the two rules a width measurement cannot supply (a newline hides text no
measurement can see; no description means no toggle) with tests for both,
including the stale-row sequence.

**The format job.** `packages/agenta-entity-ui/tests/unit/integrationCatalogFilters.test.ts`
failed `prettier --check`. Worth recording why it got through locally:
`pnpm lint-fix` runs eslint over `src/` only, while the format job runs
prettier over `**/*.{ts,tsx,...}`. A new file under a package's `tests/` is
therefore linted by neither. `pnpm run format` is the check that matches CI.

**A relative import across a package boundary.** The new ConnectDrawer story
reached into `../../../packages/agenta-entity-ui/src/...`, which `web/AGENTS.md`
forbids. `@agenta/entity-ui/gatewayTool` exports `ConnectDrawer`, and the
sibling `ConnectionManagerDrawer` story already imports through it, so the
story now does the same. The two older stories that still deep-import are
untouched: their components have no exported subpath, which is what their
comments say.

Also tightened the comments this branch added to the one line `web/AGENTS.md`
asks for.

fix(frontend): drive dictation from intent, not the recogniser's teardown

Voice-to-text had three faults with one shape: the mic's state was read off the
Web Speech API's own events, which lag the person by an entire session teardown.
Chrome only reports back once it has flushed a trailing result and closed its
speech socket, and a start() issued inside that window throws.

- Pressing the mic again after stopping did nothing: the button stayed latched
  on for the whole teardown, and every further press was a no-op.
- Re-pressing the push-to-talk chord landed in that same window, where start()
  returned early in silence. The mic read as recording and the entire held
  utterance went nowhere.
- A silence auto-restart the browser refused ended dictation with no error.

Intent is now the source of truth. The recording flag flips on the press; a
start requested mid-teardown is queued and fires when the session actually
closes; a refused start retries and gives up loudly after ten attempts. A
separate active flag holds the editor session open through the teardown so the
trailing final result still lands, and start() reports whether it opened a
session so a press cannot stack a second editor session on a running one.

Separately, dictating into a composer that already held text garbled it:
"Draft" plus a dictated "hello world" came out as "Draft   hello hello hello
hello world". Lexical merges adjacent same-styled text nodes, so the session's
committed node was swallowed by the typed text, and every result re-created it
past the interim tail and re-appended the whole transcript. The committed node
now carries a visually inert style that keeps it addressable, is re-inserted
ahead of the tail when Lexical collects it while empty, and settles to plain
text on end().

feat(runner,frontend): measure how far apart streamed deltas actually arrive

The reveal fix makes a 400ms gap read as typing, but nothing said WHERE that
400ms is spent -- the harness emitter, a buffering hop, or the model. Probe
both ends of the pipe: the runner's ACP session/update handler, which every
harness goes through, and the browser transport.

Runner side is off unless AGENTA_RUNNER_STREAM_TRACE is set (a line per delta
is far too much for a normal run); the browser side is a capped ring buffer
dumped on demand via window.__agentaStreamTrace(). Gaps present at the runner
are upstream of us; gaps that appear only in the browser belong to the service
or the network between them.

The service hop is deliberately not probed: the two ends bracket it, and its
projection loop is duplicated, so a third probe would be two copies of the same
line for an answer the endpoints already give.

feat(frontend): give the sessions rail a Type facet instead of a Show automations toggle

The toggle swapped the list rather than widening it: on listed only trigger
runs and hid every chat, which is not what "Show automations" says. Replace it
with a Type facet — All / Chat / Automation — so the control reads the way it
behaves, and add the "all" state the toggle had no way to express.

otherwise bury the conversations you are having. A stored filter blob keeps its

fix(frontend): stop the sessions rail rendering the same session twice

A row's key is its session id, so a session reaching the list twice renders two
rows that BOTH match the selected key — the white selected pill landing on rows
nobody selected.

It reached the list twice because the pinned rows were taken as the pinned query
left them. Unpinning mints a new query key and the placeholder hands back the
previous rows; once the last pin goes the query disables and hands them back for
good, while the recent window now returns them too. Filter those rows by the
current pin set, and dedupe the merged list as a backstop.

fix(frontend): hold the session headings still while the rows move

The headings were emitted in the order their first row happened to arrive, and
the rows arrive in activity order — so working in a session reshuffled the
sections around it. Only the rows under a heading should move.

Each bucket now names where it sorts, and the headings are ordered on that:
pins first under every grouping, newest day first, Running before Live before
Idle, agents by name with No agent yet last.

fix(frontend): make the rail's filters reach the sessions it holds locally

Every filter is a server predicate, and the playground's open tabs are merged in
after the query — so the chat you were looking at stayed listed, and selected,
after you switched the rail to Automation, and survived another agent's filter.
Re-apply type, agent and liveness to those rows. The activity window is the one
exemption: a session you have open is current by definition.

Keep husks off the rail too — never-run, untitled, no messages — which is the
rule the sessions list already applies through isStartedSession. This is what
stops the blank tab the panel seeds after an archive from appearing out of
nowhere and taking the selection; an active husk now names no selected row at
all. isSessionHusk takes the boolean it actually needs so the rail can read a
focused per-session selector instead of re-rendering on every streamed token.

fix(frontend): spin a session row while its turn runs

The rail's dot filled on waiting or alive and never read running, so a turn in
flight rendered as the idle hollow circle. The mobile rail already spins on the
same ref, and both source comments say the row spins — this is the desktop half
catching up. A locally-created session shows it first: its ref carries running
and, having no server row yet, is never alive.

fix(frontend): keep a baseline poll so a run you did not start shows up

The rail stopped polling the moment every row looked idle, so a turn started
under another agent — a trigger, another browser — could never reach it: this
client only knows about runs in the conversation it has mounted, and the server
flag was the only other route. Only the session you were driving yourself ever
appeared to run.

Fast poll while something is alive or running, 60s otherwise. Both are gated on
the Sessions group being open with the rail expanded, and React Query holds the
timer while the window is unfocused, so a quiet rail costs one request a minute
and a hidden tab costs none.

fix(frontend): delete a session before revalidating the lists that show it

Deleting a session the playground already knows about left the row on screen.
The local verb owns the server call for a cached session, so revalidating
straight after firing it refetched a list the row was still in — and the answer
that came back put the row right back, where it sat until the next poll.

deleteSessionAtomFamily already returns its request for exactly this reason, and
says so in a comment; the seam it crosses typed the verb as returning void and
dropped it. Type the local cache's write verbs as awaitable, return the promise
from the app adapter, and await it before revalidate. Archive took the same
route and gets the same fix.

The record log stores paths as the harness reported them, which is

drivePathFromToolPath strips the workspace roots the runner builds and tags which
mount owns the path, so the agent's <cwd>-agent sibling resolves to the agent
mount. Runner plumbing is filtered again and agent files get the right origin tag.
