second account, and nothing reported any of it. Token refresh was keyed the same
way, so a renewal could spend a handle the other connection still needed; a
rotating authorization server retires a refresh token the moment it is used, so
that left the rightful connection unable to renew at all.

Address a grant by the connection that consented instead. `grant_slug` derives
the slug from the endpoint id through the same `get_slug_from_name_and_id` every
other entity uses, so the slug is stable across reconnects and unique within the
project. `_find_grant` becomes a lookup by that slug rather than a scan, which
also takes a full project secret listing off the path of every relayed call. The
written payload records its `endpoint_id`, so a reader does not have to reverse
the slug. `refresh_grant` takes the connection, and its in-worker lock is keyed
per connection rather than per server.

Client registration stays keyed on the issuer. A registration under RFC 7591
names this deployment to an authorization server; it is not an account, two
connections there legitimately share one, and registering per connection would
mint a fresh client on every connect.

The vault payload is serialized with `mode="json"`, because a field typed as
anything but a JSON primitive reaches `json.dumps` as the object itself and
raises. Every field that predates this was already JSON-native.

The local OAuth provider fixture now serves the refresh grant type and rotates
its handles, so a test can prove that renewing one connection does not burn
another's.

feat(api): disconnect an MCP connection without deleting it

There was no way to drop a connection's authorization. The only teardown was
deleting the endpoint, which took the connection's identity with it: every agent
configured against that connection lost its reference, and reconnecting meant
building the connection again under a new id.

Deleting also left the grant behind. `delete_endpoint` dropped the row and
nothing else, so the vault kept a record nothing named — unreachable, unlistable
as a connection, and still holding a live token.

Add `DELETE /gateways/mcps/endpoints/{endpoint_id}/connect`, the inverse of the
POST beside it. It deletes this connection's grant and clears the endpoint's
`secret_id`, and keeps the id, slug, name, URL and tool policy, so the endpoint
reads as needing authorization and one Connect brings it back. Idempotent: a
repeat is not an error, and the handle is cleared whether or not a row was there
to delete, because a `secret_id` pointing at nothing is what made an endpoint
report itself ready and then fail every call.

`delete_endpoint` now drops the grant before it drops the row.

Both go through the connection-keyed grant, so disconnecting one account at a
server leaves every other connection to that server working. Under the previous
URL-derived key this operation could not have existed: it would have
disconnected every connection at that server at once.

The client registration is untouched. It names this deployment to an
authorization server rather than an account, and other connections there are
still using it.

Revocation is not attempted, so a disconnected token stays live at the provider
until it expires. Recorded as OR79 in open-reviews.md and CU20 in cleanups.md
rather than left unsaid.

feat(api): migrate stored MCP OAuth grants onto the connection key

The code now addresses a grant by the connection that consented. The rows that
already exist are still under the old key, derived from the server URL, so they
need moving.

Two cases, and only two. A grant that exactly one live connection references is
that connection's, whoever wrote it, so the row is renamed to the new key and the
connection keeps working with no reconnect. A grant that several connections
reference holds the tokens of whichever consent ran last, and nothing recorded
which one that was; there is no honest way to hand it to one of them, so those
connections have their handle cleared and the row is deleted. Each then reads as
needing authorization, and one Connect makes it correct again.

Measured against the development deployment before writing this: nine
connections hold a grant, three of them own it outright and six share a single
row in one project. So three migrate silently and six need a reconnect.

Data only. No table, column, index or constraint changes.

The ambiguous set is read before anything is written, because clearing the
handles is what stops "more than one connection names this row" being true. It
cannot be recovered from the slug afterwards either: the old key and the new one
are both `oauth-grant-<twelve hex>` and differ only in which id they hash. Rows
already orphaned before this ran are left where they are, since deleting them
would be a second, unannounced behaviour.

`downgrade()` deliberately does nothing and says why in its own body. The
renames need no undo, because the previous revision's code never addressed a
grant by its slug on the read path — it scanned the project's secrets and
matched the payload's `server` field — so it finds these rows under their new
slugs exactly as it did under their old ones. The deleted rows cannot come back,
and pretending otherwise would be worse than saying so.

The test drives the revision's own `upgrade()` against a scratch database on a
real Postgres, over the real table shapes, and covers both cases together in one
project, a soft-deleted connection not making a live one's grant ambiguous, two
projects whose grants shared the old URL-derived slug, an already-orphaned row,
and a second run changing nothing.

fix(api): re-register an OAuth client when the callback address changes

Closes OR78.

A stored client registration was addressed by the authorization server alone,
and nothing compared the redirect URI it was created with against the one this
deployment would now send. A registration under RFC 7591 is bound to its
redirect URIs, and a deployment's public address changes whenever a tunnel is
added, rotated or dropped. The next connect then found the stale registration,
sent its `client_id`, and the authorization server refused it: the client it
knows is registered against an address the request no longer uses. Nothing
re-registered, so the connection stayed unconnectable until someone deleted the
vault record by hand, and the error the person saw was the authorization
server's, which says nothing about redirect URIs.

`registration_covers` answers whether a stored registration still names the
callback we would send, and a registration is reused only when it does.
Otherwise the connect registers again, written under the same issuer-derived
slug, so the fresh registration replaces the stale one rather than accumulating
beside it.

The key is left alone on purpose. Adding the redirect URI to it would strand the
stale row under a slug nothing reads instead of replacing it, and the redirect
URI is not an identity: the issuer is what a registration is for, which is also
why two connections at one authorization server share one.

The comparison is exact after dropping a trailing slash, the one difference an
OAuth client library can introduce without changing where the browser lands.
Nothing else is normalized, because the authorization server matches exactly and
a looser comparison would reuse a registration the server will refuse.

fix(api): derive an MCP connection's slug and stop swallowing a refused create

Posting a create with no slug returned `200 {"count": 0}` and wrote nothing. The
column is NOT NULL, the insert raised a not-null violation, the DAO's
`suppress_exceptions` decorator swallowed it, the DAO returned `None`, and the
route turned that into a success with a zero count. A success that creates no
record is worse to debug than a refusal: every client reads it as done.

Both halves are fixed.

The slug is derived rather than typed. A connection's slug is its identity —
agent configuration references it, the data-plane route is built from it, and its
grant is addressed by the id beside it — so it has to survive every later edit to
the display name. Asking a person to invent one at setup put identity in the same
field as a label. `derive_endpoint_slug` seeds it from the display name, falling
back to the server's hostname, and takes uniqueness from a `uuid4` suffix the way
secrets, testsets and evaluators do. Two connections may legitimately carry one
display name, and a derived slug must not be what refuses the second. A slug the
caller supplied is still honoured, so existing callers are unaffected.

And a write the database refuses now reaches the caller. `IntegrityError` joins
the DAO's exclude list, so the slug-unique case is still converted into the
`EntityCreationConflict` callers expect while everything else propagates, and the
route raises instead of answering with a zero count.

feat(api,sdk): make an agent name the connection it means, not a label

An agent configuration said which MCP server it meant with one string, and that
string was both the label a harness renders in front of the server's tools and
the identity of a stored connection. So an agent could not express which of two
accounts at one server it wanted, and renaming a server silently moved it to a
different connection or to none.

The two are separated. Identity is the connection reference the SDK already
understands: connection = {type: "gateway", namespace: "custom", slug}. The slug
is what the platform derives once and never changes. The name becomes a label,
frozen at save, and stays the tool prefix.

A rename therefore changes the settings row and the picker and nothing else. The
alternative renames every tool inside a saved agent the moment someone edits a
label, which invalidates the permission rules already rendered against the old
names and any prompt that named a tool.

The name-matching route is deprecated in place, not deleted. Committed agent
revisions are immutable, so every server declared before the connection
reference existed still arrives at that line and has to keep resolving.

Because a name is now the tool prefix and nothing else guarantees it is
distinct, create and edit refuse a name another connection in the project
already answers to, as a 409 the person can act on. Compared on the rendered
prefix rather than the raw string, using the runner's own normalization: it maps
everything outside [A-Za-z0-9_] to an underscore, so "Acme Notion" and
"Acme-Notion" are one name as far as a tool call is concerned, and an exact
comparison would let that pair through for the runner to refuse later by killing
the whole registration.

An unnamed connection is not checked, because it renders no prefix worth
colliding and a name has never been required.

One test from the slug-derivation commit asserted that two connections could
share a display name, which this refuses. It tested the property at the wrong
level: what matters is that the slug takes its uniqueness from the suffix rather
than the seed, because a name is free again once its connection is deleted and a
slug must never be reused for a different connection. Restated against the
derivation itself, and the docstring that justified it corrected.

fix(api): treat an upstream that refuses the stored grant as a reconnect

A connection whose credential the provider had retired went on reporting itself
connected while every call failed. OR83.

The relay renews a grant only when this deployment can see it has expired. A
provider can retire one long before that: someone removes the application, an
administrator revokes the account's authorization, a server expires a token
sooner than the lifetime it issued. The stored row still looks live, nothing
renews it, the relay sends it, and the upstream answers 401.

kept reading valid, so the settings screen showed an account that was connected
and did not work, and the caller was handed an authentication error with no
route to re-authorize and nothing a retry could reach.

connection invalid and raises the reconnect the refresh-failure path already
raises, which the proxy renders as a 409 auth_required envelope carrying the
connect affordance. The insufficient-scope 403 beside it has behaved this way
since WP18; the 401 was the case nobody wrote.

401 is that server's own answer about a credential Agenta did not issue and has
no consent flow to send anyone back through, so it still passes through byte for
byte.

state the connection is left in.

renews once and the caller never sees it; a withdrawn renewal handle asks for a

feat(api): add a read-only MCP server probe

The connect journey asks for a server URL first, and nothing could answer a
question about one. The only code that reaches a user-supplied MCP URL needs an
endpoint row to exist, and OAuth discovery refuses any row that is not already
auth_mode=oauth, so a person had to declare a server's authentication before
anything had looked at it.

POST /gateways/mcps/endpoints/probe takes a URL and reports whether the server
answers, what it calls itself, and whether it wants OAuth. It creates nothing,
reads no row, accepts no credential and sends none.

The order of the checks follows the protocol. An unauthenticated `initialize` is
the handshake's first call, is not a tool call and is the only call that reports
serverInfo, so it goes first. A server that needs authorization answers it with
a 401 naming its protected-resource document, and that challenge, rather than a
guess, starts OAuth discovery.

Discovery that fails reports `unknown`, not `api_key`. A timeout, an unreadable
metadata document and a refused registration are not evidence that a server
wants a key, and a key field offered on that evidence asks someone to paste a
credential into a form that may have no use for it.

The route is gated on EDIT_MCP_ENDPOINTS, not VIEW: it makes the deployment
fetch an address of the caller's choosing. It runs the same URL guard a create
runs, so a URL the first step accepts is one the last step can save, and it goes
through the shared egress boundary, inheriting the address checks, the pin and
the no-redirect policy rather than repeating them.

feat(web): disconnect an MCP server without deleting it

Settings offered Delete and nothing else, so the only way to revoke a grant was
to remove the row. The row carries the identity agent configs reference, so that
took the connection with the credential.

Disconnect calls DELETE /gateways/mcps/endpoints/{id}/connect and keeps the
endpoint: its id, slug, name, URL and policy stay, and one Connect reconnects
it. The row action appears only where there is a grant to revoke, so a server
that is not connected offers Connect instead, and it confirms first because
agents using that server stop working until it is connected again.

The answer is written straight into the list cache rather than invalidated. The
route returns the endpoint in the shape the list holds, and refetching would
leave the row reading Authorized until the round trip landed, which is the wrong
thing to say about a credential that is already gone. The row is replaced whole:
the response omits the secret_id the disconnect removed, and merging would put
it back.

The route is owned by the identity work and is not on this branch yet, so the
tests drive the client and the cache write against the agreed contract.

feat(web): replace register-then-connect with one URL-first journey

Adding an MCP server took seven actions across two dialogs, a row menu and a
popup, and asked for a slug and an authentication mode before anything had
looked at the server. Both are internal facts: the slug is an identifier the
platform can derive, and the auth mode is the server's to state.

The journey asks for the URL first, probes it, suggests a name from
serverInfo.name or the hostname, and then takes whichever path the server turned
out to need. OAuth goes to the scope checklist and the provider; a server that
needs nothing is connected outright; a server whose authentication could not be
discovered gets an explicit fallback offering both answers, a credential or
none, because a 401 is not evidence that a key is required.

The decisions live in a reducer with no React, no timers and no network in it,
because the states worth getting right are the ones nobody clicks through by
hand. Two invariants it exists to hold: cancelling deletes only a pending row
this journey created, never a working connection and never one it is
reconnecting; and no failure reads as a success, so every non-success path lands
somewhere that carries an explanation.

Names are checked against the project's existing ones on the form the API
deduplicates, so a suggestion is never one the API would reject and a collision
is caught in the field rather than on submit.

Nothing is written to the row after consent. The edit route is a full replace
and the callback has by then stored a secret_id this client never saw, so a PUT
to flip a flag would wipe the grant the journey just obtained.

Settings, agent configuration and the in-chat connect request all mount the same
component, so the flow cannot drift between them, and the agent-config path is
how the mobile app reaches it. McpConnectDialog is gone: keeping a second connect
dialog is the drift this removes. Its unmount case went with it, and the watch's
own suite remains the standing guard for OR67.

feat(web): move the MCP servers list into a shared settings section

The list lived in web/oss, so the mobile app had no MCP surface at all and a
person on a phone had to open a blank chat session and find an accordion. The
section moves to @agenta/settings-ui, which is where the integrations section
next door already lives and why that one takes a copy override.

It reads the query route instead of the list route. The list route mixes in
synthesized builtin and provider rows that carry no id, and every caller already
filtered them back out; a list called "MCP servers" means the project's own
connections, and provider-managed rows belong with the integrations they come
from.

Opening a connection shows what it is, what it exposes and how to end it. Tools
are read-only here: a permission belongs to an agent's configuration, not to the
connection, because two agents can share one server and be allowed different
things. There is no control-plane route for a tool list, so it goes through the
JSON-RPC data plane the agents use, minting a gateway credential first because
that plane reads X-AG-Credentials and ignores Authorization.

Renaming says out loud that it changes the label and nothing else, since
renaming something an agent uses invites the opposite assumption.

Remove and Disconnect are now distinct actions with distinct warnings.
Disconnecting keeps the connection and one Connect brings it back; removing
takes the identity with it, so reconnecting later makes a different connection.

The register/edit modal is gone. It asked for a slug and an authentication mode
that the journey now derives, and its API-key option created rows it gave no way
to supply a credential to.

feat(mobile): add the MCP servers settings tab

The mobile app listed no MCP tab, so a deep link to it fell back to Preferences
and the only way to reach an MCP server on a phone was to open a blank chat
session with the configuration pane showing and find the MCPs accordion.

It now renders the shared section, the same one the desktop mounts, so a
connection added on either surface is the same connection. Like Tools, this tab
is writable rather than read-only: the section brings its own journey and
dialogs, so nothing here depends on the app supplying them.

feat(web): let an agent pick an MCP connection instead of describing one

The agent config form authored a server: URL, authentication, header name,
secret. Saving one registered an endpoint row, deriving its slug from the name
and upserting by slug equality, so renaming a server silently repointed the
agent at a different connection or collided with someone else's.

The form now asks the one question that belongs to an agent: which connection,
of the ones this project has. Adding one opens the same journey settings uses,
and the new connection is selected for this agent only.

The item writes {name, connection: {type: "gateway", namespace: "custom", slug},
policy}. The older {type: "http", url} shape is still read, because saved
configurations carry it, and is no longer written; an item on it says so and
re-picking moves it across.

The two fields are not the same thing and the form now says which is which.
`connection.slug` is the endpoint the gateway resolves and comes from the API,
never from anything typed. `name` is the prefix the model sees on this server's
tools, frozen from the display name when the connection is chosen, so renaming a
connection in settings does not rename tools in an agent that is already saved.

The row's connect action reads the slug the item points at rather than
re-deriving one from its name, which is what made a rename repoint it.

mcpEndpointRegistration and mcpServerAuthentication go with the flow they served.
Nothing registers an endpoint at save any more: the journey created it.

fix(web): render an agent's MCP tool prefix the way the platform does

The config item's tool prefix was built with its own character rule, replacing
anything outside [A-Za-z0-9._-] with a hyphen and trimming leading punctuation.
The platform renders it differently: tool_prefix in the MCP gateway service
strips, then replaces every character outside [A-Za-z0-9_] with an underscore,
case preserved. A connection called "Acme Tools" therefore reached the model as
Acme-Tools while the project had deduplicated its name as Acme_Tools.

Both now come from one normalization, so the prefix a config stores is the one a
harness shows and the one names were checked against. The reserved runner prefix
is refused in either spelling, since a display name can only normalize to the
underscored form but a config could carry either.

Also folds the create-secret drawer into the journey's manual credential step. A
project with no secret yet could select from an empty list and go no further.

The UX document now records what a pending record actually is: an ordinary row
carrying no credential, which every surface reads as needing authorization.
Cancelling deletes the row the journey created, a reconnect deletes nothing, and
nothing is written after consent, so an attempt abandoned by closing the browser
leaves a connection reading "Needs authorization" rather than disappearing.

fix(web): send a refused duplicate name back to the name field

The client checks a name against the project's existing ones before submitting,
but it cannot win a race and it is not the authority. When the API refuses one,
it answers 409 with a typed envelope saying the name is taken and what to do.
That arrived as an ordinary create failure, so the journey offered Try again,
which would have submitted the same name and been refused the same way.

The refusal is now told apart by its code and returns to the naming step with
the server's own sentence under the name field, keeping the URL and what the
probe found so only the name has to change. Editing the name clears it.

fix(api): stop a transport failure from quoting the credential it failed to send (review round 1, D1)

Nine call sites across both gateway planes turned an httpx.RequestError into a
caller-visible error by copying str(exc) onto a detail field, which the proxies
render as the error message. OR86.

That text is not safe to show. h11 validates the request while building it and
its refusal quotes the bytes it rejected, and when those bytes are a header they
are the credential the gateway just injected. Reproduced against a real socket:
a grant whose value ends in a newline comes back as an "Illegal header value"
message with the whole bearer token inside it.

The ordinary way to get such a value is a trailing newline on a pasted key,
which the person pasting it cannot see, and nothing stripped or validated a
credential on write. Two of the nine sites carry more than the MCP relay does:
the OAuth token exchange sends the client secret and the authorization code, and
the probe interpolated the exception into a message the connect dialog shows.

OR75 does not cover this. That scanner reads a relayed response for an echoed
credential; this value never reaches a response, it reaches an error the gateway
authors itself.

classify_transport_error maps the exception to a closed vocabulary and returns a
fixed sentence per cause, so no caller-visible string interpolates an exception.
The table ends at RequestError itself, so a class a future httpx release adds is
classified rather than falling through to a quote.

The same table decides what may be logged. A log is not a caller but it is not a
vault either, and two classes quote material we must not record: a local
protocol error quotes the request bytes and a remote one quotes the upstream's.
Those log their class and cause only. The reachability classes keep their text,
so an operator can still tell a DNS failure from a refused connection.

A credential is also no longer storable in the state that triggers it. Provider
keys, OAuth access and refresh tokens and client secrets are stripped of
surrounding whitespace and refused if they carry an interior control character.
Free-form custom-secret content is deliberately untouched, since a stored PEM
legitimately spans lines. Those models also hide the rejected input in
validation errors, which Pydantic renders by default and which would have
carried the credential onward to whatever logs it.

feat(web): choose what an agent may do with each MCP tool

An MCP server was allow-or-deny as a whole, so an agent that needed one tool got
every tool, including the destructive ones. Per-tool policy exists in the SDK
now and nothing could write it.

The editor sits in the agent's configuration rather than beside the connection,
because that is whose decision it is: two agents can share one server and be
allowed different things. It reuses the integration permission select, and the
mobile app reaches it through the same configuration pane the desktop does.

Three rules the table has to show, not merely obey. A tool with no rule of its
own is not unrestricted, so every such row says what it inherits instead of
displaying a bare value with no provenance. The pair of fields is an opt-in, so
while it is off the whole-server permission governs and nothing per-tool is
written, leaving an agent configured before this existed untouched. A tool an
include filter hides cannot be given a permission at all, because the API
refuses the whole policy rather than dropping the entry, and a control offered
there would build a configuration that fails on every run instead of once at
save.

Rules for tools a server has stopped advertising are shown rather than pruned. A
server can drop a tool temporarily, and discarding the author's decision would
re-admit it under the new-tool default when it came back.

The decisions live in a pure module mirroring MCPPolicy, including the detail
that makes the difference: an unlisted tool floors at ask rather than falling
through, so a run default of allow cannot widen a server whose author took the
trouble to write a table. Keys are the tool names the server advertises, never a
harness-rendered one.

Also gates the mobile MCP tab on the gateway flag, in the tab resolver and at
the render boundary. The desktop gained that gate while this branch was in
flight; without it a deep link renders a surface whose every action the gateway
refuses.

fix(api): write a credential transition as two columns, not a whole row (review round 1, D3)

Connect, disconnect and invalidate each replaced the connection row from a
snapshot the caller had read earlier. Two consequences, one found by each
reviewer, and the merged version is worse than either.

Fields the builder did not set were nulled. The edit mapping assigns tags and
meta unconditionally and the credential builders never set them, so a connection
created with either lost it on the first connect.

Fields the snapshot held stale were written back. An administrator who
deactivated a connection or tightened its tool filter while a relay was in
flight had that change reverted by the 401 that eventually arrived, because the
relay recorded a dead credential by replaying the row as it was before the call
went out.

A credential transition is not an edit of the connection, so it no longer
borrows one. bind_endpoint_secret points a connection at its stored
authorization, or at none, and marks it valid. invalidate_endpoint_secret
records that the authorization is dead. Each reads the row under its own lock
and writes the columns it owns; both are read-modify-write on one JSON column,
so the lock is what stops two of them each writing the flags they read.

invalidate_endpoint_secret deliberately does not take the handle. The relay
decides this after a round trip the connection may have been reconfigured
during, so the handle it read at the start is the one value that must not be
written back, and a connection holding none is left alone rather than marked
dead just as someone repaired it.

One full PUT stays, on the discovery step, because caching discovery metadata
genuinely is an edit of the connection's data. It now carries tags and meta
through instead of defaulting them away.

fix(api): drop a connection's outstanding consents when it is disconnected (review round 1, D5)

Disconnect deleted the grant and left the authorization attempts alone, so a
consent already in flight completed against the record it was issued and
reconnected the account afterwards. The person who pressed Disconnect was never
told, and the connection they believed they had revoked was working again.

The window is the attempt's time to live, and the ordinary way in is a browser
tab opened before the disconnect and finished after it.

Disconnect now drops that connection's outstanding attempts first, so there is
no window in which the grant is gone and a callback can still write a new one.
The handle a late tab presents then names no record, and the callback refuses as
it does for any spent or unknown handle, which is already the path the person
sees when a consent times out.

Scoped to the one connection and the one project. Two accounts at one server are
two connections, and disconnecting one must not cancel a consent the person is
part-way through for the other; the same connection id in another tenant is a
different connection.

This is the cheaper half of what the reviewer proposed. An authorization
generation stamped on the connection and checked by both the callback and the
refresh would also close an in-flight refresh, which this does not; that is
recorded against OR81, which already tracks disconnect being local and
best-effort.

fix(api): D4 make the grant rekey migration survive an occupied destination

The migration renamed a legacy grant row onto the slug derived from the
connection that references it. If a row already sat at that slug, the unique
index on (project_id, slug) rejected the rename and the whole migration failed.

The state that produces it: the connection consented under the new code, which
stored its grant at its own key, and something failed before the endpoint was
repointed at it. An interrupted callback is the way to get there. So the endpoint
still names the legacy row while the row at its new key already exists.

The occupant is that connection's own grant, by construction, since nothing else
computes that slug. So the endpoint is repointed at it, which is what the
interrupted callback was about to do, and the legacy row is left as an orphan
rather than deleted, matching what this revision already does with every other
orphan. The connection ends up naming the newer of the two credentials and needs
no reconnect.

That adoption also makes the rename a no-op for those rows rather than a
conflict, since the endpoint now names a row whose slug already is the
destination. A NOT EXISTS guard covers what adoption cannot: the unique index
does not look at kind, so a row of another kind on that slug would break the
rename as surely as a grant would, and this revision now skips that one rename
instead of aborting. Both outcomes are reported rather than passed over.

Bounded waits, per the same finding. Every statement touches a table a running
deployment writes to, and an unbounded lock_timeout lets this queue behind a long
transaction and hold the migration slot. Failing and being re-run is the better
outcome, because the revision is idempotent.

Four cases added to the existing scratch-database suite: the occupied
destination, one interrupted connection beside an ordinary one in the same
project, a destination held by another kind, and a re-run after an adoption. All
four fail against the previous revision with the unique violation the finding
describes; I checked rather than assumed.

fix(api): D13 report the grants the rekey migration leaves behind

The rename joins a grant row to its referencing endpoint on the project, so a row
whose project does not match its endpoint's is passed over: not renamed, not
counted, and not mentioned. OR62 records that the schema does not constrain the
two to agree, so such a row is possible by construction.

Leaving it alone is right. The connection reads as needing authorization and one
Connect fixes it. The silence is what the finding is about, because the counts
the revision does print would otherwise read as "everything was handled".

It now counts every connection still naming a grant that is not at its key once
everything else has run, split into the cross-project case the finding names and
the residual case a skipped rename leaves, and says so. Both lines appear only
when there is something to say, so an ordinary run's summary is unchanged.

Reporting only. No row is treated differently than before.

perf(api): address a stored client registration instead of searching for it (review round 1, D14)

Reading a client registration listed every secret in the project and matched on
the issuer URL, which decrypts each row to find one. The grant half of this
class moved off exactly that pattern when its key moved to the connection; the
provider half was left behind, and both reviewers named the same fix.

The registration slug has always been a pure function of the issuer, so the row
can be addressed. The scan stays as a fallback and is not dead code: a row
written under an older naming, or one with no slug, is still reachable by its
issuer, and losing track of a registration means registering a fresh client at a
server that may rate limit it.

A row found at the slug is accepted only if it also names this issuer, so a
collision cannot hand one authorization server another's client.

fix(api): release a connection's refresh lock once nobody is holding it (review round 1, D15)

The lock dictionary was setdefault with no removal, so a worker accumulated one
asyncio.Lock per connection it had ever refreshed and kept it for the process's
whole life. Small per entry and unbounded in time. Moving the key from the
server URL to the connection was right for the semantics and strictly raised the
cardinality, which is what made it worth closing now.

Holders are counted rather than read off lock.locked(), because a coroutine
waiting to acquire is a holder too: evicting the entry while it waits would hand
the next arrival a different lock and defeat the serialization the lock exists
for. A rotating authorization server retires a renewal handle the moment it is
spent, so two exchanges leave one caller holding a token the server has already
retired.

The eviction sits in a finally, so a renewal that fails releases its lock too.

docs(gateways): correct two comments that describe behaviour the code no longer has (review round 1, D16)

why they are worth the commit.

The plane-switch module said `env` is read per call so a test can set the
variable without rebuilding the app. The attribute is read per call, but the
value behind it is a Pydantic field default parsed from the environment when the
class is defined, so setting the variable later changes nothing. A test patches
the attribute directly, which is what every case in the plane-flags suite
already does.

The runner's permission table said the wire's server name IS the connection's
stable key and the gateway route is `custom/{name}`. That was true until the

and a credential-resolution failure each leave the relay without an audit event.

Deferred rather than fixed. The two early checks sit before the authorization

perf(api): only scan for a name collision when the name moved (review round 1, D12)

Both reviewers flagged that the display-name check reads every connection in the

fix(api): D6 keep a client registration the grants issued against it still need

Reworked onto D14, which addresses a registration by slug instead of searching
for it.

Closing OR78 made a connect re-register whenever the stored registration did not
cover the current callback address. The fresh registration then overwrote the one
mutable row this deployment kept per issuer, and every grant already issued was
bound to the old client. Their renewals presented the new one, and an
authorization server refuses a refresh from a client it never issued those tokens
to. So OR78 traded a connection that could not connect for connections that
silently stopped refreshing, which is the quieter failure of the two.

A registration is now addressed by the issuer AND the callback address it was
created with, so a changed address writes a NEW row and leaves the old one where
it is. A grant records which registration issued it, and a renewal reads that one
rather than whatever the issuer holds by the time it runs. An old registration
therefore survives for as long as a grant references it. There is no collection
step: deleting one would mean proving no grant in the project still names it, the
rows are small, and the retention is the property the fix is for.

D14's two properties are kept and extended rather than replaced. Lookups still
come before the scan, now one lookup per candidate slug, and the scan is still
the last resort for a row under an older naming or with no slug at all; such a
row is returned with whatever slug it actually carries, so a grant referencing it
either addresses it or falls back to the same search rather than to a slug
nothing is stored under. D14's issuer check moved into the shared per-slug read,
so every path keeps it.

Nothing needs migrating. A grant written before the reference carries none and
resolves the issuer's registration, which is exactly where it was already being
resolved, and every registration written before this is under that same issuer
slug, which stays in both the read and the write path for a caller that knows no
callback address.

The identity-document strategy is unaffected: it persists no registration, so its
grants record none and rebuild the client deterministically as before.

Four tests. The regression itself, driven through a mock authorization server
that issues a distinct client per registration and refuses a refresh from the
wrong one: connection A connects, the address changes, B's connect re-registers,
and A still renews. Plus the bookkeeping it rests on, the no-reference fallback,
and a grant whose registration is gone getting no substitute, because any other
client at that issuer was never issued its tokens.

One existing assertion inverted rather than added to. It asserted that the fresh
registration replaced the stale one, which is the defect stated as an
expectation; it now asserts the old row survives beside the new.

fix(runner): D10 refuse a wire name two configured servers answer to

Reworked onto D2 (8a2a59f76a) so there is one rule rather than two mechanisms
for one situation.

D2 refuses a rendered tool name more than one configured server could claim. It
does not reach this case, and the new test says why: D2 enumerates its candidates
from the permission table's KEYS, and two servers named Acme are one key, so the
split is unambiguous and the collision has already been decided by the map before
D2's code runs. Two different ambiguities — D2's is in parsing the rendered name,
this one is in which connection the name denotes.

So intake marks the name ambiguous instead of overwriting, and mcpToolPermission
refuses an ambiguous entry with D2's own verdict. That is the one place all three
consumers read: the ACP gate, the Pi gate, and the Pi extension's registration
filter, which now declines to advertise such a server's tools at all. Putting the
refusal in the ACP resolver instead would have left both Pi paths deferring.

The collapse-to-single-verdict merge is dropped. A merged verdict would be a
second, quieter policy nobody configured, which is the objection to two
mechanisms restated.

Deferring is not an option here either. The run's default permission is
allow_reads out of the box and may be an authored allow, so "we could not tell"
would become execution. The operator configured a policy for each candidate;
running under neither is not a choice this code gets to make.

The logging stays, once per colliding name at intake. D2's refusal is per call
and says nothing about why two servers share a name; this is the line that tells
an operator which name to fix.

Eight cases: both declaration orders, neither naming a permission, a per-tool
allow one of them declared, distinctly named servers left alone, the log, and the
two that pin the boundary — a shared name reports resolved to D2 while still
answering deny, and D2's own prefix pair still reports ambiguous.

fix(api): let the credential write's tenant refusal reach its caller (review round 1, D20)

The new bind method carried a bare exception suppressor, so the refusal raised
when a write would bind a credential the project does not own was swallowed and
the method returned None.

Tenant isolation held either way: the exception aborts the transaction before
the commit, so nothing cross-tenant was ever written. What was lost is the typed
refusal. The sibling edit method already excludes this exception for exactly
that reason, and the bind now matches it.

Both callers also stop reporting a write that produced no row as a success.
Disconnect answered count 1 with no endpoint, which says the authorization is
gone while the connection still names it; it now answers not found. The connect
callback showed the success card, which is worse, because the grant is written
before the connection is pointed at it, so a person was told they were connected
over a connection that still read as needing authorization; it now shows the
failure card.

That is the same "a success that did nothing" shape this branch already fixed
once for create, and the reading recorded in the comment above it.

fix(api): invalidate a credential only while the connection still holds it (review round 1, D21)

The narrow remainder of the race D3 closed. Invalidate guarded only against the
handle being absent, which covers a disconnect landing while a doomed call is in
flight. It did not cover a reconnect that landed with a different credential: the
late failure saw a handle that was not None, marked the connection invalid, and
a freshly repaired connection read as needing another reconnect.

The relay now passes the handle the call was actually made with, and the write
happens only while the stored handle still equals it. That is a precondition,
not a value to write, so it keeps the property the original change was
protecting: what the relay read before dialling out is never written back, since
the connection may have been reconfigured during the round trip.

Nothing was lost or exposed by the old behaviour. The cost was one unnecessary
reconnect in a narrow race.
docs(gateways): verify the round-1 fixes for D6 and D10

docs(gateways): record what a host-side gateway integration run needs

The gateway integration suites reach Postgres on a published port but name compose
hostnames for Redis and the mock upstreams, which a container resolves and the host
does not. Run from outside the network the Redis half fails misleadingly: the cache
sits in front of the endpoint lookup, so a whole-directory run reports a different
connection missing each time while every file passes on its own. That is why a green
single-file run has been worth less than it looked.

The preconditions now list all five addresses such a run has to override, note that
Redis is the one service compose does not publish, and record that the two mock
upstream addresses are needed by the OAuth endpoint-write and recovery suites as
well, not only by the mock upstream tests.

Also recorded: the mock upstreams are single-process, so under pytest's default
parallelism their HTTP tests occasionally time out behind the deliberately slow one.
Serial runs are deterministic.

feat(gateways): give the mock OAuth issuer a registration endpoint

Consent against the mock could not complete on a stack that is not publicly
resolvable. The issuer advertised no registration endpoint, which leaves the
gateway only the client-identity document, and that branch requires the
deployment's own API URL to be public https. A loopback stack therefore got 424
"advertises no registration endpoint" every time, so the mock could not stand in
for a real provider on the machine where the flow is developed.

It now advertises and implements RFC 7591 registration by default, which is the
branch Linear and Axiom take: a client-id metadata document is a draft almost
nothing implements. Registration binds the client to the redirect URIs it was
given and authorize refuses any other callback, so a stale registration cannot
pass as working, which is the failure registration_covers exists to catch.

The identity-document branch keeps a second issuer at /noreg, sharing the
authorize and token endpoints. That is legitimate: the client compares the issuer
identifier and never checks where the endpoints live. Because that issuer carries
a path it also covers the RFC 8414 s3.1 path-inserted metadata location, which
nothing reached before, every real issuer met so far being path-less.

test(gateways): cover both ways the gateway names itself to an issuer

The consent suite only ever met an issuer that offered no registration, so it
covered one branch of client identity and, since that branch needs a publicly
resolvable API URL, covered it nowhere the flow is actually developed.

Two tests close that. One pins the mock to refusing a callback the client did
not register: without it a gateway that never re-registered a stale client would
still pass every other test here. The other drives the issuer that offers no
registration, asserting the gateway names itself with the URL of the identity
document it publishes. On a deployment that is not publicly resolvable it asserts
the 424 refusal instead and then skips, saying which address it was reached at
and why the branch cannot be taken there.

That second issuer carries a path, so the test also covers the path-inserted
metadata location for the first time.
docs(gateways): verify D20 and D21 and close review round 1

refactor(api): share the gateway run claims and the plane-disabled refusal

Four call sites read `gateway_run_id` off request state with their own `getattr`
and their own idea of what counts as present: two required a non-empty string,
two took whatever was there. One accessor pair in `core/gateways/run_claims.py`
now answers both questions, so a change to the claim has one place to follow.

`flags._refuse` and `handle_gateway_exceptions` each assembled the same 403 and
envelope for a switched-off plane; a router dependency refuses before the
decorator wraps anything, so both surfaces stay, but they now share the
assembly.

Also collapses two identical `_as_edit` flag branches, merges the two mock
adapter tool-result shapes that read the same key, computes
`_contains_tool_result` once per relay instead of twice, and corrects the
`_find_grant` docstring, which claimed the old scan sat on the relay path. It
did not: a relayed call reads its credential through the endpoint's `secret_id`.

refactor(sdk): drop two derivable values from the gateway fallback path

`_llm_gateway_is_unavailable` took the HTTP status beside the refusal built
from it, so two parameters carried one fact. The refusal already records the
gateway's status as `gateway_status`; read it there.

`MCPPolicy.is_per_tool` was a public property with one private caller. Inlining
the condition keeps the opt-in rule beside the resolution that depends on it
and stops the model publishing API surface nothing consumes.

refactor(runner): overlap MCP handshakes and drop three redundant lookups

`registerPiGatewayMcpTools` runs on `before_agent_start`, so every turn waits on
it, and it discovered each configured server in turn. A `discover()` is three
round trips through the gateway to the upstream, so N servers cost 3xN
sequential hops before the first token. The handshakes now run together and the
results are consumed in configuration order, which is what the collision rules
depend on; only the I/O overlaps. Each server keeps the client its handshake
opened, so a tool call still reuses that connection.

`splitMcpToolName` found the table entry, returned its key, and left the caller
to look the entry up again. It now returns the entry it already had.

`normalizeMcpServerPermissions` computed two intermediate booleans and a nested
`if` for one ladder; written as the ladder, it reads in the order its docstring
states the rules. And the Pi extension, which already imports this module, kept
its own `isRecord` beside the imported one, so both were compiled into the same
bundle.

refactor(api): lift the shared OAuth integration fixtures into the conftest

`project` and `connect_service` were defined identically in both new MCP OAuth
integration suites, 48 lines in two places for the same two objects. Moved to
the directory conftest, where the provider and the seeded project they build on
already live. No call site changes: pytest resolves both by name.

refactor(api): share the LLM-plane skip and correct the tool-prefix comment

Three sites asked whether the deployment serves the LLM gateway plane and each
carried its own copy of the reason string. The two inline copies exist for a
real reason, a class-scoped setup fixture is refused before a function-scoped
skip runs, so they stay as call sites of one shared callable rather than a
fixture.

`tool_prefix` claimed to be exactly the runner's normalization. It is not: it
strips surrounding whitespace first and `piMcpToolName` does not. The comment
now states the difference, which direction it errs in, and why converging it is
a behaviour decision rather than a cleanup.
docs(gateways): reconcile the MCP release status with candidate 1

fix(hosting): stop unrelated edits from restarting the gateway mocks

Both mock services run uvicorn with a bare --reload, which watches everything
mounted at /app, and this image mounts the whole api source tree. Any edit
anywhere under api/oss/src therefore restarted them. On a shared dev box that
happens continually, and a restart kills whatever request was in flight, which
is the occasional timeout seen in integration/gateways/test_mock_upstreams.py on
a host-side run.

It also wipes the mock OAuth issuer's registered clients, authorization codes
and bearer tokens, which are process-local by design, so a consent flow spanning
a restart fails for a reason nothing reports.

They now watch the gateway code these apps are, plus utils for the env they
read, the way the services container already scopes its own reload dirs.

Adding workers would not fix this and would break the issuer: its state lives in
one process, so a second worker would answer with no knowledge of a client the
first one registered. There is nothing to serialise either, both mock slow paths
await rather than block, and a health check answers in three milliseconds while
a thirty-second request and ten twenty-second tool calls are in flight.

fix(web): let the connect journey finish

Running the new acceptance spec against a stack found three defects that reading
the code had not.

The journey never left tool discovery. Reaching "connected" moves it to a busy
state that waits for a tool list, and nothing ever fetched one, so the dialog sat
with both footer buttons disabled and no way to close it. Every case that
connects a server hung there. The hook now reads the tools and the dialog drives
it, so the journey reaches a terminal state whether the list arrives or not: a
connection whose tools cannot be read is still connected.

The connected state showed two buttons both labelled "Done", one of them
disabled, because the footer renders a cancel and a confirm and neither had
anything left to say. ModalFooter can now hide its cancel, and a finished journey
shows one action.

Closing a finished journey went through the cancel path. Nothing is cancelled by
closing a connection that succeeded, so it now closes directly.

The spec closes the journey in every case that connects, which is what surfaced
the first defect: the next step is behind the dialog.

chore(ci): ignore two test placeholders gitleaks flags in an earlier commit

gitleaks fails this branch on two matches in a credential-normalization test. The
value it matched is the literal sk-live-abc123, written to show that a key pasted
with a trailing newline gets trimmed. It was never a credential and nothing leaked.

The tip is already clean: 20ac2f008d replaced that literal with
placeholder-provider-key, and the branch tip contains no occurrence of it. The scan
fails anyway because gitleaks reads the pushed commit range rather than the working
tree, so a later correction cannot clear the commit that introduced the string.

Fingerprints are anchored to a commit, a file and a line. Both lines must be
regenerated if this branch is ever rebased or squashed, and they belong last in the
sequence before a final push, or they silently stop matching and the scan fails
again. Verified: the range scan reports no leaks with these two lines present.

chore(ci): repeat the organization's CodeRabbit exclusions in this branch's filters

The first review of #6049 ran with the organization's lock-file and generated-code
exclusions dropped. Asking @coderabbitai configuration returned a path_filters list
sourced entirely from "Repository YAML (base)" holding only this file's entries, so
for that field a repository list replaces the organization's rather than appending to
it, and inheritance: true does not change that.

Nothing broke, because the review still fitted under the file cap. The cost was that
a lock file, a generated JSON and five generated Fern client types were reviewed as
though someone had written them, which spends review attention and invites findings
against files that are regenerated rather than edited.

The three patterns are now repeated at the top of the block, marked as belonging to
the organization so a later reader keeps them in step by hand. The status note records
the replacement behavior, since it applies to any array a repository config sets, and
carries the corrected file count.

fix(api): keep a grant's client registration across renewals (review round 2, D24)

The reader that resolves which registration a stored grant was issued against
returned it without recording which one it had resolved. The token write
persists whatever that field holds, so the first renewal rewrote the grant with
no registration reference at all.

The pin therefore survived the consent and died on the first refresh, and every
refresh after that fell back to resolving whatever registration the issuer holds
now. That is the failure D6 closed, reappearing one renewal later: once a
deployment's public address has changed there are two registrations at one
issuer, and the fallback can return the client these tokens were never issued
against, so the refresh is refused and a working connection dies until someone
reconnects it.

Both branches now record what they resolved. The pinned branch records the
grant's own reference even when the row behind it has been deleted, because a
slug naming a registration that is gone still says which client these tokens
belong to, and dropping it would silently downgrade the next renewal to
"whatever this issuer has now". The by-issuer branch records the slug the row
was actually found under, so a grant written before the reference existed gains
one and the renewal after it is pinned.

D6's test connected, changed the address, and refreshed once, which is why this
survived it. The new case refreshes twice and asserts the reference after each.
fix(sdk): D37 generate Claude MCP rules that resolve the way the runner gate does

fix(api): compare the credential a reconnect changes, not the row that holds it (review round 2, D33)

The D21 fix skipped invalidation when the connection no longer held the handle
the failing call used. That handle is the vault row's id, and an OAuth reconnect
does not change it: the grant is found by the slug the connection's identity
derives and rewritten in place, so the row keeps its id and only the tokens
inside it change.

A late 401 earned by the old token therefore still passed the check and marked a
freshly repaired connection invalid. D21's test substituted a different secret
row, which is the disconnect-then-connect path; the Reconnect button does not go
that way, and neither does a token refresh, which replaces the tokens in the
same row for the same reason.

The relay now passes the access token it actually sent, and the connection is
marked invalid only while it still holds that token. The row-id precondition
stays in the write, where it is transactional and covers the disconnect.

Nothing was lost by the old behaviour and the state corrected itself on the next
reconnect. What it cost was a person being told their repair had not worked.

test(services): skip the LLM-plane acceptance cells when the plane is off

CI failed test_agent_gateway_refusal.py for all three harnesses with
failure_code None instead of endpoint_not_found. The cause is the new default:
AGENTA_LLM_GATEWAY_ENABLED ships off and nothing in .github/workflows sets it,
so the preview deployment serves no LLM gateway. The resolver then falls back
to the vault, finds no connection under a never-registered slug, and raises
ConnectionNotFoundError, which carries the same 422 and no failure code. Only
the control-plane test failed because it is the one cell that provisions
nothing, so it is not already skipped by the gateway-mocks gate.

The suites now ask the deployment which planes it serves, the way the api
acceptance suites do, and skip naming the variable to set. The probe is a
module-scoped fixture matching mod_api, and the skip is a plain function so a
provisioning fixture can call it in its own body: these suites register
endpoints through the very routes that are refused, so a skip that runs merely
before the test is too late.

This buys back a green CI at the cost of no coverage for these cells until a
deployment turns the plane on.

chore(railway): serve the LLM gateway in preview environments

The plane ships off, so a preview deployment served no LLM gateway and the
acceptance cells that prove a gateway refusal reaches the caller with its code
skipped themselves. A preview is a test environment rather than a default
self-host, so it opts in and keeps the coverage.

Declared on the api service beside AGENTA_INSECURE_EGRESS_ALLOWED, which is
the only service that reads it; the MCP plane needs no entry because it
defaults on. The reason lives in notes.gateway-planes, since JSON carries no
comments.

Per the template change protocol this is additive-first: it reaches clones
only once apply.sh converges the live template, and until then the daily drift
check fails by design.
docs(gateways): verify the round-2 fixes for D22, D24, D33 and D37

fix(api): give discovery its own write instead of replaying the endpoint row (review round 2, D31)

The API half of the finding. The connect route's discovery step read the
connection, made an outbound call, and then wrote the whole row back from the
snapshot it had read, carrying that snapshot's secret_id and flags over anything
that had happened in between.

D3 narrowed the service's credential writes and did not reach this route, which
is why it survived. The window is real but narrow: a slow discovery has to
overlap a callback writing a grant.

Discovery now writes the one key it owns, merged into the row as it stands
inside the transaction, the same shape as the two credential transitions. With
that, the helper that built these full replacements has no callers left and goes
with it, so no route can express a credential lifecycle change as a row
replacement any more.

The duplicate discovery call the finding also names is in the web layer and
belongs to that agent.

fix(api): bound what the probe reads and how long it waits (review round 2, D38)

The probe dials an address a person just typed, so both the size of the answer
and the time it takes were the far end's choice. The body was buffered whole
before anything looked at it, and the client's timeout is an inactivity timeout,
so a server sending one byte just inside it kept a worker occupied indefinitely.

The handshake is now streamed and stopped at a megabyte, which is generous
against a real handshake of a few kilobytes, and the whole exchange sits under a
total elapsed deadline of twice the inactivity timeout. A server that exceeds
either is reported the way any other unusable server is, through the probe's own
result rather than an exception: too much data reads as not an MCP server, and
too slow reads as unreachable.

The bytes that were read are handed on as an ordinary response, so everything
downstream parses the handshake the way it always has.

The caller must hold the permission to edit connections, so this is an
authorized capability rather than an open one, which is why it is a bound rather
than a redesign.

fix(web): start a new connect journey on every opening

The journey's state lives in a hook inside the dialog, and the settings section
and the chat widget both keep the component rendered while toggling `open`. So a
second opening landed on the previous journey's final screen, with no URL field
in sight and nothing to do but close it again. The component now renders nothing
while closed, which unmounts the hook and starts a fresh journey each time.

Found by the acceptance spec: the three cases that open the journey twice were
the three that failed, and no other.

The spec also stops addressing the journey as "the last dialog". The settings
page mounts the connection detail drawer, which is a dialog too, so the last one
is whichever the DOM happens to order last; both the fill and the close were
landing on the wrong element and the close then passed while the journey was
still open. It is addressed by the dialog containing the journey's test id
instead, which is what that id is for.

The OAuth case was missing its close, so every later step in it ran behind an
open dialog.
fix(api): restore a measured Codex fallback so the harness matrix tests the call it claims
docs(gateways): verify the round-2 fix for D23

test(web): cover tool discovery after a connect (D22)

The fix landed without the test the finding asks for, so nothing stopped the
driver being removed again. The reducer's tools states each had their own test
and all of them passed while the journey was unfinishable, because the defect
was never in the reducer: nothing dispatched them.

These drive the hook instead, which is where the gap was. They assert the tools
are read for the connection just made, that an empty list reads as empty rather
than as a failure, that an unreadable one leaves the connection connected and
retryable without going back to consent, and that a retry re-reads without
connecting again. One asserts the symptom directly: the journey does not come to
rest in `discovering_tools`, which is a busy state and therefore a dialog with
both footer buttons disabled and no way out.

They mock the api module the hook imports rather than the package barrel. The
barrel is the wrong seam here and a test that mocks it passes while the hook
talks to the real client.

fix(web): bind each connect attempt to its own connection (D23)

The journey reads `reconnect` twice and only at mount, in the reducer's lazy
initializer and in the ref that holds the endpoint. The settings section keeps
the component rendered and toggles `open`, and destroyOnClose destroys the
modal's children rather than the component that owns the hook, so a second
opening inherited the first attempt's state. Reconnect opened at URL entry with
no endpoint bound, which repairs nothing and, carried through, makes a second
connection to a server that already had one.

The component already unmounts itself while closed, which covers open and close.
This adds the other way in: a key per attempt, so choosing a different
connection while one is open rebuilds the controller rather than keeping the
endpoint it was mounted with.

The tests assert what a mount is for. A reconnect starts in scope discovery,
bound to its endpoint and slug, never re-probing a URL nobody is choosing, and
keeping the name someone already picked so discovery cannot overwrite it. It
also cannot delete the connection it is repairing. A fresh attempt after one has
run starts at URL entry with nothing carried over, and a second reconnect binds
the connection it names rather than the first one's.
docs(gateways): verify the round-2 fixes for D31 and D38 and open their two residuals

fix(web): speak the whole MCP handshake when listing a server's tools

D32. The browser's tool-list client sent `initialize` and then `tools/list` with
nothing between them, read only a decoded JSON body, and turned everything it
could not read into an empty array. A conforming server that enforces
`notifications/initialized`, or that answers over an event stream, therefore
appeared as a connected server exposing no tools, which left the permission
editor with nothing to edit and gave no sign that the conversation had failed.

It now speaks the sequence the specification describes and the runner's own
client already uses: `initialize`, `notifications/initialized`, `tools/list`,
carrying the negotiated protocol version and any session id, declaring both
answer shapes it accepts, and following the pages a cursor announces. A refusal
or an unreadable answer raises with the server's own wording, which the three
callers already render as a failure state. An empty `tools` array still means a
server with no tools.

The data plane refuses in JSON-RPC rather than in `detail`, so the gateway
refusal reader learned that envelope too.

fix(web): read the MCP gateway switch the way the API reads it

D35. `AGENTA_MCP_GATEWAY_ENABLED=0` stopped the API and left the whole
interface standing. The API parses the flag against its `_TRUTHY` set, so `0`,
`off` and `no` all turn the plane off there; the browser read only the literal
"false" as off, and `entrypoint.sh` flattened every other value to "true"
before the browser ever saw it. The operator was left with an MCP settings tab,
a connect journey and an agent-config surface whose every request the API
answers with a 403.

Both halves now parse the flag as `_parse_bool_env` does: unset or blank takes
the default, which stays on, and anything else is on only when it is one of the
spellings the API accepts. `isSandboxLocalEnabled` was already carrying its own
copy of that vocabulary and now shares the one parser.

The entrypoint block is covered by running the script's own text, so a later
edit to it cannot leave the test passing against a copy.

fix(web): keep an undeclared custom connection undeclared on save

D36. A custom endpoint connection whose record declared no protocol opened the
card on the form's OpenAI default, and the form sent `protocol` on every save.
A name-only edit therefore turned that default into a declaration, and a
declared protocol gates harness eligibility: an Anthropic-compatible gateway
narrowed this way loses every Claude Code row in the model picker, which the
code already warns about in `declaredEndpointProtocol`.

The card now holds "declares none" as a state of its own. A connection being
created declares the default, since the person is describing the endpoint as
they make it. An existing record declares what it already declared, and one
that declared nothing keeps declaring nothing until someone presses the
control. The control still shows the default so the keyboard and the thumb
behave; showing it is not the same act as saving it.

This runs whether or not the LLM gateway plane is enabled.

test(api): prove the discovery write keeps a credential bound beside it (review round 2, D31 residual)

The unit cases for the narrow discovery write use a store that merges by
construction: a dictionary that assigns only the key it is handed cannot lose a
column, so they could not have caught the defect they cover.

This drives the real column. It reads the connection the way the connect route
does before dialling out, binds a grant the way a callback landing meanwhile
does, then performs discovery's write from that pre-call snapshot and asserts
the handle is still there, along with the connection's route, tool filter,
settings and name.

Confirmed load-bearing by making the write clear the handle, which turns it red.
docs(gateways): record the D22 and D23 test cover and what it does not reach
docs(gateways): record candidate 2 and review round 2 in the release status

fix(api): bound the metadata fetches a challenged probe makes (review round 2, D46)

The handshake got an elapsed deadline and a size cap; the branch a 401 takes did
not. That branch is discovery, which walks several candidate URLs, each with its
own inactivity timeout, so the guarded path could outlast the guarded-against
one.

Every URL discovery dials is attacker-influenced. The server URL is tenant data,
the protected-resource location arrives in the server's own challenge, and the
endpoints below it come from the issuer's metadata. A metadata document is a
small JSON object either way, so each fetch now reads with a cap and a candidate
that exceeds it is skipped the way any other unusable candidate already is,
ending in the discovery error the probe already turns into a result.

The whole discovery now also sits under the same elapsed deadline as the
handshake, reported through the probe's own result as authorization it could not
read in time rather than as an exception.

The cap is on the OAuth client rather than the probe, so the connect flow's own
discovery gets it too; the deadline stays on the probe, which is the
unauthenticated path a person's typed address reaches first.

test(web): run the MCP browser suite by default (D25, D26)

All seven cases skipped unless AGENTA_MOCK_MCP_GATEWAY_URL was set, and the
OAuth case needed a second variable. Neither is set anywhere in the repository,
so the only end-to-end coverage this feature has never ran and every run
reported green. That is how D22 reached a review: a suite that would have caught
it was invisible.

The mock URL is defaulted to the compose address instead of gating on it, and
the two skips are gone. A stack without the mock upstream now fails once, in
`beforeAll`, with a sentence naming what to bring up, rather than seven times
with a sixty-second timeout apiece. A run without the host-resolver mapping
fails with the exact line to re-run with, because the consent page is the half
of the flow only a browser can prove and a run that quietly drops it is the
failure mode this finding is about.

It is deliberately not wired into the Railway workflow. That job points at a
deployed preview which runs no mock container, so enabling it there would fail
for the absence of a fixture rather than for a defect, and a red CI that means
nothing teaches people to ignore it. The release status now says in those words
that this is a manual gate step, why, and what would close the gap.

All seven pass against the integrated EE dev stack, with no MCP variables
exported, which is the recorded pass that row was owed. D26 goes with it: the
suite could not pass while the modal stayed open, and it does now.

test(api): stop the loopback refusals depending on the shell they run in (review round 2, D47)

Two cases assert that a loopback address is refused, and both turned green for
the wrong reason when the documented host-side mock URLs and the mocks flag were
exported: the exempt-host list then contains loopback, so the address under test
was exempt and the guard never ran.

That is the shape this project has been bitten by before, a check that reports a
pass while testing nothing, and it is reachable by following the mock
documentation.

Both modules now clear every source of exemption for their own run: the operator
host allowlist, which the adapter module already cleared, and the mocks flag,
which neither did. Verified by running the suite with the variables exported,
with the flag alone, and with neither.

Cleared rather than asserted, so the cases mean the same thing from any shell.
The exemption itself stays covered where it belongs, beside the function that
grants it.
docs(gateways): record how the D32 and D35 fixes were verified

test(web): make the journey tests render the product (D48)

The D22 and D23 suites drive the hook and supply the step the product is meant
to take: the test calls the tool loader, and the test unmounts. So deleting the
effect that starts discovery, or the wrapper that unmounts a closed journey,
left all thirteen green. A test that performs the behaviour it is checking
proves nothing about the code that was supposed to perform it.

Two rendered cases, one per finding, touching only the controls a person
touches. A connected journey lists its tools with nobody calling the loader, and
a journey closed and reopened through a host that keeps it mounted — which is
what the settings section does — asks for a URL again rather than reopening on
the previous attempt.

Both were checked against their own defect: removing the discovery effect fails
the first and nothing else, removing the wrapper fails the second and nothing
else.

Two things cost time here and are worth leaving written down. The dialog renders
through a portal, so a query scoped to the host node finds nothing and the
symptom looks like a component that rendered nothing at all. And the fields do
not label themselves the same way: the URL field carries an aria-label matching
its visible label, while the name field's visible label is "Name" and its
accessible name is "Connection name", so a helper that only reads one of the two
mechanisms silently finds nothing.
fix(runner): CR9 stop the MCP handshake probe following redirects with credentials

fix(hosting): allocate the gateway mock ports per stack (CR8)

The two mock gateways were the only services in the dev compose files publishing a
literal host port. Every other published port is templated and allocated per worktree
by env.sh, so a second dev stack on one machine failed to bind 9091 and 9092 and the
mocks never came up.

Both ports are now templated with a default matching the old literal, so an existing
stack keeps the addresses it has, and env.sh allocates them alongside the others on
both paths: derived from --port-offset, or from the free-port search, where each new
port also excludes the ones already chosen so the two mocks cannot collide with each
other or with Postgres, Traefik and the store.

OSS is fixed with EE. The finding named the EE file, but the same two literals sit in
the OSS dev compose and the collision is identical there.

Verified: bash -n passes; an offset allocation yields 9791 and 9792, and a free-port
allocation yields two distinct ports outside the existing set; both compose files
still parse.

fix(hosting): resolve an output path whose parent does not exist yet (M3)

absolute_path resolved a path by cd-ing into its parent, which fails when the parent
has not been created. Under set -euo pipefail that aborts the script, and it aborts
before the mkdir -p further down would have created the directory, so env.sh could
not write an allocation to a new folder even though it creates folders itself.

realpath -m resolves a path whose trailing components are still missing, which is
exactly what --output needs.

Verified: bash -n passes; an allocation to a two-level path that does not exist now
completes, and a real run creates the directory and writes the file.

fix(hosting): name the prepared env file in the printed start command (M2)

prepare accepts --output and writes the merged environment wherever it points, then
printed a start command with no --env-file. Copying that command starts the stack from
whichever env file the edition defaults to, so a prepared file at any other name is
silently ignored and the stack comes up on the wrong ports and project name.

The command now carries --env-file with the file's basename, which is the form run.sh
documents and resolves against the edition directory.

Verified: bash -n passes, and a prepare to a custom output prints
run.sh --ee --dev --env-file <that file>.

fix(api): resolve this deployment's own address off the event loop (CodeRabbit M18)

The check for whether the deployment can name itself to an authorization server
calls socket.getaddrinfo, which blocks and carries no timeout of its own. Both
callers are coroutines, so a slow or unreachable resolver stalled every request
the worker was serving rather than the one that asked.

The lookup now goes to a thread and the wait is bounded. A timeout answers
false, which is already the answer for an address that does not resolve, and
both callers read false as this deployment being unable to name itself: the
consent path falls back to dynamic registration or reports the server as
unusable, and the probe reports the same before anyone consents. That is the
reading a genuine resolution failure already got.

The judgement itself stays synchronous and is what the async wrapper delegates
to, so the cases that inject a resolver keep exercising the logic directly.

Three new cases cover what the finding is about rather than only its symptom:
the resolver runs off the loop's thread, a resolver that never answers costs one
coroutine, and other work on the loop keeps running while it is stuck.
