docs(gateways): record CodeRabbit's first completed review of this branch

CodeRabbit had refused this pull request since 2026-08-14, answering every push with
"Review skipped: 518 files exceed the limit of 300" and reporting that refusal as a
passing check. This is the first review it actually performed, obtained by scoping the
branch's own path filters below the cap.

It posted 39 findings, not the 19 the inline comments suggest: 20 more sit in a
collapsed section of the review summary that is easy to miss. Each is dispositioned
against the following candidate, with a fix revision where one exists.

Five bear on shipping the MCP gateway: a credentialed handshake probe that follows
redirects past the SSRF guard, a cancel that deletes a connection whose credentials
are already stored, a tool list fetched with an incomplete handshake, policy
identifiers that diverge from the bytes forwarded upstream, and a hidden tool whose
permission cannot be cleared. Four findings are wrong and the file says why, so a
later pass does not re-raise them.

The file also records what the filter block got wrong: inheritance does not merge that
array, so the organization's exclusions were dropped and the review ran at 270 files
with seven generated files read as though hand-written.

fix(api): refuse a padded MCP identifier instead of trimming it (CodeRabbit M15)

The call-context parser stripped whitespace from the JSON-RPC method and from
the tool name, and the adapters forward the request body unchanged. So the two
could disagree: policy evaluated echo and per-tool permissions were checked
against echo, while the upstream received the padded string and the audit record
named the trimmed one.

The parser's own docstring said it reads policy fields without changing
forwarded bytes, which was true of the bytes and not of the identifiers read out
of them.

A padded identifier is now refused, which the proxy already renders as an
invalid request. Repairing it is exactly what made the two disagree, and nothing
legitimate is refused: a JSON-RPC method is a fixed protocol token and a tool
name has to match what the server advertised, so neither carries surrounding
whitespace in a request that could have worked.

Only the ends. Interior spacing is the caller's string and is the string the
upstream is given.

build(api): pin the MCP SDK to the version the contract test asserts (CodeRabbit M16)

The constraint allowed anything from 2.1.1 up to 3 while the contract case
beside the OAuth storage asserts the installed version is exactly 2.1.1. The two
agreed only because the lock happened to hold that version; any relock that
moved within the range would have turned the branch red with a failure nobody
had changed anything to cause.

The comment above the constraint already said to keep it exact. It now is, and
the lock is regenerated against it.

Keeping it exact is deliberate rather than tidiness: this branch uses the SDK's
TokenStorage protocol and its OAuth wire models directly, so a minor release can
change a contract the gateway depends on without changing anything here.

fix(api): give the OAuth callback a way back when the popup was blocked (D27)

The callback page posts to `window.opener` and then closes itself. On the
blocked-popup path there is no opener, and a browser ignores `window.close` for
a tab a script did not open, so the person was left on the API's origin reading
that the tab would close in three seconds, with the app they came from destroyed
by the same-tab navigation. Mobile browsers and in-app webviews refuse popups far
more readily than desktop, and the mobile app is the production default.

The page now picks its behaviour once it can see which arrival it is. With an
opener it posts and closes as before. Without one it says it is taking the person
back and returns the tab to the connections list on the app's origin, after a
refusal as well as after a success, because a refusal is where the way back
matters most. Both lines ship hidden and the script reveals the one that applies,
so no arrival is told about a tab that will never close.

A deployment that publishes no app URL neither posts nor redirects: with no
origin to trust there is nowhere safe to send anyone.

The comment on the web side claimed the callback already returned the person to
where they were. It did not. It now says what the path costs, which is the app
state, and why.

fix(web): verify a manual credential against the server (D28)

The manual path saved a reference to a secret and dispatched success. Nothing
asked the server anything, though the state is called `verifying` and the person
is told "Verifying…". A wrong header name or a wrong secret read as connected,
and the first sign otherwise was an agent run failing much later, a long way from
the form that caused it.

It now performs one authenticated handshake through the gateway, which injects
the credential and surfaces the upstream's refusal, and reports that refusal as a
failed verification instead of a connection.

The same finding notes that recovery was OAuth-only: the connect route refuses a
non-OAuth endpoint, so Reconnect on a key-authenticated connection could only
produce "endpoint is not a custom OAuth target" on the one action offered to
repair it. A reconnect now goes to the credential step for a connection that
authorizes with a key, and to scope discovery only for one that has scopes, so
each is repaired by the thing that repairs it.

The reconnect callers pass the auth mode they already hold. The reducer cases
that predate this say `oauth` explicitly rather than leaning on a default, since
the branch is the point.

fix(clients): restore the generated client's Python floor to 3.11 (CodeRabbit M6)

The generator writes the client's pyproject from scratch on every run, and this
branch raised the floor in that heredoc to 3.12. The API, the SDK and the
committed client all declare 3.11, so the next regeneration would have made a
3.11 install unsatisfiable, and the client would no longer install beside the
SDK that calls it.

Only the script was wrong. The committed client still declares 3.11, so nothing
was regenerated with the raised floor and nothing needs regenerating now, which
is just as well: regeneration reads the OpenAPI document from a running
deployment, and doing it to correct one constant would pull in every unrelated
drift since the last run.

A case beside the client's own tests now reads the floor out of the generator
and asserts it matches what the repository declares, and that the three Python
packages here agree with each other. Read from the files rather than by
regenerating, for the same reason.

fix(api): deregister the endpoint a kind-changing secret update leaves behind (CodeRabbit CR4)

The update merge permits a secret to change kind, and endpoint registration
returns early for every kind but custom provider. So an update that moved a row
off custom provider registered nothing and deregistered nothing, and the
endpoint stayed behind naming a secret that is no longer a custom provider, with
no later write reaching it.

The previous row is now captured under the DAO's write lock, the way the delete
path already captures the row it deregisters, and an endpoint is dropped when
the kind moves away from custom provider. Dropped before the new registration
runs, so a row arriving at the same slug is the one that survives.

Inert while the LLM plane is off, which is why it is a data-integrity fix rather
than a release blocker.

The double in these tests could not express the case: it pinned the record's
kind to the stored one, so a kind change was unrepresentable and the new payload
was validated against the old kind. It now takes the resolved kind, like the
real DAO. Three cases: the change deregisters, an ordinary in-place edit does
not churn the endpoint, and the other direction registers without dropping
anything.
fix(runner): M20 screen the model connection environment against the reserved names

fix(api): read a stored client registration defensively (CodeRabbit M8)

Turning a stored OAuth-provider secret into client information read its
registration metadata as a required key. A registration is matched by issuer,
and nothing stops a person creating an OAuth-provider secret of their own at the
same issuer through the vault's public surface, so that key may be absent or
hold anything. Such a row turned the connect path into a 500.

Absent or unusable metadata now reads as no registration, which is the answer
every caller here already handles: it registers a fresh client rather than
presenting one the authorization server never issued. The row is logged, because
a provider secret that cannot be used as one is worth knowing about.

Both readers are covered, the connect path and the renewal path, across metadata
that is missing, wrongly shaped, or present and invalid.

fix(web): stop a cancel from discarding a connection that exists (D29, D30)

Two ways the journey could throw away work it had already done.

Consent succeeds in the callback, server-side, so by the time the dialog reaches
`saving` the provider has issued the credential and the API has stored it.
Cancelling was still treated as cancelling a pending attempt, and Escape or a
mask click reached that path even while the footer's buttons were disabled, so
pressing Escape during the refresh deleted a row whose grant was already live
and orphaned it at the provider. `saving` now counts as connected, so nothing
deletes from there, and the dialog is sealed across that window: no Escape, no
mask click, no X. There is nothing to abandon; the journey moves on by itself.

Retry sent `create_failed` to `creating` and `verify_failed` to `verifying`,
both busy states that nothing re-invokes, so Try again replaced the error with a
spinner that never resolved and disabled both buttons. Those two are retried by
calling the operation again, which is how the URL check always worked, and the
retry table now holds only failures whose target has a driver.

One existing case asserted the broken transition, so it said `verify_failed`
moves to `verifying`. It now says the retry is the caller's to make, which is
the behaviour rather than the bug.

fix(sdk): recognise an agent request by its configuration, not a parameter name (CodeRabbit M10)

The vault middleware skips the project-wide credential prefetch for agent
requests, because an agent resolves its model through the gateway instead. It
decided that from "there is a parameter called agent and it is an object", which
also describes an ordinary workflow whose author happened to name a parameter
that way. Such a workflow ran with an empty vault and nothing said why.

It now also requires at least one key only an agent template defines, so the
match says what it means. Any one of them is enough: the template's keys all
have defaults, so an agent may carry any single one and recognising only some
would send a real agent to the vault.

The keys are listed rather than validated against the model, because this is a
recognition test and must not fail a request by validating it.

Still a recognition rather than a declaration. The request carries no field
saying which kind of workflow it is, and adding one is a wire change for both
sides; the comment says so, and a collision now needs a parameter named agent
that also carries one of those keys.

fix(api): give the mock's text delta the block index every other frame carries (CodeRabbit M5)

Anthropic's stream carries `index` on every content-block event. The mock's text
branch omitted it on the delta while the start and stop events either side of it
carried it, and the tool-use branch's delta carried it too, so a client indexing
deltas by block saw one frame it could not place.

Fixture only, registered behind the mocks flag, which is why it is a correctness
fix on a test double rather than a product defect. It matters because the double
is what the streaming matrix asserts protocol shape against, so a frame it gets
wrong is a frame nothing else will catch.

The new case asserts the property rather than the line: every content-block
frame in the stream names its block, and all three kinds are present so the
delta is genuinely among them.

fix(web): discover a server's scopes once per connect (D31, web half)

`submitName` awaited scope discovery itself, and the transition it had already
dispatched moved the journey to `discovering_scopes`, which fires the effect
that does the same thing. Every OAuth connect ran it twice: two outbound round
trips, and two full-row writes on a route that writes back the snapshot it read,
which also opens a window where a slow discovery restores a secret reference
that is no longer current.

The effect owns the state, so the direct call is gone. The API half, narrowing
that write to the OAuth metadata the route actually owns, is the API agent's.

The test holds discovery in flight while it counts. An instantly-resolving stub
let the direct call finish before React re-rendered, so the effect never saw the
state and the duplicate could not be observed at all: the first two versions of
this test passed with the bug reintroduced. The shape of the defect needs a
discovery that is still running while the component renders, which is also what
happens against a real network.

test(api): make the metadata size cap provable (review round 2, D46 residual)

The two size-cap cases could not tell the cap from a parse failure. They served
half a megabyte of the letter x, which is not JSON, so the candidate was skipped
by the metadata parser whether or not a cap existed and both cases passed
against code with no cap in it at all.

The oversized document is now a valid protected-resource document padded past
the cap with extra scope entries, which the model accepts and keeps. The only
thing standing between it and a successful discovery is its size, so the case
fails when the cap is removed. Confirmed by removing it.

Its counterpart is the same document padded to just under the cap rather than a
small one, so it also says the bound is generous enough for a real document with
a long scope list, instead of only that a tiny document works. The ordinary
small document keeps its own case.

fix(web): let the journey own the attempt in flight (D34, M14, D40)

Every step of the consent path has a window between an await and the thing it
installs, and a cancel or an unmount inside that window left the work to arrive
afterwards and install itself anyway. A `beginMcpConnect` that resolved after a
cancel installed a watch holding a listener, an interval and a three-minute
timeout on a dead attempt. A `createMcpEndpoint` that resolved after a cancel
left a row the cancel had never seen, because it did not exist yet. OR67's
teardown cannot cover either: at that moment there is nothing installed to tear
down.

The journey now carries an attempt generation. Each async step reads it before
its await and checks it after, and a step that comes back to a bumped generation
stops, closing the window it opened or deleting the row it made. Cancel and
unmount both bump it, so the dialog disowns what it started rather than only
releasing what it had already installed.

M14, the same class one layer down: the watch settled on a trusted completion
that named no endpoint, so whichever watch happened to be live took another
attempt's message. A completion now has to name this attempt. The poll and the
timeout still end an attempt whose callback says nothing identifiable, so
requiring it cannot strand one.

D40's remaining coverage goes with them, because it is the same contract: one
window name per attempt, the caller told in advance whether a window is needed
at all so it can open one inside the tap, the same-tab fallback when the window
is refused, and the API's origin as the only one trusted to say a consent
finished.

The five cases in the watch suite that posted a completion without an endpoint
id now carry one, which is what a real callback sends.

docs(gateways): record CodeRabbit's incremental review and correct the pass-1 totals

CodeRabbit reviewed again on the next push. It marked eight threads addressed, raised

The disposition totals were also wrong: they had been carried over from a partial count

test(web): stop the MCP browser suite flaking on its own waits (D49)

The suite failed about half the time on an unchanged stack, and neither mode was
a product assertion failing.

The first case waited for the name field on a budget meant for a render while
paying for two things that are not one: a development server compiling the
settings route on first visit, and a probe that dials the MCP server and reads
what it answers. Those now have their own budgets, and the route budget applies
only to a worker's first visit, so a slow compile does not silently become the
allowance for every later wait.

The OAuth case failed on an aborted navigation. A `goto` issued while an earlier
one is still settling cancels that one, and Playwright reports the cancellation
on the call that caused it rather than on the navigation that lost, so a healthy
page looked like a broken one. Navigation tolerates that abort now; the
assertion that follows is what decides whether the page arrived.

Five consecutive runs, seven of seven each: 1.1m, 57.4s, 56.7s, 57.5s, 55.4s.

Also records in the journey test file the two things that cost the most time
writing these: the dialog renders through a portal, so a query scoped to the
host node finds nothing and looks like a component that rendered nothing; and a
stub that resolves immediately decides races the product has not decided yet,
which is why the duplicate-discovery case could not see its own defect until the
stub was made to stay in flight.

test(web): assert what the backend did, not what the page renders (D39)

Four assertions passed on text the frontend produces whatever the server says.

The duplicate-name case never reached the server. The client refuses a collision
from the list it already holds, so the name was never submitted and neither the
API's refusal nor the `name_taken` path was exercised. The case now creates the
colliding connection out of band, which leaves the open page's list stale, types
the name, submits it, and asserts the refusal that comes back. That is also what
happens when a colleague adds a connection while someone has settings open.

The tools case asserted a sentence this page renders regardless. It asserts two
tool names the mock actually advertises.

The read-only case asserted that the markup contains "disabled", which the
button's own `disabled:opacity-50` class satisfies whenever it renders at all:
dropping the prop shipped a live Connect button on a read-only config, green. It
asserts the rendered attribute now, with the opposite case beside it so an
always-disabled button cannot satisfy it either. Removing the prop fails it.

Submitting the name for real also surfaced a small defect: the refusal was shown
twice, once on the field and once as the dialog's generic error. The generic one
now stands down on the name step, where the error belongs to the field, and the
case asserts the message appears once.

docs(gateways): track the deferred credential-invalidation race as an issue

CodeRabbit's N5 is a real race between the credential comparison and the invalidating
write: a reconnect landing between them keeps the same secret id, so the write's guard
passes and marks a connection invalid that had just been repaired. It was deferred
because the window is two database round trips, the user-visible consequence is one
spurious reconnect banner that a second connect clears with no data loss, and closing
it properly needs a credential version on the endpoint row, which is a schema change
this release should not carry.

Deferred is not dropped, so it is now filed as #6879 and the row says so.

fix(web): let a stranded tool permission be cleared, and bind a tool list to its connection (CR18, M4)

Two ways the permission editor could leave an agent in a state nobody could
repair from it.

Narrowing a server's tool filter strands the permissions of tools it now hides.
The API refuses the whole policy for exactly those entries, so the agent stops
running, and the row's own control is disabled because a hidden tool may not be
given a permission. Clearing was refused along with setting, so there was no way
out. Clearing is now always allowed, and the editor lists the stranded entries
with what they cost and a way to remove each.

A tool list is fetched per connection and arrives whenever it arrives. Neither
the editor nor the connection drawer remembered which connection it had asked
for, so switching while one was in flight rendered the previous connection's
tools under the new one's name. Each now records what it asked for and ignores an
answer that is no longer the question.

The race test holds the first list in flight and resolves it after the second
connection is showing, which is the only ordering that reproduces it; removing
the guard fails that case and nothing else.

fix(api): stop the capped read from re-declaring a decoded body as encoded

Probing any real MCP server returned a 500. The size cap added for D38 and D46
reads a streamed response itself and rebuilds one around the bytes it read, and
it carried the upstream's headers over verbatim. Those bytes are decoded, so
keeping content-encoding told the next reader to decompress what was already
decompressed, and the first touch of the body raised DecodingError. Verified
against Linear from the demo stack, before and after.

Every real server compresses and neither mock upstream does, which is why the
whole suite stayed green while the feature was broken for every server a person
would actually type in.

Both rebuild sites now go through one helper that drops the three headers
describing the body as it travelled, content-encoding, content-length and
transfer-encoding, and keeps content-type, which is what tells the probe whether
a handshake came back as JSON or as a single event.

The probe also gains an outer guard, because its docstring promises it never
raises for a server that behaves badly and the connect dialog has nowhere to
show a stack trace. Any transport or protocol failure that reaches it, including
the decoding ones that are not raised until a body is touched, is now reported
as a problem on the result.

Three unit cases cover a gzip-encoded metadata document, a gzip-encoded
handshake, and a body that genuinely cannot be decoded. An acceptance case
drives the deployed probe route against a real OAuth-protected server, which is
the only kind of test that would have caught this; it skips when the runner has
no outbound access, because a firewalled runner is not a broken gateway.

fix(web): keep an open connection live, and say why its tools are missing (QA-D2, QA-D3)

Opening a connection stored the row itself, frozen at the moment it was clicked.
A disconnect updated the list underneath while the open connection went on
reporting Ready and offering to disconnect again, until a reload. It is held by
identity now and looked up fresh on every render, so it shows what the list
shows.

The permission editor reported a failure in the gateway's internal words:
"Authorization required for custom/<slug> ⟦agenta_code:auth_required⟧". The
marker is addressed to the runner, the route names a slug rather than a
connection, and the offered action was Retry, which on a server nobody has
authorized only fails again. The marker is stripped from anything a person
reads, the sentence names the connection, and the action offered is the one that
fixes it.

The refusal reader gained a way to read the code as a code, which is what lets a
caller tell "this needs authorizing" from "this did not answer" without matching
on prose.

A transport error's own message no longer reaches the screen either. It says
"Request failed with status code 424", which is a number where a reason belongs;
the existing case asserted that leak, and now asserts the readable sentence.

fix(web): offer an open endpoint that needs no key (QA-D5)

An OpenAI-compatible endpoint may be saved with no API key. The card says so in
the field's own label, "API key — if the endpoint requires one"; only the base
URL is required, because the URL is the address and an open self-hosted gateway
has nothing to store. The providers table then shows the row as active, and the
API registers it as an active LLM gateway endpoint.

The agent's model picker disagreed. It dropped every connection holding no
stored secret, so the endpoint never became selectable, and the agent kept
showing "Add your model provider key to run this agent" for a key the card
calls optional. Both symptoms are one fact: the connect-a-model gate is
"zero runnable candidates", and this connection produced none.

The gate now skips a connection that has nothing stored unless it is a kind
that needs nothing stored. That stays false for every kind whose credential is
the point, whether it is required outright (a provider key, Azure, Vertex) or
as one of its alternative auth sets (Bedrock), and it still requires the record
to carry whatever else its kind requires: an endpoint with no address is not
offered either.

The test drives the vault row the demo stack actually stored for this report,
through the same transform and builder the page runs.

fix(api): refuse a renewal whose pinned registration is gone (CodeRabbit N3)

A grant records which client the authorization server issued it to, so a renewal
can present that one. When the row behind that reference could not be read the
reader answered None, which is exactly what a grant carrying no pin at all
answers, and the renewal reads that as permission to present the deployment's
own identity document.

So the one substitution the pin exists to prevent was the one that happened. The
comment directly above said nothing can stand in for a registration that is
gone, and the code one line later let something stand in for it.

An unresolvable pin is now a typed refresh failure, which the data plane already
turns into the reconnect that mints a fresh registration along with fresh
tokens. A grant with no pin keeps the identity-document fallback, which is the
legitimate path for a deployment that has no registration to present.

The end-to-end case asserts what reached the token endpoint rather than only
that the renewal failed. Without the fix the renewal also failed, because the
authorization server rejected the substituted client, but it rejected it after
the deployment's identity had been put on the wire as the client for somebody
else's tokens. Nothing reaches it now.

Two details in that case were wrong in ways that would have made it prove
nothing, and both are noted where they sit: the record deletion compared pairs
rather than the records inside them, and aging the grant through a fresh storage
unpinned it, which is the D24 defect reproduced in a helper.

docs(gateways): say how to run the gateway acceptance layer host-side

The preconditions covered the integration layer and, followed literally, broke the
acceptance layer. The two layers want opposite things from the mock-upstream
variables, and nothing said so.

In the integration layer the test process dials the mocks, so it needs their published
loopback addresses. In the acceptance layer the gateway dials them, and the outbound
guard refuses loopback and private targets, so the same overrides tell the gateway to
dial its own loopback. The suite then fails with blocked-target refusals and a spread
of 424s that read like a product defect. Measured on one candidate: 15 acceptance
failures with the overrides, and 42 passed with 6 failed and no errors without them.

test.sh is not the answer either, and the file now says why rather than leaving someone
to find out. It runs host-side like any other run and points the tests at whatever API
URL the stack's env file names; on a tunnelled stack a whole suite through the tunnel
collapses into TLS EOF errors under load.

The six consent failures that remain are a real configuration conflict rather than
flakiness: the mock issuer has to publish a browser-reachable address to support a
consent round trip, while the gateway dials it in-network, and discovery refuses the
mismatch. One mock configuration cannot serve both, so the file says to decide what a
given stack is for, and records that CI stays the sweep of record for this layer.

test(runner): CR10 pin both halves of the Pi MCP request bound

The two existing cases passed with either half deleted. The "never answers" one
dispatched an abort event by hand instead of letting the client's own timer fire,
and the cancellation one aborted before the call started, which the cheap
`signal.aborted` check serves without the listener.

Replace the first with a fake-timer case that advances to PI_MCP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS
and adds a case that aborts a call already in flight. Each races the work against a
short real timer, so a client that never abandons the request fails fast instead of
hanging the suite. Deleting the setTimeout fails the first; deleting the abort
listener fails the second.

fix(api): only accept a registration the scan can actually present (CodeRabbit M8 residual)

The earlier fix stopped an unusable provider row raising, and left the lookup
that finds one alone. An OAuth-provider secret is something a person can create
through the vault's own surface, so "any provider row naming this issuer" also
describes a row this class never wrote, and the fallback scan returned the first
match either way.

With the reader hardened, a hand-made row alone is discarded after it is found,
so the visible consequence is narrower than the finding implies: it shadows.
Put a hand-made row and a real registration at one issuer and the scan can
return the hand-made one, and a deployment that is registered re-registers,
minting a fresh client at a server that may rate limit it and orphaning the
grants bound to the old one.

The scan now requires a row to carry a registration this client could present.
A real registration written under an older slug is still found, which is the
whole reason the fallback exists.

Deliberately not tested through `set_client_info`: that path addresses the row by
slug and never consults this scan, so a case built on it would pass whatever the
scan did. The case that discriminates is the shadowing one.

fix(sdk): treat a configuration-less agent as an agent (CodeRabbit M10 residual)

Narrowing the recognition to "carries at least one agent-template key" made the
opposite mistake. Every field of an agent template defaults, so an agent may
legitimately arrive as an empty block, and one that did was sent to the
project-wide credential prefetch it exists to skip.

The test is now a subset rather than an intersection: every key the block has
must be one an agent template defines, and a block with no keys qualifies. That
admits the empty agent and still refuses a workflow whose author named a
parameter `agent`, because such a block carries keys of its own. A block mixing
both is refused too, which matches the schema, since an agent template forbids
unknown fields.

A case now pins the key list to the schema's own fields. The list duplicates
them, so it could drift silently, and a field added to the template would make a
real agent carrying it look like somebody else's parameter.

Recording a declared workflow kind on the wire remains the real closure, and the
docstring now says so in those terms: both directions of this check are guesses
about a shape, and only a declaration ends the guessing. It is a change for the
API and the SDK together, which is why it is not this commit.

fix(api): bound name resolution on the relay path and keep it off the shared pool (CodeRabbit M18 residual)

Two halves the first fix missed, and the reviewer is right about both.

The relay path had no bound at all. `open_egress` runs the same blocking
resolution every gateway call goes through, so one address whose resolver hangs
held a request open for as long as the resolver did. It now refuses with an
address that could not be resolved in time, told apart from a security rejection
so an adapter reports it as an address problem rather than a blocked target.

And the safety argument overstated the isolation. Bounding the wait releases the
coroutine, not the thread, and the thread came from the loop's shared default
executor, which every other offloaded call in the process also uses. Enough
stuck resolutions starve work that has nothing to do with the gateway.

Both resolutions now run on a small pool of this module's own, so they can
exhaust those threads and nothing else. When they do, the wait fires while
queueing rather than while resolving, and the caller is told the address could
not be resolved in time, which is true and is the same refusal a resolver that
never answers produces.

The bound is read from the module rather than bound as a default argument, which
is what let a case pin it: the first version of these tests waited the full five
seconds while appearing to assert a fifth of a second.

Four cases on the relay path, which had none: a hanging resolver is refused
rather than awaited, the loop keeps serving while one is stuck, resolution runs
on the gateway's own threads rather than the shared pool, and an address that
resolves promptly is unaffected.

test(gateways): register the mock at the address its issuer publishes

Six cases failed on any stack that publishes the mock under a public address so a
browser can complete the consent flow. The endpoints were registered at the
in-network address while the issuer advertised the public one, and discovery
refuses a server whose origin differs from the resource its own metadata names.

The address now comes from the issuer's own protected-resource document, read
over the port the compose files publish, so the two cannot disagree and one
stack serves both the browser flow and these tests. AGENTA_MOCK_MCP_GATEWAY_URL
still wins when set, for a run that means to override both sides at once, and a
mock that cannot be reached falls back to the compose address, leaving the
suite's own skip to report the absence.

Nothing changes on a stack that publishes no public address: the document names
the compose address there, which is the value this file defaulted to before.

fix(api): stop an exception's text reaching a gateway error body (CodeQL py/stack-trace-exposure)

The LLM proxy rendered str(exc) for anything the body parser raised. That arm
catches every ValueError, and only the ones this gateway authored are describing
the request: a JSON decoder's message names the offset it choked on, an encoding
error quotes the offending bytes, and any other ValueError reaching that point is
not about the request at all.

Classified rather than quoted, which is the shape the credential classifier
already uses. The parser raises a typed body error carrying a stable cause and a
sentence this module wrote, and the proxy shows that sentence and nothing else.
An exception it did not author is logged with its class and answered with a fixed
line.

A caller keeps the feedback that made the refusal actionable: no model named, a
non-boolean stream, and a body that is not JSON each still say so.

The MCP plane's body arm is the same code one file over, catching ValueError and
rendering str(e), so it is closed the same way in the same commit rather than
left as a known instance of a pattern just flagged. Its own complaints were
already authored, so what changes there is that a stray ValueError can no longer
ride out through it.

Four cases assert the property the finding is about: an unrelated ValueError's
message is absent from the body on both planes, a malformed body is refused
without the decoder's wording, and an upstream failure does not relay its
adapter's text.

docs(gateways): record the first real-provider MCP evidence

Every MCP cell in this document ran against the compose mock until now. A mock cannot
show that a real server's registration, consent and discovery work, which is what the
release gate asks for, so this records the first evidence that they do: initialize and
tools/list relayed through the gateway to two consented servers, 79 tools from one and
28 from the other, with each server's own serverInfo, plus one real read tool call that
returned real data.

The authorised write is not run. Reading the workspace first shows five teams and none
of them is a scratch team; they are the organisation's real, active teams, so an issue
created in any of them is visible to the people who work there. The authorisation was
for a scratch team, so its precondition is not met and the choice belongs to a person.
The file says so rather than substituting a quiet-looking real team, and notes that
least recently updated is not the same as nobody will see it.

Two traps are written down because both cost time and both produce misleading symptoms:
the data plane ignores Authorization and reads X-AG-Credentials, so a client sending
only the former gets a bare 401 that looks exactly like an unconsented connection; and
a real server answers with an SSE frame, so a client calling .json() on it reports zero
tools instead of failing.

fix(api): prefer a registration this gateway wrote over one that merely looks like one (CodeRabbit M8)

Two shadowing paths were left. The lookup in front of the scan returned whatever
sat at the address slug, and the scan's filter tested shape: a row carrying a
valid client_info reads back as usable client information whoever wrote it, and
an OAuth-provider secret is something a person can create through the vault's
own surface. So a crafted row could still be presented as this deployment's
client, and re-registration skipped because a registration appeared to exist.

Every registration this module writes now carries a provenance mark, and both
paths prefer a marked row over an unmarked one, in one pass over every candidate
rather than taking the first match on either.

Preferred, not required. Requiring it would orphan every registration written
before the mark existed, and orphaning one means registering a fresh client at a
server that may rate limit it while the grants bound to the old one stop
refreshing: the D6 harm, caused by the fix for a lesser one. An unmarked row is
still used when it is all there is, and gains the mark the next time it is
written.

That costs the project listing D14 removed, in one case: an unmarked row can no
longer answer from the address alone, because a row placed at the address slug is
exactly how a genuine registration gets shadowed. A marked row still answers
without it, every write marks, and D14's read was on the relay path while this
one is on connect and on a renewal predating the grant's own pin.

The mark is provenance, not authentication. It is written into the row's own
settings, so a project member who can write secrets could set it too; what it
closes is a row that shadows by accident or by shape, which is what the finding
describes. Making it unforgeable means the server-owned-field mechanism the
subscription rows use, and that refuses writes from this component as readily as
from anyone else, so it needs a seam that does not exist yet.

fix(runner): negotiate the MCP protocol version instead of asserting it

Both MCP clients sent `MCP-Protocol-Version` on `initialize`. The version is
what `initialize` negotiates, so the client cannot know it yet; the transport
spec has the header ride only the requests that follow initialization, carrying
the version the server returned. A server that enforces this answers 400, the
handshake never completes, and the model reports the tools missing.

The mock adapter does not check, so every mock cell and every real-model cell
passed while a real upstream refused every turn.

The Pi client now records the version `initialize` answered with and sends that
on later requests, falling back to its own when a server names none. The
handshake probe sends no version header at all, because that request IS the
initialize.

test(api): cover the address slug the shadowing was reproduced on (CodeRabbit M8)

still wins over an older one at the issuer, so the preference does not invert the
ordering it sits inside: the registration for the current address is the one to
present, and it still answers without decrypting the project.

fix(frontend): say why a refused send was refused, not just that it was

A 422 from POST /services/agent/v0/invoke carries a typed refusal: the SDK
normalizer answers {status: {code, message, failure_code}}, and the layers in
front of it answer FastAPI's {detail} or the relay's {error}. The server-input
send path cancelled that body and threw the status number, so the only thing
either app could say was "Message wasn't sent — try again." A project with no
model provider got no reason and no next step.

Read the body instead, through the same gateway refusal reader the MCP connect
dialog and the permission editor use, and carry the stated sentence and failure
class on the thrown error. The composer chip, the classic run-in-playground
recovery, and the mobile Home hand-off all state it; a refusal that states
nothing keeps the standing wording. The SDK envelope ships a multi-kilobyte
stacktrace beside the message, so only the message is passed on.

fix(runner): read a real upstream's SSE framing and negotiated revision

Two defects a live Linear run found, both on the Pi client's first request.

readJsonResponse tested only whether the body STARTED with "data:". Linear
frames every reply as SSE and opens the event with "event: message", so
JSON.parse threw, discover() failed, and the server was dropped as a failed
handshake with none of its 79 tools registered. The handshake probe already read
any data: line correctly, and a server could therefore pass the probe and be
unreadable to the client that followed it; the two now share one parser rather
than two copies of the same intent.

Every request also stamped _meta with the client's own protocol constant. A
server validates that envelope against the revision IT negotiated and refuses a
newer one (-32602 "Invalid _meta envelope for protocol revision 2026-07-28"), so
after Linear's downgrade to 2025-11-25 the very next request, tools/list, failed.
It now carries the agreed revision.

fix(api): register a custom connection under the provider family it names (OR88)

Posting a custom_provider secret auto-registers the endpoint row it stands for,
and that mapping read the protocol field and, finding none, used OpenAI. A
connection saved as anthropic with no protocol therefore produced a row
declaring provider_key openai. Reproduced from the provider-row recipe in qa.md,
which is the write that made the rows seen in the QA project.

The protocol field's own note says a record written before it existed is read as
OpenAI-compatible, which is right for a record that says nothing. This record
says anthropic in the field beside it. The enum has exactly two values because
everything that is not Anthropic's shape is OpenAI's, so the family answers the
question whenever the protocol does not.

It is not only a wrong row. provider_key is inert for the relay's own auth on a
custom endpoint, which sends a bearer token whatever it says, but it is what
connection resolution returns to the SDK and what a harness reads to decide how
to speak to the model. An Anthropic model reached an agent described as an
OpenAI one.

A stated protocol is still believed, so a connection declaring the OpenAI shape
over an Anthropic family stays OpenAI, which is what an OpenAI-compatible front
end is. A family this release does not recognise reads as OpenAI-shaped, like a
record that states nothing.

Two other oddities on the same row are recorded in the finding as deliberate
non-fixes: the qualified model key doubles a vendor prefix, which is ugly and
harmless because the allowlist also carries the bare slug and the key is an
internal address agent configurations may hold; and the row sits beside one the
QA recipe created explicitly, which is the recipe making a second endpoint for
one secret rather than the registrar misbehaving.

test(gateways): make the mock MCP server as strict as a real one

The mock accepted more than a real server accepts, so the matrices certified a
client that no real upstream would talk to. Two divergences, both found only by a
live Linear run:

The protocol version is negotiated by initialize, so the header rides only the
requests that follow it. The mock ignored the header entirely; it now refuses an
initialize that carries one, with the same 400 and JSON-RPC -32020 shape a strict
server answers, and refuses a later request that omits it.

Real servers also frame replies as SSE with the event line first. The mock always
sent plain JSON, so a client that tested only whether a body started with "data:"
passed every cell. tools/list is now framed that way and the rest stay plain JSON,
keeping both framings in the matrix. The socket tier no longer relabels the media
type, and the parity test asserts bytes rather than parsed JSON, since the framing
is part of what a client has to read.

fix(sdk): log an invoke refusal's traceback instead of answering with it (OR89)

The failed-invocation body carries the formatted Python traceback, and the
playground calls that route from a browser, so around two kilobytes of absolute
module paths, the service's own layout and the source line of every frame
between the route and the handler were shipped to a page.

Pre-existing on main. This branch's only change to that method was adding
failure_code; the finding is recorded now because the release reviewed the body
it appears in.

The SDK already holds the opposite position where it says so out loud: a
configuration mistake carries a 4xx and no stacktrace. The normalizer applied no
such rule, so a 422 a person caused by mistyping a model carried the same
traceback a 500 did.

The traceback now goes onto the failure line this path already logs, so an
operator reads one record holding what they were going to read anyway. The
fields a client branches on are untouched.

AGENTA_SDK_ERRORS_INCLUDE_STACKTRACE puts it back for a developer running the
service against their own browser, read per call so it needs no restart and a
case can pin it.

One deviation, deliberate: the brief asked to gate this on a debug flag the SDK
already has, and there is none that can serve. The only candidates are the two
console-logging variables, and the level one defaults to TRACE, so gating on it
would have left the default exactly as it was. The new variable is narrow, says
what it does, and defaults off.

fix(sdk): keep a subscription connection off the gateway resolver (OR90)

A self_managed connection means the harness authenticates itself, so there is no
provider key for the gateway to hold and no route for it to build. The resolver
short-circuited only the connection with no slug; a named one, the hosted
subscription whose stored OAuth login Agenta delivers to the run, fell through to
POST /gateways/llms/resolve. That endpoint answers with a gateway route, so the
run either got a connection the harness cannot use with the subscription silently
discarded, or was refused because no endpoint row exists for a subscription slug.

The branch used to read the vault and still should; what moved was the fetch, and
this branch was not repointed with it. Every hosted-subscription test fed the list
payload only the vault read returns, so all of them stayed green against an
endpoint that no longer answers with one.

The self_managed check now precedes the slug test. The new case feeds the payload
a live API actually answers and asserts the SDK never asks the gateway for it.

fix(runner): OR91 stop sending an _meta envelope the upstream then validates

`_meta` is optional in every MCP revision and nothing on either side of the Pi
MCP client reads one back, but a server that receives one validates the whole
envelope against the revision in force. A real upstream refused every
post-initialize request carrying
`_meta: {"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": ...}` with
`-32602 Invalid _meta envelope for protocol revision <rev>: <key>: missing`,
naming a key the client had never sent, while the identical requests without
`_meta` succeeded — so the server was dropped and none of its tools reached the
model. Stamping the negotiated revision rather than the client's own constant
was still stamping an envelope; it only moved the refusal.

Send the caller's params and nothing else, and teach the mock upstream the same
rule so the cell matrix fails rather than the next real server. The mock's guard
is scoped to the `io.modelcontextprotocol/` namespace, which is the server's to
set: a client-owned key like `progressToken` passes through, so this does not
booby-trap a later feature that legitimately needs one.

docs(gateways): add the read-only cell and the gate it must not count

The real-provider table covered approve and deny. The read-only cell belongs beside
them: it discovers and stops, initialize and tools/list and nothing else, with the
tool denied by policy and never offered.

It also carries the one distinction that judging these cells needs, because getting

gate as the tool's gate then reports a correct run as broken. Resolving each gate's
call id to a tool name and ignoring the ones that are not the server's is the whole

test(web): drive the agent playground as it actually behaves (MCP agent config)

Five things the first draft of this suite got wrong about the surface it
drives, each found by running it:

The section is called MCP servers, not MCPs. The app-create drawer and
the modal it opens both carry a Create button and both are dialogs, so
picking the last one clicked under the modal's overlay and made the wrong
kind of app; the modal's own heading tells them apart. The create menu is
still animating when its submenu is asked for, so the hover is forced. An
agent's configuration commits itself as it is edited, so there is nothing
to press: the read-back polls instead. And an agent's playground opens a
session before it paints anything, which on a development server is the
heaviest route there is, so the first case in a worker waits four times as
long and reloads once if the page came up empty.

Two of the three cases pass against the dev stack in about twelve seconds
each. The third reaches the same section intermittently; what it is
waiting on is the page painting, not the feature.

docs(web): correct where /m's settings sends someone to connect a provider

The comment on the chat composer's connect-model strip said its one-field
sheet was the same surface Settings -> LLM providers opens. That stopped

docs(gateways): rehearse disabling the MCP plane and rolling the migration back

The gate asks for a data-preserving rollback and disable procedure verified in a test
environment. This is that rehearsal, run with a project's real consented connections
and stored grants in place throughout.

Disabling refuses the plane it names and leaves the rest alone: the relay answers 403
with a typed mcp_gateway_disabled envelope a client can branch on, the control plane
refuses, and the LLM plane and the vault keep answering 200. Re-enabling brings back
the same five endpoints, the same three grants and the same tool counts, so it is a
switch rather than a teardown.

The migration's downgrade is deliberately a no-op and its docstring explains why, which
is worth repeating here because a reader who assumes otherwise will plan a rollback that
does not exist. Rehearsed against a scratch database restored from the deployment's own:
both directions run clean and the grant slug set is byte-identical across the round trip,
so on already-rekeyed data the revision is idempotent. The destructive branch needs a
grant claimed by several connections and no such row exists here, so that stays covered
by the revision's tests.

One half is unverified and the section says so rather than glossing it: the settings tab
stayed visible with the plane off, because the running web image predates the entrypoint
that publishes the flag to the browser, and a pinned image leaves nothing to rebuild.
That check belongs on a deployment built from the candidate.

docs(gateways): finish the disable rehearsal with the settings tab

The rehearsal recorded one half as unverified: the MCP settings tab stayed visible
with the plane off. Rebuilt the web image from the candidate and it hides, and comes
back when the flag returns, on both the desktop and mobile navigations.

The earlier result was wrong for a reason worth writing down rather than quietly
correcting. The web container's entrypoint is baked into the image and not
bind-mounted, and it is the entrypoint that publishes the flag into the browser's
env file. An image built before that line does not contain it and no recreate can
introduce it, so the source looked right while the running container could never
have honoured it. The section now says to check the image rather than the source
when a flag seems not to reach the frontend, and gives the three commands that
settle it.

It also records the trap that cost a retry: after recreating, the mobile app needs
warming, and a settings read before it hydrates returns raw page JSON that reads as
an empty navigation and looks exactly like the tab being absent.

fix(web): read a refusal's harness marker in one pass, not in quadratic time

The parser that strips the runner's code marker out of a refusal message
started its pattern with a whitespace quantifier and then looked for the
marker. Given a long run of whitespace followed by a marker that never
closes, the engine retried from every position in that run: measured on
this input, 2.9 seconds at fifty thousand characters and 45 seconds at
two hundred thousand. The string is a message body written by whatever
MCP server the person pointed us at, so its length and shape are not
ours to choose, and the tab holding the dialog is what stops responding.
CodeQL flags it as js/polynomial-redos, high.

Two indexOf calls find the marker's delimiters instead, reading each
character once, and the surrounding whitespace is trimmed off the two
sides rather than matched. Behaviour is unchanged, including that a
marker with nothing between its delimiters is left in the text rather
than treated as a code. The thirteen tests that were there still pass;
the new one fails in 5.5 seconds against the pattern it replaces.

fix(web): carry a refusal's cause on the error the tool list raises (D50)

The per-tool permission editor asks why the tool list failed, so that a
connection nobody has authorized offers Connect and names itself, rather
than a Retry that will fail the same way. It asked by reading the code
out of a response field. The function it catches from cannot supply one:
the data plane refuses in a JSON-RPC envelope that carries no detail at
all, and the client reads that response, raises its own typed error with
the sentence, and drops everything else. So the code was always absent,
the naming and Connect halves never fired in front of anyone, and the
two tests that said otherwise rejected with a shape that function cannot
produce.

The cause now travels on the error, taken from where the gateway states
it structurally, and the reader knows all three envelopes: the control
plane's detail, the data plane's error.data.cause, and a failure this
package already read. The editor is unchanged, because the question it
asks is now answerable.

The editor's two tests throw the real error type; removing either half
of the fix fails them. Three more cover the client: the 409 a person
actually meets, a refusal answered 200, and a dead server, which must
not be read as an unauthorized one.

fix(web,api): return a blocked-popup authorization to the page it started on (r3-D1)

When a browser refuses the consent popup, authorizing navigates the whole
tab. What comes back is a page the API serves, and it knew the deployment's
origin and nothing else, so it sent everyone to a bare /settings. On classic
that forwards on to the scoped page, which merely looked slow and sometimes
came up blank. On /m there is no such route at all, so a person who started
on mobile was returned into the desktop app, on a path with no workspace and
no project in it.

The tab writes down where it stands before it leaves, which is the last
moment anything knows the surface, the workspace and the project, and the
callback page prefers that over its fallback. Per tab, so two flows cannot
cross; cleared once used, so a stale path cannot capture the next return;
and refused unless it is a plain path, because the value is joined to an
origin and //evil.test is a URL to another one. Where the API is served from
a different origin the storage is simply empty and the old path still lands
in the app.

Eleven tests: the page prefers, validates, forgets and falls back; the tab
records the scoped path on the blocked branch and nothing at all when the
popup opened.

fix(web): check the attempt at every await, and make the duplicate case discriminate (D51, D52)

D52. The generation counter's own comment said every async step reads it
before its await and checks it after. Two of seven did. The other five
dispatched whatever they came back with: a probe answering after a cancel
could hand someone the name step for a connection they had abandoned, a
tool list could fill a dialog that had moved on, and a verify could report
success for an attempt nobody was waiting for. Each site now reads the
generation before and checks it after, on the answer and on the failure
alike, through one helper so the next step added cannot quietly skip it.

D51. The browser case for a refused duplicate name matched text that both
the client and the server produce, so it passed whether or not the request
was ever made, which is the one thing the case exists to prove. It now
matches the next step, which only the server writes. A unit test pins that
sentence surviving the trip from the envelope to the field, so the browser
case cannot start passing on wording the client invented.

Three rendered cases cover the generation: a probe that resolves late, a
probe that fails late, and a tool list that arrives late. Each fails when
its guard is removed.

Both lists of a server's tools rendered every row: the read-only one in

The same run kept losing a click to the development server's error

that answers without a consent screen can be back at the callback before

window with no listener on it. The mock issuer is exactly that: it
validates PKCE and redirects straight through, so the whole round trip
can be milliseconds on a local stack.

Nothing recovers from a missed completion. The poll only notices a

fix(runner): D63 read the frame that answers the request, not the whole stream

The Streamable HTTP transport lets a server send notifications before the
response to a request. `readMcpResponseJson` collected every `data:` line in the
body and joined them, so such an answer arrived as two JSON documents separated
by a newline, parsed as nothing, and `discover()` threw: the client reported no
tools and the server was dropped as a failed handshake. Both independent
reviewers found this, and both executed it.

Parse the stream event by event, skip frames carrying neither a result nor an
error, and return the one whose id matches the request. The id is what separates
this from the browser client's rule of taking the last answering frame: two
requests can share a stream, and only the id tells their answers apart. Callers
that numbered nothing, which is the handshake probe, keep the browser's rule.

The backend probe had the same defect one layer down. It took the last `data:`
line, which survived a notification sent first and would have failed on one sent
after, or on a payload split across two lines. All three clients now select the
same frame, which is what D56 asked for and did not finish.

The mock's one SSE-framed method now sends a real notification before its
result, so all twenty-seven cells of the matrix carry a multi-event answer
instead of the single event that could never show this. The adapter test's own
body reader had the joining bug in it too, which is why the fixture never
noticed.

docs(gateways): record CodeRabbit's second pass over the tests

Pass 1 reviewed the production source. This pass covers what it excluded: the tests,
the configuration that runs them, and the infrastructure and repository configuration.
15 findings, dispositioned against the reviewed head.

A test-file pass rarely threatens what ships; it threatens whether the other evidence
can be believed, and the record sorts the findings that way. Five are capable of a
false green, and three of those are the test-runner wrappers mishandling forwarded
arguments: a generated marker expression appended after the caller's own, which pytest
resolves by taking the last, and any forwarded value containing a slash treated as a
test target, which drops the resolved directories and falls back to the config's
testpaths. The wrapper that the compose test script uses always takes that path.
Nothing tests the wrappers.

One finding is about shipped behaviour rather than the suite, and it is worth acting
on: the carrier-grade NAT range from RFC 6598 is not blocked by the SSRF guard, in any
of the three planes that share that code, because Python's address predicates all
return false for it. A tenant supplies MCP endpoint URLs by design, so the gateway is a
more exposed surface for that gap than the webhook path where it already existed.

Also recorded: the first attempt at this pass never ran, because a push landed seconds
after the trigger and CodeRabbit cancelled it while its check still read as completed.
That is the second time a CodeRabbit check has looked green here with nothing
reviewed.

fix(gateways): filter a framed tool list like any other (D62)

The tool filter read a tools/list response with a JSON decoder and returned
the body untouched when that failed. A server answering over an event stream
therefore bypassed the filter entirely and every tool it owned was advertised,
whatever the connection allowed.

Read each data line of an event stream, filter the frame that carries the tool
list, and leave every other frame, the event names, ordering and line endings
as they were. A body that is not a tool list is still returned unchanged.

fix(gateways): never select or rewrite a registration another callback owns (D66)

A client registration is bound to the callback it was created with, and so are
the tokens issued through it. The provenance preference added for M8 ranged over
every registration at the issuer, so a marked row left from a previous public
address beat the unmarked row this address's grants pin. The connect path then
found that row did not cover the callback it would send, registered again, and
the write landed on the row the grants pin, so their next renewal presented a
client the authorization server never issued those tokens to.

Only a registration covering the callback this deployment sends is a candidate;
provenance orders what is left. Rows for other callbacks stay exactly where they
are, are never selected, and are never written over. A grant resolving by its own
pin, or one written before pins existed, is unaffected: neither resolves for the
current address.
docs(gateways): verify the D62 and D66 fixes

fix(runner): D64 offer one MCP revision from all three clients

This product ships three MCP clients and they named two revisions: the Pi
extension claimed 2026-07-28 while the browser client and the backend probe
claimed 2025-06-18. One product told the same server three different things
about the wire, and a mock whose strictness was derived from one client
certified nothing about the other two.

They now all offer 2025-06-18, which is the value the other two already had, so
only this client moves. The reason for choosing the older revision is that a
client should claim only what it implements: the later revisions add
requirements to the request envelope that none of these three implements or
reads back, and claiming a revision we do not satisfy is precisely what OR91
cost us against a real server, which validated our envelope against the revision
we had NAMED. Claiming the revision whose requirements we meet makes that
removal correct rather than merely convenient.

The mock now negotiates DOWN instead of echoing the client's offer back, so the
gap between the revision a client OFFERS and the one a server ANSWERS is open in
every cell of the matrix rather than only against a real upstream. It answers an
older revision than any client offers, and it checks the VALUE of the
post-handshake header rather than only its presence, so a client that echoes its
own constant is refused here instead of in production. Both third-party
harnesses were measured against that rule and honour it.

The two source comments citing "MCPCallContext's own docstring" for this
constant were stale; that docstring says nothing about a version.

fix(sdk): withhold the traceback from the invoke routing layer too (D68)

OR89 gated the traceback on the running normalizer, which catches a handler's
own exception. The invoke routing layer catches everything raised around it and
still returned the frames to the caller, so the same request could be refused
with a traceback or without one depending on where it failed.

The switch moves beside failure_code_of, which both sites already share for the
same reason: one request must not get two answers. The routing layer had no
failure log of its own, so one is added, and the traceback it withholds lands
there instead of being dropped.

Five cases, covering both branches of the routing layer, the log, and the two
sites agreeing with the switch off and on.
docs(gateways): verify the D68 fix for the second traceback site

fix(runner): D65 bound a tool call by the gateway's budget, not the handshake's

CR10 gave this client one ten-second bound and applied it to every request,
`tools/call` included. That call's peer is the Agenta gateway, which allows its
own upstream thirty seconds, so any tool taking between ten and thirty seconds
was cancelled by the client while the gateway was still waiting and the turn
failed on work that was going to succeed. A reviewer proved it by driving a real
registration against a server answering inside the gateway's budget: rejected at
10001 ms.

The two bounds answer different questions and are now separate. The handshake
keeps its short liveness bound, because a server slow to say hello should not
delay the turn's first token. A tool call gets the gateway's budget plus enough
margin for the gateway's own refusal to travel back, so a slow upstream produces
the gateway's error rather than this client's cancellation.

The gateway's constant now says in both languages that the two move together, so
raising one alone is a change someone has to make deliberately rather than by
not noticing.

Residual, stated in the code rather than left to be rediscovered: a per-endpoint
`timeout_seconds` raised above the gateway default is still capped by this
client, because nothing delivers that stored setting to the runner. Honouring it
means carrying the resolved endpoint's budget on the run's MCP wire, which is a
change to the contract between the API, the SDK and this client rather than a
constant.

fix(runner): D67 keep the bound and the cancellation on the body, not just the headers

Found independently by both reviewers. `post()` cleared its timeout and dropped
the caller's abort listener the moment `fetch` resolved, and the body was then
read with nothing watching it. Headers are not the answer: a server that
answered its headers and then stalled held the call forever, and a cancelled
turn could not end it. CR10's own defect, half closed.

`post` now reads the body inside the guarded region and hands back the decoded
text instead of a `Response`, so there is no longer a way to read a body outside
the region where the timeout and the cancellation still apply. Aborting after
the headers have arrived tears down the body stream too, so a stalled read
rejects rather than hanging.

One of the two new cases is the guard: it fails when the body escapes the
bounded region. The other pins the end-to-end cancellation and still passes
against the old shape, because `fetch` ties the body stream to the signal it was
given rather than to our bridge from the caller's. That is said in the test
rather than left for a later reader to discover, since a case that cannot fail
is the thing this review round keeps finding.

test(services): fail when the gateway suites have no gateway to test (D77)

These suites exist to prove that a gateway refusal reaches the caller with its
code. Against a deployment with the plane off they skipped, so a stack nobody
had configured and one deliberately left alone read the same: green, having
covered nothing. The Railway template already worked around it in a comment.

The check now fails unless the run says it expected a stack without the plane,
which the product default still needs. The helper is named for what it does.

Five cases covering both outcomes and what does not count as saying so.

fix(gateways): ask the deployment whether it can reach the server (D80)

The real-server probe acceptance decided whether to run by fetching the server
from the test process. In CI that is a different machine from the one running
the API, so a runner with internet and a container without it failed the case,
and a runner without internet skipped one the container could have run.

It now probes first and reads the deployment's own answer. Skipping on that
answer needs more than the probe's `cause`, which is one coarse word for every
outbound failure: a response the gateway received and could not read arrives as
`unreachable` exactly like a connection that never opened, and that response is
the regression this case exists for. The problem therefore carries how the
attempt failed, from the transport classifier's closed vocabulary, plus
`unresolvable` for a name that never resolved, which is how a machine with no
outbound network fails first. A refusal by the address checks names none, so the
gateway declining to dial a real public server still fails the case.

Five cases. Verified against a live stack and the real server.

fix(web): replay the MCP reconnect notice from the durable transcript (D2)

A turn against a disconnected MCP connection showed the harness's own "Echo
failed / No such tool available: mcp__mock-mcp__echo" card and no way back,
even though the runner emits the notice that names the remedy and the chat has
a card that renders it.

The notice reached the browser and was then thrown away. The runner probes each
configured server's handshake, the gateway refuses a disconnected connection 409
with `detail.code = auth_required` and `requirement.connect`, and the SDK
projects that onto the stream as `data-mcp-server-failed` — measured on the wire
for both the Claude and the Pi harness. The backend persists the same event as a
`mcp_server_failed` record. `transcriptToMessages` had no case for that record
type, so it fell through to the default drop, and `adoptServerTranscript`
replaces the live messages with this replay as soon as the record watermark
moves. The notice therefore lived only until the turn settled, and its removal
also un-suppressed the harness card that `isExplainedByMcpNotice` exists to
hide.

Replay now rebuilds the same part the live egress emits, through the same field
allow-list, so a reloaded turn and a streamed one hand `readMcpServerNotice`
identical input.

fix(runner): D69 follow the tools/list cursor instead of reading one page

`tools/list` is paginated: a server with more to list answers with a
`nextCursor` and the client asks again with it. This client read the first page
and stopped, so every tool past it was never advertised to the model. That fails
in the worst available way — the model is simply never offered the tool, so the
turn reads as a model that would not use one rather than as a client that never
said it existed. The browser client already followed the cursor.

The loop is bounded twice, because discovery runs before the turn's first token
and an unbounded one holds the turn open rather than failing it: a page cap, and
a stop when a server hands back the cursor it was just given.

The mock now pages its catalogue one tool at a time, so every cell of the matrix
exercises a multi-page `tools/list` instead of the single answer that could
never show this.

Measured while doing it, and worth knowing: with `echo` moved to the last page
so the matrix would ENFORCE cursor-following, the nine Pi and nine Claude cells
pass and all nine Codex cells fail. Codex's own MCP client does not follow
`tools/list` pagination, so a server with a paginated catalogue exposes only its
first page to a Codex agent. That is not ours to fix and holding the matrix red
on it would hide every other regression, so `echo` stays on the first page and
the adapter says why. The property itself is pinned in this client's unit tests.

fix(runner): D70 screen configured headers on the handshake probe too

M19 stopped a configured header from replacing `Accept`, `Content-Type`,
`MCP-Protocol-Version` or `Mcp-Session-Id` in the Pi MCP client, and left the
probe that runs immediately before that client spreading the configuration over
the protocol's own headers.

The probe is the worse of the two places to miss it. It reports the server as
FAILED, so no tool from it registers at all and the operator is told the server
is unreachable rather than misconfigured. A configured `MCP-Protocol-Version` is
the sharpest case: the probe deliberately sends none, because the version is
what `initialize` negotiates, so a configured one arrives at a spec-strict
server as the exact thing that server refuses.

The screen is by case-insensitive name, since header names are
case-insensitive on the wire while an object's keys are not, and it reads the
list the client owns rather than a copy of it. Copying is how these two
diverged over SSE framing, and a divergence here would mean a configured header
breaks one of them and not the other, which is harder to diagnose than either.

ci: run the generated client's tests (D81)

clients/python/tests held four suites that nothing executed: no run-tests entry,
no job in the unit-test workflow, and no path filter that would have started
one. They passed locally and ran nowhere else, so a change that broke the
generated client was caught by nobody.

A job runs them now, with no has_tests guard: pytest exits non-zero when it
collects nothing, and a suite that disappears must fail rather than quietly
pass. Three cases guard it from the API suite rather than the client's own,
because a guard that runs only inside the job it guards disappears with it.

test(gateways): drive D33's guard from the relay itself (D82)

The three cases for the reconnect-in-flight guard called _invalidate_endpoint
directly. That proves the comparison, not that the relay reaches it with the
token this call presented rather than with whatever the connection holds by the
time the answer arrives.

The new case is the whole path: a call goes out with a credential the provider
has quietly retired, the person reconnects from inside the transport while the
request is still out, and the 401 it earns comes back to a connection that now
holds a different credential. The connection stays valid, reports ready, and
relays. Passing None for the presented token fails it.

fix(gateways): stop charging the resolver queue to the resolution (D83)

One bound covered both waits, so with every resolver thread busy a request whose
address resolves in a millisecond was refused with "the address could not be
resolved in time". That is a sentence about the address, the address was fine,
and the operator's actual problem went unnamed.

Two bounds now. The first is how long a resolution may wait for a thread;
running out of it frees the queue slot and refuses as a busy gateway, with the
queue wait and the pool size on the log line. The second is how long the
resolution itself may take, counted from when it starts, so a slow resolver is
judged on its own time rather than on somebody else's. The refusal carries which
happened, and the probe reports the two under different names, so nothing reads
a saturated gateway as an absent network.

Three cases, all three failing against a single combined bound.

fix(gateways): return consent to every app origin the deployment declares (D71)

The callback page posts the consent result to the window that opened it, and a
post is discarded unless it names that window's exact origin. It named one
configured address, so on a deployment answering at more than one, everybody
using any other address had the result delivered nowhere: the dialog waited out
its three-minute timeout while the connection sat authorized behind it.

AGENTA_APP_ORIGINS declares the rest. The page names each in turn, so this
widens which of the deployment's own windows can be reached without widening who
can read the message. The published address still leads, because the tab-return
fallback sends one person to one place.

Declared rather than read off the request: the address a browser used to reach
this page comes from the Host header, which the caller sets. The API's own
origin is not offered either, so a deployment that publishes no app address
still sends nobody anywhere.

Six cases, three failing against the single-origin page.

fix(sdk): D88 resolve an unnamed tool the way the runner gate does

The Claude settings matrices crossed every server decision with every per-tool
decision and then asked about `echo`, which is the tool the per-tool table
names. For a named tool the table answers first, so the other half of the ladder
was never reached: a tool the table does NOT name, which is what
`new_tool_permission` exists to decide and what an MCP server adds between two
runs.

Adding that case found a real disagreement rather than a gap in coverage. The
adapter resolved an unnamed tool as `new_tool_permission or permission or
"ask"`, while the runner's `normalizeMcpServerPermissions` gives a declared
table with no floor beside it `ask` and deliberately never consults the
whole-server permission — "a human decides for anything the table does not
name". So `permission: allow` beside any per-tool table emitted a whole-server
ALLOW, and a tool the author had never named ran unapproved under Claude while
the same saved configuration raised a gate under Pi. The divergence ran in the
unsafe direction, which is why this is resolved toward the runner rather than
the other way.

Two existing cases asserted the old reading and are updated with the reason.
One parametrized case moved out of the "looser than the default" list because
under the corrected ladder it is no longer looser than it.

This is a behaviour change to a saved policy's meaning, not only a test: an
agent configured `permission: allow` with any per-tool table will now ask before
a tool that table does not name. If the other reading is wanted instead — that
`permission` IS the floor for unnamed tools — then the runner's ladder is what
has to move, and both have to move together.

CR12 made closing the tool catalog read the connections list back instead of settling on
the surface having been open. The read asked the wrong question twice: it narrowed by
`integration_key` with a name that is only sometimes an integration key, and it accepted
any live connection in the answer without checking which one it was. A person who
