docs(channels): rename the two ledgers; design connection identity from platform docs

findings.md becomes review-findings.md and open-design.md becomes
design-findings.md, so the two ledgers are named for what they hold.

Connection identity checked against each platform's own documentation rather
than reasoned by analogy, and three results changed the design. Telegram puts no
bot identifier on the payload at all -- the bot is identified by the transport,
so the mechanism is the secret token echoed as a header, and resolution must
read the whole request rather than only the body. Slack sends the workspace as a
flat field on events and a nested one on interactivity, so an extractor reading
one shape returns nothing for a button click. Discord omits the server entirely
in direct messages.

So the bot is the key and the tenant is a qualifier: the bot half is always
present while the tenant half is variously absent, plural, or missing. Each
adapter composes its own key.

docs(channels): own the connections table rather than share the gateway's

Channels gets channel_connections with an external_key, so a connection reads
like every other external identity in the domain -- a locator plus a key
composed over the fields the adapter declares -- and so channels is not coupled
to a table whose future belongs to someone else.

Nothing is released, so the migration is edited in place rather than layered.
Only four channels files touch the shared connection today.

It also unblocks two things the shared table could not give: a globally unique
key, which ingress needs because it resolves the tenant from it and which would
be wrong for a gateway where two projects legitimately reach the same product,
and a credential schema that does not impose itself on other rows.

Corrects the grain to connection rather than bot. Grains name the row they key,
and bot is the product word. The bridge disproves the bot framing outright: many
bridges, many connections, one provider, each fronting a platform we never see.

cannot be part of the identity. The bridge disproves the other half.

and one function composes it, as the space and thread grains already do.

The grain-named locators on the inbound event are dropped by the ingress

The entities decision to reuse the shared table rested on channels

docs(channels): design Agenta as a first-party channel

The channel that needs no credentials, so the whole path can be driven
before any platform is involved. A real channel in the registry, not a
harness: if anything after the inbox row branched on it, the port would
be wrong.

The API is permanent and the UI is throwaway, built together because an
API designed against no consumer is how the mock adapter ended up
complete and undriveable. The UI goes in web behind the per-user flag
mechanism that already carries two flags, since the thing being tested
is our own node vocabulary.

One deliberate divergence: inbound uses an authenticated project-scoped
route rather than the public ingress, because the ingress exists to
establish a tenant that a session has already established.

docs(channels): correct the Agenta ingress; record the pre-implementation gate

The Agenta channel does not need its own inbound path. Its route is an
ordinary literal route that is simply absent from the public-endpoint
list, so the normal auth middleware applies and the same _ingest runs.
Exactly one step differs, and it differs in implementation rather than
shape: verification proves the caller may speak for the connection, and
a session proves that as well as an HMAC does.

The earlier draft claimed a divergence and would have built a second
inbound path for no reason.

What both designs do need is more of the request than the body: Telegram
its headers, a per-bot URL its path, Agenta its session. One change, not
three special cases.

Also records what actually blocks returning to implementation, split
between deciding before the packages are written and finishing after.

docs(channels): write the Agenta and Slack journeys step by step

Designing either alone left both in the air, so they are written
together: every step names the screen, the call, the row and the
credential moved.

Reading the codebase rather than assuming changed the credential design.
An encrypted secret store already exists, project-scoped, encrypting in
Postgres through a column type, which is what the architecture doc meant
by the vault. Credentials become a secret row referenced by the
connection rather than a new encrypted column, under a channel-owned
kind so machine-written rows do not land in the bucket a user browses
and deletes by hand.

Reading Slack's own documentation supplied the step the research set was
missing: a link that opens app creation with the manifest pre-filled, so
customer-owned setup needs no OAuth app of ours and no public redirect.
The manifest builder for it already exists and has no caller.

The schema shrank to two fields on the rule that we ask for what only a
human can copy and discover the rest.

docs(channels): restructure journeys on two axes; correct the manifest generalisation

Config time and runtime, crossed with Agenta and Slack. The runtime rows
must be the same code reached two ways; the config rows are where the
channels genuinely differ, and the design effort is keeping the
difference contained there. Adds the half both journeys were missing:
renaming, disabling, rotating a credential, drift, revocation from the
platform side, and teardown.

The manifest claim did not survive checking the other platforms. Discord
has no manifest and configures through portal toggles no document can
carry; Telegram has no app object at all and inverts the direction,
since setWebhook is ours to call. So setup shape is a fifth thing a
channel declares, not a rule taken from Slack.

What does hold across all four is that we never own or create the
customer's app, which also decides what a removal page must say.

The secret kind is nested, matching the provider kinds already in the
store, and that nesting is the credential schema rather than a second
mechanism beside it.

docs(channels): grants by kind with allow and deny; a conversation is a thread

Permission was encoded as 'somebody pre-created a space row', which only
topics can be. A private space is one per user and exists because
someone talked; a group is an ad-hoc set of people. So every DM is
silently refused today, against a declaration that says private spaces
are supported.

Space rows keep their real job -- they own the message log, the backfill
guard and a policy level -- and get created on first contact like
threads. Permission moves to the grant, which can now name a kind rather
than an id, with allow and deny rows evaluated deny-first.

A narrow deny beating a broad allow is not an override: it is the
existing rule that a stated false wins. What that rule forbids is the
opposite direction, and this does not do it.

Also corrects an invention from earlier in the same design: a
conversation is a thread, not a space. Threads are per agent, spaces are
per place, and Agenta is shaped like a DM -- a private space per user
with a thread per agent inside it.

gateway's own use of it) and redirects to Slack's authorize URL; refuses

adapter whether an inbound payload signals a stopped installation
(Slack's app_uninstalled/tokens_revoked) and deactivates the connection
without touching its grants, spaces or threads; removing a connection
from our side now asks the adapter to revoke the installation and
supply its own removal notice, defaulting to the existing customer-owned
wording when an adapter declines to override it.

fix(channels): root a top-level Slack message's thread under its own ts

Slack puts thread_ts only on messages inside a thread; a top-level message
has none. The THREAD key composition declares thread_ts required, so every
plain channel message raised ChannelLocatorIncomplete in the dispatch worker.
Slack showed nothing, with no error anywhere the operator can see.

parse_event now falls back to the message's own ts, which is Slack's own
threading model: a top-level message roots the thread its replies live in
(a reply's thread_ts IS the parent's ts). This also makes the agent's answer
land as a thread reply under the mention it answers.

The one existing test that pinned the old shape asserted a locator the rest
of the system could not consume; it now pins the new semantics: a parent and
the replies threaded under it resolve to one unit.

(cherry picked from commit f26abb5e61689ea660f79c7bf4b7d1aff3206e30)

fix(channels): target the thread's locator on a turn's first post

The delivery worker's first post for an item has no receipt yet, and that
branch passed an empty locator to the adapter. The Slack adapter needs
locator['channel'], so it raised KeyError and the first answer on any thread
was silently never delivered — the playground showed the answer, Slack showed
'Working…' forever.

The thread row already holds the full target (team, channel, thread_ts);
_send now takes the thread and uses its locator for the no-receipt post.
Same defect class as the bridge's F63: a read with no writer, surviving
because fixtures seeded the receipt directly.

(cherry picked from commit 60a54b13e247f66f2246a150927624cc7760385a)

fix(channels): close the bot-echo cascade and the empty-answer delivery path

Three defects found and hotfixed during a full day of live QA on Slack, then
run for the rest of the day against the live deployment.

The bot's own indicator edit came back as a `message_changed` event whose
author sits in the nested message, so the authorship check read it as human
input: the adapter rooted a phantom thread off the edit's synthetic ts, ran a
paid turn, posted, edited that post, and went round again. Edit and delete
subtypes now drop at parse, and authorship is read one level down too.

A turn-ended event can outrun the final record commit, so the fold read an
empty answer and rendered an empty Slack section, which Slack rejects
wholesale -- the indicator then sat on "Working..." forever. The read is now
retried twice before rendering; an empty section block is never emitted; a
still-empty fold leaves the indicator alone and logs loudly rather than
delivering a blank bubble; and a blocks rejection falls back to text-only with
the rejected payload logged.

(cherry picked from commit 0b62e154f18dd4ae644f435be42aaf30dd023872)

  published from the record INGRESS, before the record committed, so the

[fix] Channels: live-QA fixes for Slack, Telegram, and phone UI

Batch of fixes found and verified during live QA of the Channels feature
(PR #6644), on an isolated Slack/Telegram stack.

- Slack: recognize a native <@bot> mention in ordinary message events and
  drop the redundant app_mention copy, so a real @mention opens a turn
  without double-running installs subscribed to both. (+ 4 regression tests)
- Telegram: clear resolved approval-card buttons only after answer admission,
  with interaction/thread/token guards.
- Telegram setup: in-flight guard so opening setup cannot issue two link
  requests / report a spurious existing connection.
- Channels: post a fixed "run could not be started" notice when an invoke
  fails before any turn-start event, idempotent on the turn's outbox key so a
  redelivery posts nothing and a started turn's row is left to the outbox.
  (+ 4 regression tests)
- Approval cards: redact secret fields, humanize the title, show arguments
  and one-call scope instead of the internal tool name.
- Phone agent overview: Channels controls visible at 390px.
- "Chat bound elsewhere" now shows a clear message instead of a misleading
  invalid-link error.

ci(api): declare the absent database for the acceptance layer on Railway

The Railway job has no route to the preview's Postgres. The acceptance
cases that read the database directly (channels bridge/differential and
the mounts/sessions attachment cases) went through require_core_uri and
errored at setup. Declaring AGENTA_TEST_NO_DATABASE for the acceptance
layer too makes them skip with the declared reason and counts them in the
job summary; local runs without the declaration still run them, and a
misconfigured local run still fails loudly.

test(channels): address the bot in the two-bridges resolve case, and say what the live channel conversation held

case never ran in CI because the database guard errored first.

The live Agenta-channel case now prints the conversation it polled when
no answer arrives, so a timeout says whether nothing, a working indicator
or an error was posted.

fix(channels): never fail an archive after the row is archived

Archiving a hosted Slack connection wrote deleted_at and then 500'd: the
teardown notice called auth.revoke with the stored row, whose bot token
lives behind a vault reference, and ChannelConnectionIncomplete escaped
the best-effort revoke. The client saw a failed disconnect for a
connection that was already gone, and every retry 500'd again.

Hydrate the credentials before revoking, treat a missing token or a
transport error as a skipped revoke, and never let the notice raise.

fix(channels): show a failed disconnect next to its button and re-read after it

The disconnect error rendered at the top of the manage panel. In the /m
bottom sheet the user is at the Disconnect button at the bottom, so the
error was off screen and the click looked like it did nothing. A failed
call also skipped the reload, so the row kept claiming a connection the
backend had already archived.

Show the disconnect error inside the disconnect block, always re-read the
connections after a disconnect, and close the panel when the connection
is gone even if the call reported an error.

The setup route takes optional name, description and handle query
params. The Slack adapter puts them in display_information and
features.bot_user.display_name, fitted to Slack's limits (35/140/80),
the handle keeping only the characters Slack allows and derived from

feat(channels): let the user name, describe and pick the handle of a new Slack app

fix(frontend): wait for the agent to be ready before the first queued send

The durable send built its request once, so the first message to a newly

fix(channels): queue a follow-up sent while the thread's turn is running

A message sent in a channel thread while that thread's agent turn was still
running reached the runner as a second start. The runner refused it
(session_turn_in_use), and since the strict-start change the refusal read as a
failed start: the chat got "The agent run could not be started" and the message
was lost. Before that change it was dropped silently.

The inbox dispatcher now admits the message to the thread session's
pending-input queue first, through the same SessionInputsService.admit the
playground uses. A busy session holds it as a pending input that the sessions
queue promotes and runs as the next turn when the current one settles; a free
session runs it now as before. The admission is keyed by the trigger id, so a
redelivered task never queues the message twice. A refusal that still arrives
(another turn won the race) re-admits and queues. Without a queue, a lasting
refusal gets one deduplicated "still working" reply instead of silence.

unchanged.

message, after any bot mention or agent sigil; Telegram's /new@bot form is

backlog at the current conversation's start. A channel thread now does the
same once an earlier conversation exists under its key. A first mention in a
thread still sees the discussion that led to it.

fix(runner): fail an ACP request when its connection closes instead of hanging

@agentclientprotocol/sdk 0.16.1 settles a pending request only when a response
arrives. When the transport gives up for good (every POST answered 502 because
the harness process cannot start, or the stream dies mid-turn), the SDK's reader
loop throws into an unhandled rejection and the request waits forever. The turn
awaiting it heartbeats running=true with no deadline.

Patch the SDK the way its later majors behave: when the connection closes,
reject every pending request with the transport's error, and reject a request
sent after close at once. The caller now sees the daemon's error, so a failed
session/load falls back to session/new and a failed session/new fails the turn.

fix(channels): claim an outbox reply atomically so two workers never post it twice

Two consumers of worker-sessions-channels-outbox (deploy overlap, scale-out,
or a reclaimed pending entry) can each hold a copy of the same turn event.
_send read the row, saw it not yet sent, and posted, so both posted.

Delivery now takes a claim first: one conditional UPDATE that succeeds only
when the row is not already SENT with this content and no live claim
(status code 'sending', stamped by the database clock) exists. A claim older
than 60s is taken over, so a worker that died mid-post does not lose the
reply. The loser polls briefly, skips when the row went out with its
content, and otherwise raises so the stream entry is redelivered. A turn's
answer is marked final, and progress edits never overwrite it.

The outbox consumer now runs the reclaim pass (30s idle, 5 deliveries,
then dropped), so a transient platform error is retried instead of lost,
and a thread whose space or connection is gone is acknowledged.

fix(channels): answer in threads and groups only when addressed

In a Slack channel thread, a Slack group DM or a Telegram group, one
mention used to make every later message in the thread a turn: an active
channel_threads row admitted everything until !new. The trigger gate now
admits a shared-space message only when it mentions the bot, is a
command, or resolves the choice the agent has pending in that thread
(resolve passes resolved_token into the gate). A 1:1 DM still answers
every message, and a mention in a specialist's thread still goes to it.

Unaddressed messages are still stored and reach the agent as context on
the next mention.

fix(channels): carry context since the last turn, and never drop a mention

Context rules on top of the mention-only gate:

- The range is (latest counted trigger on an earlier event, this event]:
  a message that lands mid-compose goes to the next turn.
- A trigger counts unless it provably never ran: REFUSED, or FAILED with
  status code never_sent (WorkflowDetachedStartNeverSent). An uncertain
  failure moves the offset, so input that may have run is never replayed.
- An approval answer is marked consumed before its decision is sent;
  consumed events and button clicks never become conversation.
- Every addressed message gets its own turn; the unique (thread, event)
  trigger is the only dedupe. The sender's identity lookup runs before the
  trigger is claimed, so a failed lookup no longer drops the mention.
- Dispatch is not serialised: when messages in one thread arrive within
  about a second and run out of order, context can repeat or be missing,
  but no mention is dropped and none runs twice in the same thread. A !new
  between a task retry and its first attempt can run it again (#7131).

fix(runner): stop reporting context-window size as a run's token usage

When the harness's PromptResponse carried no usage, the runner fell back to the ACP
stream's `usage_update.used` value and reported it as the run's token total. That
value is not a token count of the run. It is how full the agent's context window is
at that point in the turn. Measured on one stack: 6,041 root spans shaped
`input 0 / output 0 / total 63369`, with no cost.

A wrong number here is worse than no number, because a reader cannot tell a real
63,369-token run from a context-size artifact, and any token aggregate built on that
path is silently poisoned.

Fixing the usage merge alone would not have removed those rows. The tracer keeps its
own usage record built straight from the stream, and handing it nothing is a no-op
rather than a clear, so it kept stamping the context size on the root span anyway.
So the stream handler now drops `used` and keeps only the reported cost, and an
update carrying neither is not recorded at all.

The stamping function now also skips a usage record with no tokens and no cost. All
zeros is the absence of a measurement, not a measured zero, and asserting that a run
spent nothing is its own wrong answer.

Nothing consumes the context size. The only readers of the merged usage object are
the span attributes and the Python SDK's `record_usage`, and both treat every number
in it as a token count.

Tests: the full runner suite passes, 1,486 tests across 97 files, plus nine new cases
covering a context-size-only stream, a cost-only stream, a half-reported split, and a
normal split delivered through the harness.

fix(runner): let one span own each token observation

The runner published the same token count twice inside one OTLP batch: on the
per-call `chat` leaf spans, and again as the run total on their `invoke_agent`
ancestor. `gen_ai.usage.*_tokens` is the incremental bucket by contract, so ingest
read both as separate observations.

Nothing showed it, because the roll-up never ran on the runner's batch at all. The
span tree was seeded only from spans with no parent, and the runner's batch has none.
Once the roll-up runs, it adds the parent's own incremental value on top of the
children it just summed, and the agent span reports exactly twice the real count.

Measured live before this change, on a four-turn Pi run:

  invoke_agent   incremental 7776   cumulative 15552
    turn 0 -> chat  1850
    turn 1 -> chat  1926
    turn 2 -> chat  1983
    turn 3 -> chat  2017

The four leaves sum to 7776, and the parent reported 15552.

The producer owns this, not the roll-up. Adding a span's own incremental value to its
children's cumulative is the correct general definition, and making the API skip a
span by name would trade one bug for a wrong rule that breaks any producer whose
parent span legitimately makes its own model call.

So the token attributes come off `invoke_agent` in both tracers. `gen_ai.usage.cost`
stays, because ingest maps it to the cumulative bucket, which makes it the explicit
summary a parent should carry rather than a repeated incremental one.

Both harnesses had the same shape. Pi gave each turn's `chat` span that turn's usage
and the agent span their sum, so the error scaled with turn count. Claude ACP creates
one `chat` leaf per prompt in `start()` and stamped the same run total on both it and
the agent span. Moving ownership to the leaf loses nothing in either case. Turn spans
were already clean; they never carried usage.

Live after this change: a one-turn run reports 1739 against a leaf sum of 1739, a
three-turn run reports 5413 against 1777 plus 1809 plus 1827, and a four-turn run
reports 7414 against a leaf sum of 7414. Cost survives on every run.

Tests: the full runner suite passes, 1,490 tests across 98 files, and `tsc --noEmit`
is clean. Four new tests assert, for both tracers, that no span with children carries
token attributes and that the leaf sum equals the run total.

feat(runner): declare that our input token count excludes cached tokens

The API prices a model call by handing token counts to litellm, which expects an
inclusive prompt count and derives ordinary input by subtracting the cache details
from it.

This runner emits the opposite. `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` holds uncached tokens
only, with cache read and cache creation counts beside it. The pinned Pi
implementation confirms it; it reconstructs a prompt count as input plus cache read
plus cache write.

The OpenTelemetry GenAI contract says `input_tokens` already includes cached tokens.
Agenta ingests OTLP from third-party instrumentation as well as from this runner, and
ingest maps both into the same bucket, so the API cannot tell the two contracts apart.
Whichever it assumes is wrong for the other, and the wrong assumption misprices by
about tenfold in either direction.

So say which one this is. Every span that carries an input token count now also
carries `agenta.usage.input_tokens_includes_cache = false`. One shared constant, and
both tracer paths stamp it at the same place they stamp the token counts.

The tests assert the two as a biconditional: a span carries the marker exactly when it
carries an input token count. A future stamping site that forgets the marker fails the
suite rather than shipping an unpriceable span.

The API side of this contract maps the attribute and treats an absent marker as
inclusive, per the OpenTelemetry meaning, so an older runner reaching a newer API
produces the pre-existing undercount rather than a new overcharge.

Tests: the full runner suite passes, 1,495 tests across 99 files, and `tsc --noEmit`
is clean. Five new tests cover both tracers, a parent that carries no input tokens and
so needs no marker, a cost-only run, and a turn with no cache counts.

refactor(api): recompute trace totals in the ingest worker, per touched trace

Replace the Redis totals queue (batch-id sets, delay window, claims,
leases, recovery, in-memory retries) with a direct recompute: after the
tracing worker stores a batch, it recomputes the totals of every trace
the batch touched. The DAO's advisory lock serializes recomputes of one
trace, and each runs after its own batch committed, so the last one
sees every stored span. The HTTP path is unchanged.

This also removes the lost-work case where a worker restarted after
acking a batch whose scheduling had failed.

The recompute now reads ag.flags too, so a workflow span marked
aggregate_usage keeps its run total instead of adding its children.

fix(api): remove a cleared cumulative value instead of writing zero

The dashboard counts any stored errors.cumulative as a failed trace, so a
recompute that clears a trace's errors must drop the value, not write 0.

fix(api): retry a failed trace totals recompute before acknowledging the batch

A transient database error during recompute left the trace with partial
totals, and nothing retried after the batch was acknowledged. Retry only the
recompute, three times with a short backoff; ingestion and metering stay
outside the retry. After the last attempt the batch is still acknowledged.
docs(api): note the trace totals retry and removed cleared values

fix(api): count a handler's copied usage once over its traced calls

A workflow or task span whose own usage equals its children's total repeats
the calls traced below it: llm_v0 returns its litellm call's usage, and a
custom SDK app returns {message, cost, usage} while the litellm callback traces
the same call. Summing them doubled the root's tokens and cost. Such a span now
counts once. Model call spans still add their own call to their children's.
test(api): carry cache token counts through the trace totals recompute

A Claude turn priced from tokens (reloaded session, no harness cost) billed

Claude Code writes 1-hour entries. The runner now says so with

fix(runner): report the usage of work done around an approval pause once

A turn that pauses for an approval leaves its prompt running. Three paths lost
the usage of that prompt:

- Decision then fresh text (settleApprovalsThenPrompt): the turn let the parked
  prompt finish, then sent a second prompt and kept only the second
  PromptResponse. The first one, which holds the work before the pause and after
  the decision, was dropped for Claude and Codex. The turn now sums both
  responses (usage field by field, _meta.quota.model_usage per model).
- The same path on Pi: the trace port tore down the parked prompt's telemetry
  channel at turn start, before that prompt settled, so its native trace batch
  and usage sidecar were lost. The port now keeps the channel until the parked
  prompt ends, drains it and reads its sidecar (beginNextPrompt), then opens the
  channel for the second prompt.
- A cold pause on Pi destroys the session, and Pi publishes the pre-pause trace
  and usage as it stops. The paused turn read the sidecar without waiting for
  that write. It now drains the trace first, as a finished turn does.

A pure warm resume already reported the whole prompt once, on the resume.

fix(runner): report the pre-pause usage of a cold-paused Claude or Codex turn

A cold pause calls destroySession, which sends session/cancel. Claude
(claude-agent-acp) and Codex (codex-acp) answer the open prompt with
stopReason "cancelled" and the usage of the work before the pause. The
runner raced past that prompt at the pause and never read the answer, so
the paused turn reported no tokens, and the resume counts only its own
new prompt. The usage of the model calls before the pause was lost.

The paused turn now waits a short, bounded time (2 s by default,
AGENTA_RUNNER_COLD_PAUSE_USAGE_SETTLE_MS) for that answer and reports its
usage on the turn's spans. While it waits, only usage_update frames reach
the run; other frames are teardown artifacts (Codex writes
"*Conversation interrupted*"). Pi keeps its sidecar path. Warm parks are
unchanged: the parked prompt still reports on the resume.

fix(runner): keep a late Claude cost reading from overwriting the turn's usage

Claude Code's usage_update (the session's running cost total) arrives on the SSE stream, the prompt response on the POST body. When the reading landed after the turn set its usage, the tracer replaced the turn's usage with the running total, so the run reported the whole session's cost, and the next turn measured its share from a stale baseline.

A reading that lands after the turn's usage is set, or between turns, now leaves that turn's usage alone and only moves the session's baseline.

fix(chart): keep the autoscaler from evicting the single-replica stateful pods (#7211)

redisVolatile, redisDurable and supertokens each run one replica and hold
state, so losing the pod takes the component down. On GKE Autopilot the cluster
autoscaler consolidated a node in live traffic, deleted the redis-volatile and
supertokens pods, and every agent turn was refused for about 15 s until the
replacement pod was ready: the api could not reach Redis, the admission beat
returned 500, and the runner refused each turn.

Each of the three pod templates now carries
cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false", so the autoscaler
skips their node. The annotation does not block an operator drain or a node
upgrade, and it is inert where no autoscaler runs. Two escape hatches: set
<component>.safeToEvict: true to opt out, or override the key through
<component>.podAnnotations, which is merged over the default.

Stateless workloads are deliberately untouched; blocking scale-down there would
hold nodes for no reason.

[7200] fix(gate): accept a Kubernetes pod name in the bash journey token (#7210)

* fix(gate): accept a Kubernetes pod name in the bash journey token

The tool journey asserts on a token the model cannot compute:
`QA-BASH-$(hostname)-$(uname -m)`. The pattern required the hostname to be
hex, which holds for a Docker container id but not for a Kubernetes pod name
(`agenta-runner-7bccbff75-g9lmw`). On every Kubernetes stage the journey
reported FAIL although the tool had run and its output reached the reply.

Accept any hostname and keep a minimum length, which is the part that stops a
model from passing with a short value it invented instead of running the tool.

Closes #7200

* fix(gate): match the reply token to the shell output, not just its shape

CodeRabbit's point on #7210: the journey passed when a tool-output frame
existed AND the reply contained any token of the right shape, which does not
tie the two together. Widening the pattern to accept a Kubernetes pod name
widened that gap, because a fabricated non-hex hostname now fits the shape.

bash_token_from_output() reads the token off the tool's own output frame, and
both passing journeys now require the REPLY to carry that exact string. A model
that writes a plausible token without running anything no longer passes, and
neither does one that ran the tool and then reported a different value.

The deny journey still asserts ABSENCE against the reply, which is correct: a
denied call produces no output to match, and the property under test is that
the model did not invent a token to cover the refusal.

* fix(gate): require the reply's token to stand alone, not merely appear

CodeRabbit's second point: 'shell_token in t.reply' also accepts the token with
more hostname or architecture characters glued to it, so a mangled value could
pass both journeys.

reply_carries_token() adds boundaries. It leaves punctuation out of the boundary
classes on purpose: a reply that ends the sentence with a full stop, or wraps
the token in backticks or quotes, is still reporting the right value, and
rejecting it would turn a correct run red.

* fix(gate): scope the token to the bash call, and reject a dotted suffix

Two more review points, both right.

The hostname pattern allows dots, so 'token.extra' still satisfied the boundary
check. A dot is now rejected only when another hostname label follows it, which
keeps a reply that ends the sentence with 'token.' passing.

bash_token_from_output scanned every tool payload and returned the first shaped
token, so a token another tool printed could stand in for a bash call that
produced none. It now takes the bash call's toolCallId and reads only that
call's available output. Both journeys resolve the call through
_bash_call_outcome; _allow_rule_flow already had it and was discarding it.

* fix(gate): extract the whole token from the output, keep the reply scan unanchored

Third review point. The architecture part of the pattern ends in \w, which
stops at a dot, so an arch like x86_64.v2 would be extracted truncated and the
reply would only have to carry the shorter string.

BASH_TOKEN_FULL_RE runs the match on to the end of the token and is used only
where the token is read from the tool's own output. The suggested fix anchored
BASH_TOKEN_RE itself to a whole line, which cannot be done: the same pattern
scans REPLY prose for the deny journey, where a fabricated token has to be found
wherever the model put it, and anchoring would have made that journey pass when
it should fail.

fix(api): stop a NUL in a record body from looping the records stream

A record body holding a NUL (U+0000) cannot be stored: Postgres rejects it
from both `text` and `jsonb` with `UntranslatableCharacterError` (SQLSTATE
22P05). The record is already off the runner by the time the INSERT runs, so
the batch could only be redelivered — and it was, every 30s for over a day,
from one `tool_result` carrying console output.

It never isolated because the rejection was not recognised as permanent.
SQLAlchemy's asyncpg dialect wraps the driver error in its own generic
`AsyncAdapt_asyncpg_dbapi.Error`, which it then cannot map to a typed
subclass, so it arrives as a bare `DBAPIError` and not `DataError`.
`_append_committed` therefore returned before its one-record isolation pass,
leaving the good records in the batch uncommitted too.

Fix both ends:

* strip NULs at the producer boundary that already bounds body size, so the
  record is stored intact rather than quarantined. Record bodies carry
  arbitrary tool output, so a NUL is reachable from ordinary use — a `grep`
  over a binary file is enough.
* classify the rejection by unwrapping to the driver exception and reading
  Postgres's SQLSTATE class 22 ("data exception"), which is always a property
  of the row. Testing `DBAPIError` itself would be wrong: `OperationalError`
  and `InterfaceError` are subclasses too, and treating an outage as permanent
  is the silent record loss this worker exists to prevent.

fix(runner): time-box record ingest and keep the incomplete-records marker working

Two small, independent robustness fixes in the session record persistence path, from investigating the 2026-09-28 EU runner OOM incident (production-session-investigation).

1. Bound each ingest POST with a per-request timeout (AbortSignal.timeout, env AGENTA_RECORDS_INGEST_TIMEOUT_MS, default 30s). Without it a single stalled request holds the per-session persist chain, and behind it the turn-end drain, open for as long as the socket stays open. A timeout now throws and is retried like any other transient error.

2. Stop flush() from consuming the per-session drop count. The turn-end finally in server.ts is the authoritative reader that marks a session incomplete when a record was dropped; flush() consumed and cleared the count first, so that reader always saw zero and the session was never marked. flush() now drains only and leaves the single read to the caller.

Unit tests updated: the flush test now asserts the count survives for the caller. Typecheck clean; runner unit suite green apart from 4 pre-existing gateway-gating failures unrelated to this change.

NOTE: the larger runaway-output memory bound (the actual OOM cause: unbounded events[] and streamed-text accumulators in tracing/otel.ts) is a separate follow-up, to be placed at the otel choke point and terminalized through the existing run-limits RUN_LIMIT_TRIPPED path, pending a recorded full-stack QA pass.
